AMBROGIO MARIA FIOCCHI, S.J.

Mother Rosa GATTORNO in 1878

Foundress (1831-1900) Second edition Revised, developed and up-dated by Sr. A. ERNESTINA DEGETTO © printed 2001 By the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne Via Merulana, 177 - 00185 Rome, Italy Translated by Louis and Kate Marcelin-Rice

IMPRIMATUR

There are some many-faceted lives whose dimensions do not easily fit into the framework of a conventional biography because, with their originality and range of potential, they transcend every conventional model. This is wonderfully clear when the subject’s crucial choices obey the superior impulse of God who chose him or her as an instrument for his plans, as in the case of Rosa Gattorno.

The rich personality of the foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne is a fabric woven of many strands, each of which would be enough to qualify a life.

The human strand in Mother Rosa sets before us a woman from the Genoese middle class, adventurous and full of initiative, who grew up with a stable Christian background, but on the other hand was open to the social concerns and ideological conflicts of the time. From her father, an able business man, she inherited the practical sense and administrative capacity which she surprisingly managed to reconcile with her mystical inclinations; from her mother, a profoundly devout woman, Rosa obtained the right combination of faith and piety, free of superstition, and an exquisite feminine sensitivity which gave her insight into human situations and enabled her to feel close to the suffering. Nevertheless, this particular gift was often expressed in a form of apprehension, a weakness which she called “my terrible character”, and strove with the gift of fortitude to overcome.

Rosa Gattorno is the image of the biblical type of “strong woman” (Pr 31:10): determined, courageous and efficient. In his testimony, Fr. Domenico Serafini, the Apostolic Visitor, described her as: “a devout woman, with an extraordinary mind and untold energy”. So she proved at the critical moments of her life, first as a wife, then as a mother, a widow and a foundress. Strong and even bold in the face of obstacles, she was also endowed with serenity and balance. Combined with her cordial manner, these gave her a noble and imposing air, “like a queen of extraordinary austerity and at the same time of great sweetness”, as the Princess di Fitalia said.

In addition, sincerity and quickness shone out in her acts and in her words, and she deeply inculcated these qualities in her sisters: “Truth in the heart and on the lips!”. What she could not tolerate in others, especially in representatives of the Church, was two-sidedness or falsity.

Mother Rosa also had a cheerful and communicative nature, not exempt from a fine exuberance. In spite of this, in her Memorie she often complained to the Lord of her loneliness which became an almost cruel isolation. She repeated hundreds of times: “Alone, a hermit in the middle of the wide world. Alone, in the midst of such a large Work!…. Alone, without anyone to whom I can say a word!…”. She frequently attempted to put herself under the guidance of a servant of God, but failed. In directing the Institute, everything gravitated around her; her immediate collaborators became mere secretaries, even when, in obedience to the provisions of the Holy See, she was flanked by official assistants. This was not an absorbing personalism as some have interpreted it, but an observation of fact: Rosa Gattorno was different; it must not have been easy to tune in with her spirit. She moved in an orbit of ideals and aspirations which only persons with the same experience could enter. In her Memorie, after the umpteenth failure of her intention to have a spiritual director, she wrote: “Alone! Everything is darkness and sorrow…. I thought I was understood by my director, but it is quite the opposite! I clearly see my state of mind, but when I explain it, I see that they mistake one thing for another…. Oh! Only those souls who have loved deeply will be able to understand me, and then they will find themselves below, in the most wretched abyss” (M. 9.4, pp. 7, 38).

So there was no question of selfish withdrawal or the reticence that is dictated by self-sufficiency. Rosa Gattorno’s case, which is not unique in the history of spirituality, exceeded the common parameters, not only of psychoanalysis but also of biographical tradition. It depended partly on the gifts of her nature, mentioned above. Her standard of learning, subsequently enriched by religious formation and intensely assimilated and personified in contemplation, was certainly no higher than that of other women of her social rank; but she possessed a remarkable self confidence in communicating her ideas and feelings in words and writing, adapting her style and tone to the temperament of those whom she was addressing.

To anyone who attentively examines the whole of Mother Rosa’s opus, it seems impossible that the hand which by day wrote letters in a lively, incisive language, could be the same one which by night confided her intimate experiences to her notebook in a secret dialogue with her Supreme Good and bequeathed them to us in that marvellous sequence of allegorical images contained in her book, Travagli e conforti, the events of God’s Work. Furthermore, she wrote everything as it were in the margins of her full-time dedication to the Institute, in permanent communication with the superiors, closely following the foundation and functioning of every house and the situation of every religious, constantly traveling throughout Italy and also to France.

There was still room in her heart for concern for her sacred family duties: for her parents, while they were alive, for her brothers and sisters, and, above all, for her own children: deaf and dumb Carlotta and her family, and Alessandro who died and whom she personally nursed in his last illness. She interpreted the answer she received from Pius IX who told her to leave the care of her children in God’s hands, as inferring disengagement from her maternal responsibilities; and she refused to accept advice to the contrary that was given to her by a prelate.

However, the most important strand of Rosa Gattorno’s life, without which it would remain incomprehensible, was the supernatural dimension: God’s part. She herself, after what she claimed was a true conversion, was convinced that she was living through God — the Being of her life — and through operating and moving under God’s action.

It is precisely this intimate layer of radical sacrifices, her yearning to suffer and to torture her own body and her mystical flights to the loftiest unitive experiences which marks her spirituality, not forgetting her atrocious spiritual suffering and her constant struggle against the devil’s temptations. In examining the very precise autobiographical data found in Mother Rosa’s Memorie and in the testimonies of the causes, a question arises: how can one explain that a human organism like hers, badly nourished, with very limited rest at night, constantly subjected to penances of every kind, tightly bound, day and night, by chains and other metal objects which prevented the normal circulation and functions of the gut… as well as long periods of prayer and exhausting work, and gruelling journeys… how can one explain that with this physical body she reached the age of 69 fully functioning? It is a mystery; and continues to be such, however tempted one might be to refer to the unsuspected resources of autosuggestion.

However, all this had a vital instrumental role in relation to Rosa Gattorno’s evangelizing and ecclesial mission which she was to describe as God’s Work. One day, after hearing contempt expressed by someone who deemed her unsuited for such a task, she heard her “voice” say: “And this is why Jesus took you to fashion you in his own way, therefore no one can say that this is the work of man, but that divine wisdom alone has co-operated” (TC., p. 324f.).

It was her charism as Foundress that conferred unity on all the aspects of her personality. It was not a calculated choice nor prompted by an impulse of her own, but the discovery of God’s plan through active love and her ecclesial sense which led her to see the divine will in the authority of the Archbishop of Genoa, and to seek its supreme confirmation from the lips of the Vicar of Christ. From that moment, she never doubted that God, the true helmsman of the ship, would steer it victoriously through storms and contradictions. Indeed, she always considered herself merely a useless instrument, trained at the school of the crucified Christ; she attributed every triumph to God, “the superfine craftsman”, while she saw her own “wickedness” as the cause of difficulties and partial failures.

The Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne did not come into being for any specific service to society; it is not defined by its activities, but by the dynamism of a love that reaches to wherever there is suffering to alleviate or a need to be remedied, without protagonism, without caring for financial advantage or social prestige. “We must always go wherever the greatest need requires it” (TC., p. 481), was the norm of the Foundress.

In addition to assistance to the sick in their homes and in hospital — which was the first and favorite form of Mother Rosa’s apostolate — we find among the works taken on by the sisters, homes for waifs and strays, rooms for nursing mothers and babies, hospices, psychiatric hospitals, clinics for the treatment of lepers, assistance in prisons, nursery schools, colleges and soup kitchens…

Those were the years in which the Holy Spirit inspired in Catholic countries hundreds of religious congregations which offered consecrated women ample room for their own fulfilment, particularly in serving the working classes which had emerged as a result of industrialization. The Holy See, facing an unprecedented event in the Church’s history, endeavored to channel and to authenticate the foundations according to pre-established models, outlined by the members of the Curia. This caused Mother Rosa distress at the time when she was applying for the approval of the Institute’s Constitutions, as it did other founders and foundresses motivated by a strong inspiration to evangelize.

In the meantime, with the numerous vocations that flowed into it every year, God’s work was strengthened and spread faster and faster, much to the alarm of the “prudent”, one of whom compared this vigorous growth to that of a pumpkin plant (TC., p. 393). Thirty-four years sufficed for the Foundress to fill the most varied milieus with Daughters of St. Anne. At her death, there were 368 houses, 318 of which were in Italy, 43 in America (Bolivia, Brazil, Peru and Chile) and 7 in Africa (Eritrea); about 3,500 religious worked in them.

In the Jesuit, Fr. Ambrogio Maria Fiocchi, Rosa Gattorno had a biographer equal to the task. He was an able writer with a broad historical vision and a remarkable critical sense, as well as an enthusiast of the figure of the Foundress. In writing his work whose first volume was published in 1937 and for whose second, in 1941, he applied himself to patient research using first all the personal writings of Rosa Gattorno, then the testimonies of the various diocesan informative causes, letters and other documents from the Historical Archives of the Daughters of St. Anne, and lastly, news items gleaned from several publications of the period.

More than half a century has now passed since Fiocchi’s biography was published. In these decades, new documentation has come to complete the facts and fill the gaps with important publications on Mother Rosa’s writings; in addition, the happy continuation of her Cause of Canonization and the diligent preparation of the Positio required for this purpose have afforded an opportunity to add new historical clarifications.

Therefore a new edition became necessary, which would correspond with the current knowledge of the life and personality of the Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne. The task was taken on by Sr. Anna Ernestina Degetto, who is particularly expert in the Mother’s writings and in the Institute’s history. With the help of the sisters employed in the above-mentioned Archives, today enlarged and properly arranged, she has made a painstaking revision of the text, rectified inexact facts and information, corrected the interpretation of certain events, while respecting the plan of the work and the author’s style: in short, this is a considerably improved edition, worthy of the human and spiritual stature of Rosa Gattorno.

In as dynamic and complex a life as that of Mother Rosa, who was in constant contact with important people and institutions, the biographer inevitably finds himself confronting complicated situations and forms of conduct whose clarification would require a prolix critical analysis, more suited to a monographic study: the biography would lose its unity and interest. Therefore it was wisely decided, both for the first edition and for this revised edition, that references which might jeopardize the good name of certain figures should be eliminated; and that others, which could not be omitted, should be mentioned tactfully, but with historical fidelity.

These include the really important role played by Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, a priest of the Congregation of the Mission, in the early years and development of the Institute: he was the Foundress’ effective adviser and collaborator, in agreement with her and by her express appointment (M. 1.1, pp. 91-92; 2[3], pp. 58-65; Positio, Summarium Documenti, pp. 750; 753-754), he wrote the Rules of the Institute — approved by the Church after a long and troubled process — and for several years did his utmost for the formation and direction of the Daughters of St Anne, so as to deserve the title of Co-Founder.

This “good religious” however, as his biographer Anselmo Lipari has also recognized (Una esemplarità di vita, 1995, p. 118), did not manage to overcome “the inner conflict” between what he thought his role ought to be and the actual role the Church acknowledged him as having.

According to the procedures for the approval of religious institutes which the Holy See already followed at that time, there was a preliminary phase of diocesan right in which a priest was assigned by the bishop as director or “ecclesiastical superior”, with delegated authority. Then when the institute subsequently became of pontifical right, by virtue of the famous “Decree of praise”, the powers of this director over the whole institute ceased and it came under the jurisdiction of the Roman Congregation for Bishops and Regulars (which preceded the Congregation for Religious).

Fr. Tornatore’s assignment as director of the Institute, delegated by the Bishop of Piacenza at the beginning of the foundation and even after the “Decree of praise”, issued on 21 April 1879, thus concerned only the diocese in which the Generalate was then situated. When it was transferred to Rome, the authority of the bishop was limited solely to the houses of the institute which existed in the diocesan territory. Thus the figure of ecclesiastical superior necessarily disappeared.

It should also be noted in confirmation of this that the documents of the Holy See concerning the Daughters of St. Anne were always and only addressed to the Foundress.

However, there is no doubt about the good faith, indeed the total rectitude and positive zeal with which the Co-Founder proceeded throughout this matter that was as painful to him as it was to Mother Rosa, and should therefore be ascribed to the unfathomable mystery of God’s love alone.

To conclude, I would like to wish this new edition of Fr. Fiocchi’s biography a favorable reception, not only by the Daughters of St. Anne and by everyone who desires to be acquainted with the great witnesses of total commitment to God’s kingdom, but also and especially, by all the members of the various branches of the religious family who, in their different living conditions and social classes, attracted by the extraordinary timeliness of the personality and life witness of Mother Rosa, are inspired by her charism and experience and live in today’s world the riches of the Gospel message she has handed down.

It will serve as a worthy frame to the glorification of this great Foundress, which we hope will occur soon.

Fr. Lázaro Iriarte, O.F.M. Cap.

This new edition of the biography of Rosa Gattorno written by Ambrogio Maria Fiocchi, S.J., is prompted by the real and urgent need for a new scientific work on the Foundress’ life, to bring the historical and critical aspects up to date.

On the basis of the existing chronological material, we have therefore chosen to develop certain topics of specific interest for the Institute by closely examining documents of notable historical importance, and to communicate the outcome of recent studies, indeed, the result of an appreciable systematic research.

In this way it is possible to understand the mass of documentation which supports the development of the narrative of the events; most of the documents are autographical manuscripts and accounts by testimonies on oath, which are very reliable as they were given by eye-witnesses.

In rewriting the work, an attempt has been made to update what was considered out of date, to broaden and to summarize, reviewing certain facts in the light of the research carried out in the past ten years with a new historical approach.

The layout was also revised to facilitate consultation: the two volumes in which the work was previously presented have been combined; every chapter is preceded by a summary of the principal topics listed in the final general index; in the context of each chapter, the subjects are also treated under sub-headings, which are used in the summaries.

Mindful of the work’s purpose, in order to update it and to facilitate its use by readers, the language and style have been generally modernized but the characteristics of the original text have been respected.

It has therefore been possible to provide a better explanation of Rosa Gattorno’s activity in the Frassinetti Associations in the period of her widowhood; of events related to the birth of the Institute; of the role of Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore. In addition, through a critical interpretation of a large quantity of documents, the long and laborious history of the Rule’s approval and the development of the Institute’s first two General Chapters have been reconstructed.

Likewise, another equally important aspect of the Foundress’ life and work has been brought into focus: an activity of charitable work and extraordinarily intense governance, imbued with a deeply mystical experience against the background of a passionate humanity.

From her tender relationship with her children to her outstanding motherly feeling for the sisters, especially those who were ill whom she described as the “jewels of the Institute”, Mother Rosa was and remains a great witness to fully human values, for she was formed by the genuine spirit of Jesus Christ and was a prophet of God’s love for the lowly, the poor and the suffering.

I feel it my duty to express warm gratitude to the Superior General, Sr. Anna Virginia Sinagra, who commissioned the book, and to her Assistant and Secretary, Sr. Anna Angela Florio, for her constant guidance and support during my work.

A very special “thank you” is due to another of my sisters, Sr. Anna Roberta Frati, the archivist, who gave me her precious, irreplaceable and sisterly help whenever I needed to consult documents in the archives.

To conclude, I feel I have offered a complete but not exhaustive work of its kind; indeed, I hope to have laid the foundations for a future history of the Institute, to which we can look forward.

Sr. Anna Ernestina Degetto

A battle of words in the Camera dei Deputati ~ In the Chamber of Deputies, during the second session of 8 June 1907 of the Italian Parliament, the Hon. Mr. Santini raised an objection against the Hon. Mr. Ciuffelli regarding the recent disorders at the Universities of Palermo, Naples and Rome. In these seats of learning there had in fact been certain lectures by socialists and anarchists against which Catholic and other pacifist student groups had protested. Santini stood as the mentor and spokesman of the latter.

This brilliant and famous Roman member of parliament who normally welcomed interruptions and interjections from the opposition, was instead particularly taken aback by the veiled murmurs followed by open invective of the Hon. Mr. Federico Gattorno, a seventy-year-old “Garibaldino” and Member of Parliament for Rimini. Santini’s easy eloquence repaid Gattorno amply, abundantly covering him with deprecation, and he even went as far as proclaiming his respect for the latter’s veneranda senectus and among other names, called him “fattore delle monache di Via Merulana” (the farmer of the Via Merulana nuns).

This led to a most lively and unseemly incident; the Honorable Mr. Gattorno, having asked to speak for personal reasons, sought briefly to defend himself from the other insults, but focusing on the last one he said: “As regards what the Hon. Mr. Santini has just said with reference to my having something to do with nuns, this is a delicate matter. It is an insinuation that I totally reject. I had a sister who was a nun but in spite of this I have fully upheld my anti-clerical and anti-Catholic principles. No reproaches can therefore be made to me for having had a sister who was a nun, who indeed was a holy woman.”1

And the incident finished in general silence.

The fact was recalled with a degree of satisfaction by the Hon. Mr. Gattorno in a letter of 25 February 1913 to the Mother General of the Daughters of St. Anne, Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega: “…thank you for the printed article you sent me about my sister, a holy woman who was deeply humanitarian, as I had the opportunity to proclaim in Parliament at a time when they wanted to reproach me for the affection I always had for her.”2

This episode, however politically insignificant it may have been, was of some spiritual and historical value. The “holy woman”, sister of the miscreant Garibaldino, was Rosa Gattorno. The parliamentary skirmish, quite by chance, juxtaposed in sharp contrast two long lives of totally opposed inspiration and spent in such different ways, although the two came from the same family. This contrast, which unfortunately is not rare in the history of humanity, is rich in moral teachings and quickens the interest we may have in what sort of family gave birth to these lives, and how one was so clear and productive and the other, so troubled.

The lives of saints in the world can in many ways be compared to ocean currents which, like huge rivers, move between liquid walls from which they are so different in content and yet are of the same substance. If we seek the origin of such currents, we delve into mystery or at least uncertainty; such are saints who move in this world as men among men, born as other people and growing up among them. At a certain point, we find them very different from all others, with characters glowing with moral beauty and beneficial fruitfulness. In the midst of the stagnant indifference of others or the lazy mediocrity of the multitude, we see them move quickly to their goals of perfection, rich in love and glory; but when this all might have begun is often a mystery. Such is the case of Rosa Gattorno.

The birth-place of the Gattornos at Sturla ~ At the beginning of the 19th century the family of her grandparents was living at Sturla, a small town which then belonged to the municipality of Quarto by the sea, but is now part of the urban fabric of greater Genoa. The little town overlooking the magnificent Riviera di Levante takes its name from a torrent that flows into the Tyrrhenian Sea at this spot. In a place near the beach and to the right of the stream, at the beginning of the 1800s there was a house belonging to the Gattornos that was demolished to build a bridge for the provincial coast road ordered by Napoleon I. However, the Gattornos had no desire to leave the region and bought another house further north, towards San Martino d’Albaro, adjoining the Church of the Annunziata in Sturla. This circumstance helps us understand the family’s religious sentiments, since the Gattornos made many pious donations to this church which later became a parish, so many that they were considered its protectors. They had a great devotion to it, although they did not cease to attend the parish church of San Martino.

Rosa’s paternal grandparents, Emanuele Gattorno and Rosa Cafferata, lived in this house until they died and as we shall see, Rosa came to spend her summers there and to be spoiled by her grandmother who doted on her.

After the death of his father Emanuele, who wished to be buried in the Church of the Annunziata,3 it was from this tranquil nest that Mr. Francesco Gattorno departed in 1827, when he wanted to found a family of his own, marrying a young Genoese widow, Adelaide Campanella. She brought to their new home a baby daughter by her first husband, Gerolamo Ravano, born a few months earlier. Francesco was honest and hardworking and his wife Adelaide, devout and charitable, so that the testimonies of those who knew them are full of praise.

The marriage was blessed in the parish of Nostra Signora della Consolazione in Genoa on 20 June 1827,4 and the couple settled in this city in San Donato Parish, coming to live in the Dealbertis house in Piazza San Bernardo on the corner of the street of the same name and on the left, facing the church. It was a well-to-do house, as can still be seen; the Gattorno couple occupied the second floor from their wedding day, and here their first child, Emanuele, was born on 21 January 1828.

The birth of Rosa in Genoa and her early childhood ~ The couple were followed by good fortune and the new family was subsequently favored by a lovely horde of children, another two boys and three girls: Rosa, whose story is told in these pages, Giustina, Federico, Elisa and Francesco,5 who always got along well together and with their step-sister Amalia, for as long as she lived under the same roof. They almost all lived to be more than 70, like their parents; so longevity was a common gift to the members of this family, in which affluence was always accompanied by a very simple life style.

Shortly before Rosa’s birth, the Gattornos moved to Piazza Santa Maria delle Vigne, to a spacious flat on the second floor of Palazzo Lamba Doria, opposite the church. Here they lived for twenty years until 1852. Rosa was born here on 14 October 1831 and she was baptized that same day in the parish of San Donato by the Parish Priest, Fr. Paolo Amedeo Giovannelli; Mr. Alessandro Costa of Consolazione Parish and Mrs. Benedetta Tassara Rezzo of San Donato were her godparents.

The new-born baby was given the name of Rosa Maria Benedetta.6

Since her mother was unable to give her the care she needed, the baby was entrusted to a wet nurse from Ovada, a Ligurian village which today is in the Province of Alessandria. This good woman, although she did not know what a great treasure she had taken in, probably perceived the abundance of special graces which God had showered upon that creature for whom he had such lofty plans. So it was that she remembered them even after many years, since she outlived Mother Rosa, and spoke of her with wonder and simplicity.

Once she had been weaned, the baby girl returned to her family home, bringing it a new smile, especially in the hours of rest which Francesco would snatch between the serious concerns of his business; so she grew up among the comforts of her home and the tenderness of her loved ones who were so well able to imbue her heart with exquisite goodness.

In this exemplary Christian family, the children were given an education that corresponded to their high estate and the courteous manners of the time; but they were supervised by their devout mother who, with her example and her words, instilled religious piety in those tender hearts; she herself was so deeply imbued with it that despite her domestic chores she found time every day to recite the office of the Blessed Virgin.

Thus as soon as they reached the age of reason, the boys were sent to state schools, but the girls, on the other hand, had to have lessons at home from teachers carefully selected by their parents.

Historical context of the Risorgimento: Federico Campanella ~ Nothing particularly remarkable happened to Rosa in her early childhood; it should nonetheless be remembered that this was a time in history in which the social and political forces, intellectual trends and currents of opinion, shortly to play the lead in the Risorgimento, were acquiring their specific features.

The figure of Federico Capanella, elder brother of Adelaide, should be placed in this context. While studying law at the University of Genoa, he met Mazzini and immediately became one of his most active followers, a convinced champion of democratic and liberal principles, the founder and organizer of political associations, as well as a dogged Republican propagandist. Interested in publishing Mazzini’s works and faithful to his new method in the slogan “thought and action”, that is, an appeal to the ideal principles and a constant effort to spread them and with a lasting commitment to popular education, Federico Campanella founded schools for the common people’s instruction and gave many lectures on Mazzini’s writings.7 He likewise worked to extend the electoral law to women in particular, asserting: “…the exclusion of women from voting and their civil and political enslavement are the offspring spawned by that bestial violence exercised ab antiquo by the powerful over the weak, which are still prolonging the childhood of humanity in adult peoples today”.8

Mazzini himself wrote of him: “Federico Campanella is one of the purest, most honest, tenacious and proven patriots with whom I am acquainted”.

He also wrote of him: “Always profoundly honest, he now lives modestly, after spending all he had for the popular cause. He, like Quadrio, lived educating. As a writer he would certainly have been one of Italy’s best humorists; as a politician, he would have had the makings of a man of State. He is neither the one nor the other, because in times so sluggish he knew how to have too much character; the honors go to the opportunists, the admiration of the good to the apostles… And Campanella, without fear of being contradicted, can call himself an apostle”.9

When Mazzini founded “Giovane Italia” in Marseilles, Federico Campanella set up its Genoese Committee with the brothers Jacopo and Giovanni Ruffini, working very hard to spread this institution and secretly preparing a revolution which was to have broken out in the early months of 1833.

However, when the government authorities got wind of the plot, many of Mazzini’s followers were arrested and among them some soldiers, sympathizers, were killed. Federico Campanella escaped the police search, it is not known how, and took refuge in the Gattornos’ house in Santa Maria delle Vigne where the love of his sister and brother-in-law were his salvation. Dressed as a sailor, his face and hands blackened with tar as though he were a rough crew member, he was able to embark on a ship that was about to set sail and reached safety in Marseilles.

While these events were taking place, the Gattorno children were still very young: Rosa was only two and her eldest brother six; so they were oblivious to it all. Nevertheless their uncle’s tragic flight and the political ferment in the city had deep repercussions on their siblings who were born soon afterwards; in addition, the news of their uncle, who wandered about Europe for fifteen years unable to set foot in Italy, must have kindled a real enthusiasm for new ideas in those childish hearts.

Federico Campanella returned to Italy in 1848 and took part in several revolutionary movements during that year and in those that followed. He made no secret of his aversion to the Church and to the papacy. He courted the Italian Freemasons for a period and strove to make Masonry a decisively Republican institution. “Masonry”, he said, “if its substance and form are not reformed, is powerless and absurd”.10 He died in Florence on 8 December 1884.

Federico, Rosa’s brother, also threw himself into patriotism and conspiracy; at a young age he participated with conviction and enthusiasm in the enterprises of the Risorgimento, following in his uncle’s footsteps.

In this period, an episode is told concerning Rosa which was testified by Sister Anna Apollonia Marchetti at the rogatory process of Naples in 1913. Here a presumed visit of the future Pope Pius IX to the home of the Gattornos and of several prophetic words spoken about little Rosa are mentioned.11 On the basis of accurate and recent research of the Institute’s historical archives published in a study by Cardinal Pietro Palazzini, it can be affirmed that the episode in question is not very reliable, for not only do we have no confirmation of this visit by Pius IX to the Gattornos’ home by other witnesses or biographers, but the advocate of the cause himself, Carlo Snider, declares that it is impossible that the future Pope, then Bishop of Imola, could have made a journey to Genoa in this period.

Should all this therefore be discounted as a pure invention? Cardinal Palazzini himself offers the hypothesis that Rosa’s mother recounted the event, later published in the texts, at a time of mental confusion, evidently mixing up the circumstances and dates of her daughter’s life.12

On the other hand, it is certain that Rosa’s first meeting with Pius IX was on 3 January 1866 at the memorable audience during which the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne was to be decided, and which was the beginning of a closely-packed working relationship between the Holy Pontiff and the Mother, for the benefit of the Church and of the world.

Rosa’s precocious sensitivity to the poor ~ In the meantime Rosa had a flourishing childhood. Gradually, her gentle and perceptive intelligence became apparent and made her lovable to everyone, especially her paternal grandmother, who made no secret of her soft spot for this little granddaughter.

Her grandmother’s devotion had a great influence on the little girl’s education in those early years, especially in the summer months during the pleasant stay at Sturla, where the greater freedom of country life afforded her various opportunities to be in the company of poor girls; her grandmother had perceived her granddaughter’s gentle nature, so inclined to affection, and made the most of these meetings to direct her to deeper feelings for the humble. Little Rosa’s response was very clear then from her joy at being able to help the poor and, for the rest of her life, from her wonderful acts of charity which were later to blossom as works of the Institute she founded.

In 1841,13 when Rosa was barely ten years old, her grandmother died and the Sturla house was sold. Her father bought another house nearer Genoa, at San Luca d’Albaro, which could accommodate the whole family, now grown to eight people; All the Gattornos went there every year in the summer months and at times also in other seasons, as they did during the epidemics which ravaged those years. This stay in Albaro must have been the first place, later always remembered, where Rosa could exercise her piety and zeal.

The precise date is unknown, but probably towards the age of ten or eleven, in accordance with the custom of the time, Rosa was admitted to First Communion, and a little later, on 19 April 1843, to Confirmation, which she received at Santa Maria delle Vigne from the Archbishop, Cardinal Placido Tadini; Marchioness Eugenia Raggio, the wife of Marquis Ignazio Pallavicino, was her sponsor.

Adolescence and growth in the faith ~ These events marked a special maturity in the young girl’s character. Indeed, in their testimonies her relatives observe that her precocious intelligence from that period enabled her to share in family life and succeed in exercising “an ascendancy and a fascination” over all her brothers and sisters “which, moreover, she retained for the rest of her life”.14

Sharing a bedroom with her younger sister Elisa, she made her say her prayers, morning and evening, and kept up this habit until she married, leaving her sister pining for that devout intimacy. Her other brothers and sisters recall the thoughtful kindness with which, ridding herself of superfluous and other agreeable things, she would pander to their innocent caprices, in this way winning their hearts to lead them to goodness; her brothers Federico and Francesco, although far behind her with regard to religious practice, were also later to hold her in deep veneration and were a great help in the various works of her apostolate.

After being widowed in 1840, her maternal grandmother came to live with the Gattornos; Rosa cared for her lovingly in her ailments until she died in 1850. However, it was her mother especially, then the victim of serious illness and almost always unwell, who found great consolation in the ready kindness of the little girl, who from that time showed a rare inclination to give the sick proper care and to comfort the suffering.15

She was particularly delicate in foreseeing, hiding or alleviating anything that could afflict her mother who was extraordinarily sensitive; the good lady immediately noticed her daughter’s affectionate prudence and began to treat her as her confidant, so that their exchange of troubles, worries, joys and advice soon became a fond habit.

In those confidences Rosa learned from her mother a precious attitude to life that was later to yield the most consoling fruit. From that period she became accustomed to allocating her time wisely, so as always to be able to find some to devote herself peacefully to prayer, acts of charity and the instruction of the ignorant in the catechism. The young girl’s self-confidence in taking the initiative for various charitable works was the object of amazement.

Among other tasks, her mother had put her in charge of the household linen and Rosa could therefore make the most of this circumstance secretly to set aside what she considered no longer of use to benefit some needy person.

At that time, the summer holiday at Albaro was the most favorable season for her charitable activity: It really was a festive occasion for this fifteen-year old girl to help the poor with generous alms-giving, to comfort the afflicted and to instruct the little ones in the faith. Here, in fact, Rosa enjoyed greater freedom to gather the peasants’ children round her and to teach them the first elements of the catechism, interesting and entertaining them with the lovable arts of her charity.

Her contemporaries say that she seemed like a mother hen in the midst of a happy brood of chickens.16 From that time, her spirit of dedication to the humble formed the basis of her character; one might say that her acute intelligence and exquisite family up-bringing, far from making her vain, rather inspired the development in her heart of a wholly Christian judgment of life’s value, in other words, that life is all the more valuable the more it is spent for the benefit of others.

Her exemplary piety was not only evident in her devotional practices in which her joy at receiving Holy Communion and in adoring Jesus in the Sacrament17 was particularly noticeable, but she also strove to decorate the altar; an old lay brother of San Francesco d’Albaro showed a visiting woman a beautifully executed work of embroidery on a fine altar cloth which he said had been done for that church by Rosa Gattorno when she was a girl, and spoke of her with eager admiration, recalling her charming manners and most pleasing zeal.18

The Gattornos were in the habit of ending their holidays at San Luca d’Albaro on All Souls’ Day. Rosa would spend most of that morning distributing generous quantities of cooked beans to the poor, as was the tradition of well-to-do families in that area, and used the occasion to say an affectionate farewell to those humble and beloved people. However, in 1850 when the farewell was the last since her family had purchased another villa in Sampierdarena, everyone was overcome by sorrow and ever afterwards a number of those humble people would pay her frequent visits in Genoa, as though to a friend, and blessed her memory for many a long year.

Youth of an “eminently superior” nature — At this point in her life we already see clearly Rosa’s character as a young Christian, as she was still remembered many years later by a close family friend. The lovely qualities of mind and heart with which she was endowed were wonderfully radiant in the chaste beauty of her slim figure and her luminous, most gentle eyes, which could radiate such pure joy; her bearing had so becoming a modesty that her family were amazed at her self-control even in the most unexpected circumstances: in short, she was “the soul” of the house. Her parents had seen to the cultivation of her intelligence, according to the custom of the time, by engaging teachers of Italian literature, French, drawing and music to come to the house.

She had acquired particular skill in embroidery and singing: gifted as she was with a very sweet voice and good taste, she was often invited to perform pieces of music at family celebrations and in the homes of relatives and friends, where she sometimes also had to take part in a dance or sit at the piano; and this she did with great grace. Later, when she had become a religious and a foundress, thinking back on these youthful amusements, she showed something like repentance for them, as she once told a venerable Genoese priest when passing along Via San Rocchino, where there was a house later lived in for some time by the Daughters of St. Anne; stopping to look at it, she said sadly: “How many dances I have danced in this house!”19.

But in truth she had nothing to reproach herself with, for in this period of her life too her conduct was so balanced and upright that her acquaintances unanimously described her as most modest and angelic.

To all this was added a special aptitude and a rare perspicacity in the administrative affairs of the family, so that the running of the household was largely entrusted to her intuition, and with her persuasive words she often succeeded in softening her father’s inevitable business setbacks. Indeed, this superiority of intelligence and character was so evident that one of her sisters, Giustina, was at times jealous of it. But the finest thing in Rosa’s youth was undoubtedly the exquisite ardor of her piety, sustained not by passing emotions but by a living faith and a serious religious formation, which often moved her to show her gratitude to God for having had her born in the bosom of the Catholic Church.

According to the testimony of those who knew her, the girl Rosa grew ever more reserved and good, averse to amusements and without ambition. Inclined to a life of piety and recollection, even as a young girl she would stay up praying until late at night, as she later confided to some of her closest sisters, and it is not impossible that even at that time she practized penances20. She was exemplary in her respect and obedience towards her parents, and she also grew in spirit through frequent reception of the Sacraments, which were for her the true nourishment of the supernatural life.

By virtue of this growth, her faith could show itself robust and firm even in dealing with people hostile to the Church. After his return from exile in 1848, Federico Campanella in fact became a frequent visitor to the Gattorno house, and it seems that he even lived there for some time. More involved than ever, as has been said above, in the realization of Mazzini’s ideals, he often spoke of them and soon won over his nephews, especially Federico, Rosa’s brother, who was then barely twelve. Friends of Mazzini, Goffredo Mameli and Giuseppe Garibaldi thus often happened to be in the Gattorno house, and Rosa necessarily had to deal with them and be present at their conversations. Her brother Francesco testifies: “Of an eminently superior character with those she dealt with, and without compromising her convictions, she had an innate tolerance that commanded respect; and although very young, in a time of political upheaval and in a position that brought her into contact with some of the greatest thinkers and agitators, she was repaid with the utmost regard, and her word was always as effective as her faith and her noble examples of sacrifice”21.

It is Rosa’s character asserting itself as clearly Christian and distinguished by filial love for the Church. It is the clear, slender current, already sure in its course between the waves that flank it. The same upbringing had set the lives of these children on their way in a Christian home; at the clash of opposing ideals, some gave way and drew aside, taking other paths. At what point the parting came is difficult to establish, even though only a decade of family life is involved. The secret, however, lies in two words, gentle and terrible: fidelity to grace; a fidelity made up of ever-increasing sacrifices and therefore showing an ascending greatness, to the point where it can be called holiness. This was the greatness of Rosa Gattorno.

Marries Gerolamo Custo ~ “The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a feast for his son’s wedding” (Mt 22:2).

Among his many enlightening and practical comparisons, this one blossomed more than once on the divine Teacher’s lips. Indeed, he chose to begin his public life by taking part in a wedding feast which he sanctified and gladdened with a splendid miracle. However, every time that Jesus presents us with a wedding feast, he does not stop to let us consider the carefree joy that brightens life and seeks almost to ignore its burdens, but points out serious, even demanding aspects. It is like some unusual test in which moral strength is measured and the fruitfulness of love is radiant. The servants who watch vigilantly through the night, the strict requirement of the nuptial garment which must always be impeccable, the prompt preparation of the lamps which the virgins must keep ready even during a delay that is long, uncertain, nerve-racking and conducive to sleep; these are always intended to mean a fidelity to our own commitments that transcends all selfishness and is ready to be heroic.

Yes, because joy must also be a test of strength here on earth. It is for this reason too, that is, not only for the sake of indissoluble unity but rather because of love’s superior power in any sacrifice, that St. Paul said that marriage is a sacrament which reveals Christ’s relationship with his Church.

These things were well known to Rosa Gattorno who, approaching the age of twenty, had to look to her future and talk about it seriously with her spiritual director. She had opportunities to meet worthy priests throughout her spiritual life, but when the time came to choose a state of life, God set Fr. Antonio Accinelli on her path. With a thorough knowledge of her soul and her sincere efforts to seek God’s will, he made her decide on marriage. Indeed, he failed to glimpse the clear signs of a virginal vocation in this young woman, although he often saw her talking to nuns and much enjoying the conversation; even the great charity with which she so lovingly approached the unfortunate and went to the hospitals in Genoa to visit and comfort the sick,1 did not seem to him reliable proof of her vocation to a life wholly dedicated to helping the needy, as was the practice of certain Institutes founded at that time. On the contrary, Rosa’s lovely qualities seemed the best prerequisite for founding an exemplary Christian family; especially since Rosa, although secretly dreaming of a state of total consecration to God, also felt disposed to married life as long as it was blessed by the Church. In addition, she took the express desire of her parents in this matter as an indication of the divine will.2

The testimony of Rosa’s sister, Elisa, who was devoted to her, is of considerable importance in this regard because of her direct knowledge. This sister declares that Rosa decided to marry on the “recommendation” of her parents, at the age of twenty-two, and that “she married of her own free will and with affection”.3

While making such a demanding choice of life, Rosa certainly could not have imagined what God had in store for her: married life must have been the harshest of sacrifices for her, a beginning and a school of heroic virtues that would not fail to crown her with religious consecration in an immense apostolate of charity.

At that time, numerous Genoese would come to Palazzo Lamba Doria for business matters or to talk politics. They did not only admire the elegance of the rooms and the shrewd nobility of the merchant, Mr. Francesco Gattorno; there is no doubt that they also admired his daughter who in doing the honors of the house, combined such grace and maturity with so strong a character that she attracted attention and amazed many, especially when they saw her with self-confident courtesy keeping up the flow of conversation on religious principles or the respect due to the Catholic Church. Consequently, requests for her in marriage were not slow in coming.

A cousin of hers, Gerolamo Custo, felt close to Rosa because of her honesty and good social rank and she repaid him with uncommon affection; but her father had already accepted the request for her hand of another gentleman, the lawyer, Tito Orsini.4

He was a brilliant lawyer in Genoese circles, the brother of a well-known supporter of Mazzini, Dr. Angelo Carl’Antonio Orsini, who had been taken prisoner in the revolutionary movements of 1833. This relationship perhaps explains the lawyer Tito’s presence in the Gattornos’ house, where, as we have seen, Federico Campanella used to gather other political conspirators. Young Orsini’s gratifying position and intelligence won him the sympathy of Rosa’s father, but his conduct soon disappointed his hopes. The inexplicable postponements in bringing the already excessively protracted engagement to a conclusion and even more his conduct, which was not in conformity with the honest principles of the Gattornos, ended by disgusting Rosa’s family and he was no longer admitted to their home.5

Then her cousin Gerolamo once again presented himself and was gladly accepted by all, because of his good qualities. The necessary ecclesiastical dispensations for the degree of kinship were obtained, and the marriage was arranged for 5 November 1852.

In the meantime, Francesco Gattorno had bought a house near the cathedral, at the corner of Via Scurreria and Via Tommaso Reggio (then Via del Chiostro). It was a rather tall building and the Gattornos kept the whole of the second floor as their own home. They moved in after Easter 1852, when the appropriate alterations had been completed, thus becoming parishioners of San Lorenzo. It was therefore in this house, in accordance with the custom of many families at that time, that Rosa’s marriage to Gerolamo Custo was celebrated on 5 November and the following morning, in the chapel of the sacristy of San Lorenzo, the newly married couple received the blessing and took part in Holy Mass.6

Fr. Antonio Accinelli, parochial vicar of the cathedral, was present and blessed the marriage. Rosa’s sister, Elisa, also expressly noted that “at both ceremonies the Servant of God behaved modestly and showed her happiness without letting herself be carried away with joy”.7

Perhaps Rosa had had a presentiment that that day was the beginning of a difficult life: she had prepared for it with prayers, vigils, fasting and other rigorous practices.8 Thus it was not surprising that among the flowers, gifts and bustle of the wedding party she should have adhered to the sensible behavior to which she had long been accustomed.

It was fortunate for her that she did, since sharp thorns were soon to be entwined with the orange blossom.

Financial troubles ~ At the end of that day, the new couple left Genoa with a procession of carriages for France; their goal was Marseilles, where Gerolamo Custo’s business was based. Their relatives’ carriages accompanied them for a long stretch, as far as Varazze and there, having taken leave of everyone, the married couple continued on to Nice and Marseilles. But it must also have been their farewell to happiness.

In fact, shortly after arriving in Marseilles, the disastrous state of his affairs became apparent to Mr. Custo. A few days of trembling at the brink of the gaping abyss, his anxious silence about what was inevitable, and at the same time a few threads of hope or rather illusion, but in the end it was useless and impossible to keep the secret: he was bankrupt! In a few months, from being opulently rich he had become poor and was obliged to tell this to his young wife. It is easy to imagine Rosa’s dismay. She immediately appealed to her father who came with all haste from Genoa, and able as he was in business matters, succeeded in saving a few small things from the wreck; but Custo’s future in Marseilles was over for ever. Francesco Gattorno had to bring his daughter and son-in-law back to Genoa and give them hospitality in his house since Alessandro Custo, Rosa’s father-in-law, was not a man to open his arms to the poor shipwrecked couple; indeed, after that point relations between the two families became somewhat strained.

Birth of Carlotta and her disability ~ In the midst of these painful events, Rosa had begun a pregnancy; it is easy to imagine the negative repercussions they must have had on her health, precisely in those months when she so needed peace.

Towards the end of the year, on 8 December 1853, the day of the Immaculate Conception, she gave birth to a baby girl who was baptized the following day in the Metropolitan Church of San Lorenzo and given the names Carlotta, Francesca, Maria.9

Her first wails rekindled the hopes of the tried family and somewhat reconciled the relatives’ feelings; indeed the infant was given the name Carlotta as a tribute to Rosa’s mother-in-law; her second name was Francesca, because of Rosa’s love for her father. The Gattornos and the Custos strengthened their ties over the innocent child’s cradle, and this union served to remedy past misfortunes. In fact, shortly afterwards we find Gerolamo Custo a partner in the Gattornos’ family business.

But Rosa’s maternal affection was soon to encounter a very harsh trial. Indeed she had scarcely had time to see in her baby’s innocent face those first signs of recognition which make a mothers heart beat with joy, her bright eyes responding to her mother’s tender gaze while her uncertain tongue was already stammering the names of papa and mama, when the tender little body was stricken with a violent and mysterious illness and seized with spasmodic convulsions; in that illness her voice was extinguished and her ears stopped for ever; little Carlotta became a deaf-mute. Poor mother!

In that privation, Rosa not only felt the wound in her heart but perceived the painful dismay of all her relatives, foreseeing the dark future that would weigh upon her home.

Birth of Alessandro and Gerolamo’s departure for Russia ~ Two years passed and Rosa became a mother for the second time. On 28 October 1855, in her father’s villa at Sampierdarena, her son Alessandro was born and was baptized the next day in the Church of San Martino and Santa Maria della Cella.10

The growth of the family and, perhaps, an improvement in his business made Gerolamo decide to re-establish a business of his own; in fact during that year it seems that the Custos took up residence in the Parish of San Siro in Genoa.11

Rosa nevertheless continued to fulfill her religious duties at the Metropolitan Church of San Lorenzo, where she was well known and had the opportunity to be involved in various good works, especially hospital visits. At this time, she changed directors to be under the spiritual direction of Fr. Giuseppe Firpo, Custodian of the Metropolitan Church. She continued with him throughout her time in Genoa, and he gave her great help and advice in particularly difficult times. From this priest we know that Rosa received the Holy Sacraments with praiseworthy frequency.12

This was the period of her life when she shone for her virtues as a Christian wife and exemplary mother. Gerolamo, her husband, had surrounded her with notable comforts, but he had become increasingly bitter, perhaps because of his sad experiences, so that some held him to be bad tempered and at times violent.13

Other testimonies of considerable relevance, since they report information learned directly from the Mother, emphasize instead that Girolamo Custo had a gentle nature and that during their approximately six years of marriage, the husband and wife loved each other sincerely and had a good living relationship. In fact, Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia testified at the Roman Cause: “She told me that her husband was very kind and that it would have been a shame to do him any wrong; therefore they lived in peace and love together”.14

Other domestic and external testimonies agree in saying that Rosa loved her husband and was loved by him.15

Rosa wanted a wholly Christian spirit to prevail in her upper-class home: God had to have the first place within those walls; so in addition to the most sensitive concern for her husband and children she paid watchful attention to the servants, to ensure that they fulfilled their religious duties and kept away from any moral danger.

She was so keen on the observance of rest on Sundays and feast days that on those days she did not allow the premises to be cleaned.16

However, she was only able to enjoy this orderly rhythm of domestic life for a few months. Her husband Gerolamo barely had time to rejoice in the birth of their son, Alessandro, when he had to leave for distant Russia to join his brother-in-law Federico Gattorno who had set up a grain-trading firm in the city of Berdyansk.17

Thus towards the end of 1855, Rosa was left alone for more than a year, fully absorbed in caring for the two children.

Gerolamo’s return and birth of Francesco ~ Gerolamo’s business took a turn for the better in Russia and so he was able to amass a modest fortune for his children.18

However, his health deteriorated from day to day, so badly that at the beginning of 1857 he had to go home, and he arrived in Genoa in a very bad state. His wife’s care certainly had the effect of alleviating his mind and to a certain extent his body, but Gerolamo, who had been so harshly tried, never recovered his former strength.

In the meantime Rosa was favored by God with a third pregnancy. On 1 December that same year a third son was born: Francesco. His godparents at his baptism were his grandfather, Francesco Gattorno, and another relative, a certain Rosa Gattorno née Morando.19

Gerolamo’s illness and a premonition of his forthcoming death ~ Hardly had this last flower blossomed when the shadow of death began to fall across the young Custo family. Gerolamo, weakened by the disease that was gnawing at his innards, was forced to bed. At first it seemed a slight indisposition, but it soon became apparent that his condition was serious.

One day when Rosa was at his bedside, she raised her eyes to an image of Jesus the Nazarene that was hanging at the head of the bed; she was stunned to see Christ’s features melting into the traits of a skeleton before her very eyes! Nothing of the kind had ever happened to her and she was sure she was not mistaken; so she accepted the event as a divine warning, and was deeply convinced that her husband’s death was imminent.20

His illness proved to be tuberculosis of the lungs, already so advanced as to leave no hope. Rosa was truly an angel of consolation in those last days of her husband’s life when her strength of mind and heroic spirit of self-denial seemed greater than ever. She was kept very busy, looking after the new baby and attending to unfortunate Carlotta who was barely four years old; since she was deaf and mute, she could only express her wishes and her little miseries by crying and screaming; yet the generous woman did not want to relinquish her place beside her husband, and looked after him constantly for three months, day and night, without even undressing. Her love was so great that all her acquaintances were amazed at it and still marvelled at her many years later; the priest, who wrote a testimonial of Gerolamo’s death a few years later, felt moved to add these words: “It should be noted that during his long illness of more than six months, he was constantly and lovingly assisted by his wife”.21

This was truly total Christian love, since Rosa combined with her cares for her husband’s body the most fervent zeal for his soul, through spiritual conversations with him that detached him from the earth and imbued his soul with hopes of heaven..

The sick man also enjoyed prayers, especially the holy Rosary, which he wanted to recite with his wife every day and never missed, even when he felt very ill.22

Rosa’s widowhood ~ Comforted by prayer and the sacraments, the sick man died on the evening of 9 March 1858 when he was only 31 years old. How distressed Rosa was! She fainted when she realized he had died, as she herself recounted many years later; and when she subsequently visited her deceased husband’s grave, she promised him that she would love him for ever, as she had loved him when he was alive.23

She was then alone with three very young fatherless children; the thought of their future, the mysterious tumult of aspirations stirring in her soul, her sense of her own responsibility and the bond that tied her to those tender little lives, filled her with dismay. However, she sought refuge in her faith without hesitation.

Taking the three little ones with her, she entered a church and in front of an image of the Sorrowful Virgin, in tears she offered them, entrusted them to the divine Mother. That cry for help, that act of abandonment welling up from her heart were so determined and so profound that she immediately seemed to feel reassured and to know that the Blessed Virgin would always take care of her fatherless children. Somewhat comforted, she went home and set about facing daily life with great courage. Her silent face over which quiet grief spread a sort of veil of majesty, inspired a sense of deep respect and admiration in all who knew her.

The untimely widowhood, which struck Rosa when she was only just 26 years old, was one of those mysterious acts of Providence which determine the progress of saints. The death of her husband was the beginning of a new life for her extraordinary sacrifices and the immensity of what she was later to undertake. It seemed that God was urging her to stride through the thorny bushes of all her troubles, to lead her to sublime conquests of charity.

Family disputes ~ Indeed, the bitter cup offered to her had not been emptied at her husband’s death. A sordid quarrel about matters of ownership flared up between the Custo in-laws and the Gattornos over the still fresh grave; in this adversity those who made the arrangements for the funeral had not thought to pay its cost.

Some time later, a man presented himself to Rosa, asking her for the sum he was owed for having dressed and buried her husband, adding that he was tired of waiting. The poor widow, horrified that the sum should still be outstanding, gave the man what he asked straightaway and, retreating to her room, burst into floods of tears.24 But that may have been the last expense she could pay easily.

Indeed, very soon the two families quarrelled over the ownership of what was found in the house of the deceased and the bailiff had to order the seizure of all the furniture and household goods, including the widow’s marriage dowry. “With difficulty”, the Mother later recounted, “I was able to save a few pieces of furniture by sending them to my sisters’ house; and it was very hard to see myself suddenly dispossessed of the drawing room furniture and the jewels and linen of which our home was deprived, as well as being forced to live in a few rooms scantily furnished with the bare necessities and even, for a few nights, to sleep on a simple straw pallet”.25

Death of Francesco and Rosa’s return to her parents’ house ~ However, the bitterest drop was at the bottom of the cup. Just three months after her husband’s death, Rosa saw her tender little son die at the age of only a few months.26 He was the only one to be born in that house which she could call her own; he was the last flower of her motherhood which had bloomed as her husband’s life was waning, and he was therefore her most vivid memory of him. Death had now inexorably wrenched him from her. The poor mother’s grief was so bitter that, as she later confessed, she thought she would go mad. Her confessor, Fr. Firpo, had to come and comfort her several times, and finally resorted to a severe order of obedience to induce her bravely to resume her activities and the care of the other two children.

Meanwhile Mr. Francesco Gattorno was convinced that his daughter’s life in those tragic conditions was unsustainable. Seeing that the Custos did not want to have anything to do with them, he intervened with a generous fatherly impulse and took the widow and her children home.27

So it was that Rosa returned to the rooms of her youth barely six years after she had left them in her bridal veil; she returned in mourning, with two little children at her side on whom an irreparable loss weighed heavily.

Such a great misfortune might seem, in the eyes of the world, mysteriously at odds with the good heart and the pure and generous youth of that twenty-six-year-old woman. It seemed a life broken for ever; instead, it was precisely then that that life was beginning.
