(1858-1865) The beginning of a life of charity – Love for Christ crucified and the “vocation to suffering” – First mystical experience in Santa Maria delle Vigne; vow of chastity, obedience and perpetual fasting – Austerity of life – Aridity and spiritual consolations – Diabolical suggestions – Profession as a Franciscan Tertiary – Fr. Giuseppe Firpo’s spiritual direction – Vow of poverty.

The beginning of a life of charity ~ The rapid sequence of events in Rosa’s life and their change from happy to sad during the winter between 1857 and 1858 was strangely documented on a sheet which turned up among her letters: it is the little account of a milliner for bills for that four-month period from 15 November 1857 when she was expecting the birth of her last son, to 13 March 1858, a few days after her husband’s death. This little item, preserved out of the many keepsakes that were burned, was perhaps more than once the object of Rosa’s reflection: it certainly shows signs of long use. Whoever wrote the bill paid no attention to the different character of the articles of clothing and the painful events which had stricken the young widow; thus, in a single list, written in accordance with the custom of the period and obviously with the dates next to them, are listed hats for walking out, baptismal bonnets and such small details together with the mourning items that were then immediately required. All in a few lines on a single sheet, which seem to bring the cradle close to the coffin, as if to recall the vanity of life.1

In any case the lesson was so profoundly learned by Gerolamo Custo’s widow that from that day her way of life became an arduous spiritual ascent with a wonderful impetus of charity.

She was later to write in her Memorie:

“In the year 1857,2 free from any obligation, I dedicated myself with greater zeal to pious works, visiting the hospitals and the poor sick at home, assisting them by coming to their aid as far as I could and serving them in everything. [With] the Lord’s grace, I realized that all my earthly affections were vanishing; nothing was enjoyable, only my God was the pasture of all my delights” (M. 1.1, p. 1).

This love grew steadily to the point of heroism, since what impelled her was giving herself to the poor and lowly as she would have given herself to Jesus Christ; she therefore endeavored to sacrifice herself for the unfortunate rather than to give them material aid, although in this too she was exceedingly generous.

In her parent’s house she was given an apartment with her own entrance, so that she could come and go freely even at night, without being noticed by the family.

Indeed, in the middle of the night, when her children were fast asleep, she would often leave silently with one of her most faithful serving women, to bring some seriously ill person physical and spiritual help. She recognized that in so doing she had God’s special protection, both for herself and for her children, since nothing disastrous ever occurred.

She went to the hospital as though she were going to a party; she found complete happiness with the sick and particularly with the poorest and shyest.

With deep respect she made their beds, offered them their medicines and kissed their sores. “When I managed to do this”, she wrote, “it was a real comfort to me”.3

Financial contributions must have been a serious problem for Rosa, given her straitened means in the first months of widowhood. She would have liked to dispose of certain small ornaments and to give up some of the comforts which her parents lavished upon her, but the family’s standard of living did not allow it. Nonetheless, with the perseverance of generous love, she always managed to find something to give.

Seated at table with the rest of the family, she appeared to comply with the usual custom in serving herself; instead, she knew how to make things she did not intend to take for herself disappear, and these were the choice morsels. If it was fruit or such like, she would secretly drop it into the napkin she had on her lap and then cunningly contrive to take it away for the poor. No one at home ever noticed this; everyone believed that she abstained from meat and wine for physical reasons, and thought that in other respects she ate normally.4

Because of her liberality in giving to the poor, she sometimes got into trouble with her relatives. One day, finding that she did not have the money to help a needy family and several sick people, she called a faithful servant and sent him to sell a gun and a divan that were among the few things retrieved from the sequestration after the death of her husband. They were kept by her father in a storeroom in the house: she then delightedly distributed the proceeds among her unfortunates. But it was not long before her father realized what she had done and harshly reprimanded his daughter for her prodigality, to the point that he even wanted to expel her and the children from the house. “Oh how upset he was that evening”, Rosa told a sister a few years later, “how upset he was when, coming home late, he found me looking after my sick mother! Without thinking, at that late hour he wanted me to leave home. In this I clearly saw a test of the Lord, because I was the darling of them all and was not only loved but idolized by my father and mother. Enough; as God willed, he calmed down because he saw that even then I was prepared to obey him, since I had started to fetch my little ones to go in search of a new haven”.5

Love for Christ crucified and the “vocation to suffering” ~ These difficulties were far from impeding the generous impulses of Rosa who was learning more every day from the crucified Jesus.

The crucified Christ; Rosa called him “my Good”.

For some time she had nourished her devotion with a special tenderness for the Savior’s wounds; then her latest misfortunes had revealed to her the mystery of the Cross, and she had felt such a fascination as truly to reach a holy madness. The holy Cross, dripping with Christ’s blood and rendered worthy by his most sacred limbs, suggested to Rosa as the plan of her sanctification a determined process of identification with Christ Crucified, which she resolved to put into practice with irrepressible zeal.

As soon as her husband had died, she asked to consecrate herself to God with the vow of perpetual chastity; in the meantime, she was granted permission to do this for a year. She bound a crucifix about seven centimeters long to her breast, and kept it tightly bound to her, day and night, so that it became embedded in the flesh; when after five years she was ordered to remove it, she had to tear it from the wound it had formed, together with shreds of cloth.6

That same year, 1858, Rosa desired to gird herself with the cord of St. Francis as a Third Order Franciscan; she felt suddenly impelled by a strong urge to increase her corporal penances in a growing crescendo of mystical ardor that she called quite simply a “fire that consumes”. These were the first indications of her special vocation to suffering, which she followed at first almost unconsciously, then with ever increasing awareness.

First mystical experience in Santa Maria delle Vigne; vow of chastity, obedience and perpetual fasting ~ During the Novena of Nostra Signora delle Vigne, she received a unique grace which was to enlighten her. While she was in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, exposed for the benediction in the famous sanctuary, she felt fully absorbed in a keen perception of Christ’s blood, feeling at the same time ineffable sentiments of intimate union with Jesus and a most ardent love.

This event subsequently recurred several times, until she clearly understood that she had to take the way of Calvary if she was to be closely united with her crucified God. She was later to say: “I know that Calvary alone is the sure hill where I shall stop” (M. 1. 1, p. 16).

Towards the end of that year, during the Novena of the Immaculate Conception, she was allowed to make a perpetual vow of chastity and obedience; she would also have liked to take the vow of poverty, but her wise director, Fr. Giuseppe Firpo, did not deem it appropriate. Nonetheless, her offering marked the beginning of a new life.

“I have placed everything” she wrote, “at the feet of Mary most holy, and may she make a gift of it to my Good, Jesus, and beg him to make me his bride. Oh, what I felt! As though I had entered another state [of life] and I knew not whether I was living or who it was that was living for me!” (M. 1. 1, p. 2).

Meanwhile the tribulations of her family life were unequalled; Rosa does not say specifically what they were, but we know that as well as serious problems with the Custos she had to put up with opposition at home, both because of her life, which seemed too pious and austere, and because of the conduct of her brother, Federico, who following in his uncle’s footsteps had taken the path of conspiracy and was militant in the ranks of the Garibaldini.

To find strength in these troubles and nourishment for the inner flame of love for her God, Rosa asked and obtained permission to increase her penances. And here we touch on another secret of that great soul. What were they? From one text which she wrote through obedience, it is granted to us to know some of them, which by their very nature were already substantial tortures.

Since 1856, after the birth of her son Alessandro and when she was only twenty-five years old, she had imposed upon herself the vow of perpetual fasting, eating only one meal a day, always abstaining from meat and excluding wine. She kept up this harsh regime for forty-four years, that is, until her death, allowing herself no dispensation from it even in her last illness. She also forbade herself the use of heating in winter, and although she suffered terribly from the cold which sometimes even made her feel faint, for more than eighteen years she made no exceptions, that is, until 1876, when she was at death’s door with pleurisy which forced her to accept the relief of a little warmth.

In addition, she did anything that revolted her with deliberate determination, paying greater attention to it, in order to feel the full impact of disgust.

Austerity of life ~ In such austerity Rosa made her body a real living host pleasing to God but, attracted by what was undoubtedly an unusual vocation, she again asked her director if she could increase her penances and reiterated this request frequently throughout her life; one can say that she renewed her plea at every great solemnity or at the appearance of any particularly difficult circumstance. In 1859 she received the desired permission for the Novena of the Redeemer. She then made a leather bodice stitching piercing iron points into it; she also fabricated contrivances for her arms and legs and found a way of tormenting her feet and her head. But her most terrible instrument was a heavy iron chain with double overlapping links that formed a girdle about a centimeter thick; she bound it round her waist and pulled it so tight that she could no longer remove it. She wore it continuously for more than forty years, until her death. As time passed, the chain ate into her flesh causing her great spasms; but Rosa did not decide to remove it until the eve of her death, as will subsequently be told. Then her nurse had to use heavy pliers to break a link.7

For the same Novena of the Redeemer in 1859, she subjected her body to a stricter fast; on this occasion she spent the day before it with a little bread and barely one sip of water. “Yet”, she noted, “I felt my strength gradually increasing, as if these penances and scourging myself to the blood were a great nourishment to me” (M. 1.1, p. 4).

Aridity and spiritual consolations ~ However, while as in the past she was waiting for the divine response of great consolation, that feast of the Redeemer brought her such aridity as to dismay her and cause her to lose her peace of mind, as if some hidden sin were the impediment to divine favors.

“I did not yet know”, she wrote, “how to fight under the banner of the Holy Cross, delicious and beloved. Ah, how many [sins] are committed by being a beginner!” (M. 1.1, p, 4).

After prompt recourse to her director, serenity returned to her soul. She then understood that following the crucified Christ did not only involve corporal privations and penances, but also dark nights and anguish which torment the spirit. These could not be slow in coming and were the prelude to several extraordinary favors.

In that year of 1859, the Novena of Nostra Signora delle Vigne also brought her great spiritual consolations and inner enlightenments which would have kept her in church all day, had her obligations had not prevented it. From those moments of intimacy with God she drew great spiritual strength, so that she felt she was ready for any trial; and such was the joy she felt within that she even let it appear externally, to the point that everyone thought she was happy.

She experienced these special gifts especially after Holy Communion. At that time, after seeing a very bright light over the crown of thorns and feeling a great longing to participate in some way in Christ’s torture, she asked and obtained permission to make one for herself and to wear it on her head every Thursday night until Friday. But she was once badly hurt by one of the thorns on her forehead which caused a swelling; how grieved she felt, fearing that it might lead to the discovery of her penances by her relatives! However, she arranged her hair over her forehead to hide the affliction.

Diabolical suggestions ~ From that time Satan’s persecution became implacable. Violent and horrible temptations came to disturb Rosa’s soul: at times she would feel sinful and far from her Good, at others, the most atrocious doubts, even about the Blessed Sacrament, would lacerate her mind, yet again, she would have scruples about the penances she had inflicted on herself, as though they were a suicide or a hindrance to her duties as mother and daughter. These storms would agitate her at brief intervals, especially in the first years of widowhood, and are frequently mentioned in her Memorie. Rosa fought them with a generous heart and always continued to progress in her renunciation of the world and in the total sacrifice of herself.

In 1861, she put into practice an idea she had long contemplated: having obtained from the friars of St. Francis a length of material like that used for their habits, she sewed a sleeveless one for herself and wore it under her secular clothes, which, as was then the fashion, were loose enough to enable her to do so. She proceeded to bind it round her waist with a thick cord, from which the skull dangled on one side.

She wore this habit day and night, and one can imagine how uncomfortable she was, mostly because of its weight, and the other instruments of penance she had about her person.

That Franciscan habit can be seen among all the other penitential contrivances in her cell in Piacenza, mentioned above,

Such austerity and moral suffering seriously undermined Rosa’s health so that at the beginning of summer she had to go to the country, to San Francesco d’Albaro with her family. She had grown so thin and pale that she looked as though she were sickening with phthisis. Yet even then the devil bombarded her with temptations; these seemed to reach their peak in mid-July.

During the Novena of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, she had terrible battles and an abyss of tribulations: more than anything else, she was wounded by the diabolical suggestions that incited her to desperation, and tried to convince her that she would never have the grace to be loved by Jesus Christ; it seemed to her that she had uttered blasphemies in those moments of agitation, she was therefore left with deep regret, as it is easy to imagine.

However, with great wisdom, even from afar she turned to her spiritual guide in whose prudence and fortitude she had full trust. Certain letters from Fr. Giuseppe Firpo which have been preserved are a clear documentation of the Mother’s struggles and the state of her soul.

In one rather lengthy one, he soothed her with regard to evil thoughts and doubts about the Most Holy Eucharist. He wrote, “Therefore, daughter, you must thoroughly understand what I am saying to you: do not be in the least afraid of these diabolical machinations; continue the career you have begun with honest determination, and fear nothing, even should these forces be redoubled. If you can, I recommend that you always receive Holy Communion: this will be a shield to you against any assault of hell…”.

And again, “…whatever temptation comes to you, do not force yourself to tackle it face on, but embrace the cross of your crucified Spouse and Love, Jesus, and rest there in peace, with certainty that nothing can harm you…”. And he concluded “I am very glad that you have been able to receive Holy Communion every day […]. If I think of the great benefits which Holy Communion has brought you, I am right to tell you that the Lord loves you and loves you as the apple of his eye. Believe me, after receiving it, you became different from what you were before. Now you belong totally to your Jesus. As regards the second part of your letter, I tell you that for the time being you should limit yourself to no more than the penances I have permitted you, with which the Lord will be pleased”.8

This soothing reply was accompanied by sweet consolations, although her inner strife continued.

Profession as a Franciscan Tertiary ~ On 24 September 1861, on holiday at San Francesco d’Albaro, she made her profession as a Third Order Franciscan and chose this saint as her special patron, ever afterwards retaining a great devotion to him. Shortly after the ceremony, she was gladdened by new divine favors which were: vivid experiences of Christ, visions of his blood, the keenest desire to suffer for love of him and to be consumed by his love; Rosa used to call these the “caresses” of her Good.

This is not the right place to investigate the nature of the extraordinary gifts that Mother Rosa was privileged to have been given; She tells of them simply and plainly in the pages of several notebooks as facts that were interwoven with all her interior life, but attached no fundamental importance to them.

At this point it would be appropriate to quote a valuable study on Rosa Gattorno’s personality written a few years ago by Fr. Lázaro Iriarte, in which among other things he says: “Another premise to be borne in mind is the following: Mother Rosa endlessly cited her interior lights, her penetration of hearts, her predictions of future events, her visions […] but she never spoke of revelations, or of messages to be given to other people and we never see her modify her own behavior or her own decisions in the light of what she saw […]. She felt guided by God, tutored and supported by her Good…”.9

Rosa’s holiness did not depend on the exceptional quality of the charisms with which she was favored, but there is no doubt that they bore precious fruits in her soul: a growing fervor of love for Christ, an insatiable thirst for sacrifice under the guidance of obedience, true humility which spurred her to concealment and to jealously guarding her inner life, which was besides so rich and extraordinary; all this so that nothing would leak out about those gifts which would have attracted esteem.

In the space of four years Rosa had achieved such heights in the purification of herself and in her union with Christ that the crescendo of her aspirations have the style of the greatest of saints and the hallmark of folly of the Cross: “My suffering grew, and I thanked my Beloved for it, he who provided me with such sweet food” (M. 1.1, pp. 17-18); “Oh, Love, you who have suffered so much for my sake, make me suffer and die for you!” (M.1.1, p. 20).

Fr. Giuseppe’s spiritual direction ~ In answer to this thirst for suffering, God lavished upon his beloved aridity and inner desolation which became habitual and very painful to her. Her spiritual director, Fr. Giuseppe Firpe, was now certain that at every meeting this subject would be discussed.

“Concerning your letter”, he wrote to her on 20 August 1862, “before opening it I more or less imagined what it would contain: tribulations and crosses, crosses and tribulations. This, daughter, is the heritage of chosen souls here on earth. I certainly did not expect you to communicate consolations to me: true consolations are certainly in store for you in heaven”.10

Later, on 17 September: “The time for consolations, that is, spiritual dainties, appears to be over for you, and you must henceforth quench your thirst with the bitter cup of tribulation alone. It is in tribulation that your lover, Jesus, wants to be more closely united to you. God’s favorites, the predestined, the elect to glory”11.

What is even more surprising, however, is how readily her director now granted Rosa new penances, whereas before he had been rather firm in refusing them during the holiday season. In that year, 1862, she had fallen ill again, yet she would never give in, either by agreeing to see a doctor or by going to bed. Her parents, seeing her reduced to such a state and exhausted, were annoyed with Fr. Firpo for allowing her things that were harmful to her health, and so they took her out of Genoa to the countryside. But from there Rosa continued to press her director for new mortifications and penances. The wise priest answered her on 1 August: “I grant you everything you ask of me in your letter, for that is how I feel inspired for the present”12. And a month later, on 7 September: “As to what you ask me in your letter, may the Lord’s will be done: I grant you all that you can do and all that the Lord seems to want of you”13.

The confessor had come to this decision because a few months earlier he had received a sign of God’s will in an unexpected event. During the novena of Pentecost he had allowed Rosa additional penances but had told her to suspend them all on the day of the feast. Rosa, though very reluctantly, obeyed without the slightest remark; but at once she fell into such a state of prostration that, unable to stand, she had to go to bed.

She then sent a note to Fr. Firpo, asking him to allow her to put on all her instruments of penance so that she might be able to get up. A good part of them was granted to her and she immediately recovered her lost strength. Her director was thus convinced that Rosa’s was a genuine and extraordinary vocation to suffering, and from then on he was more generous in his permissions. Vow of poverty ~ Towards the end of 1862, on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, she was also able to make the vow of poverty; beneath her secular clothes she was now a person entirely consecrated to the Lord. In the arduous school of the Crucified, Rosa had reached heights and depths humanly unimaginable, and her spiritual life, from the first steps of her widowhood, appears to us in gigantic or, rather, in Christianly heroic proportions.

The extraordinary lies in the things themselves and in their measure; on reflection, one can also see the goal willed by God taking shape, though it was still hidden from this humble creature, who thought only of pleasing her crucified Spouse. He drew her powerfully towards conquests of boundless horizons; she, with the calm faith of the strong and almost unaware, climbed the steep slope of the mountain whose summit was still veiled in mystery. She did not yet know of the great mission she would one day have to fulfill, but she was now certain that her whole life must be solely a longing for holiness and a journey towards it.

(1858-1865) Rosa’s care for her children — Lofty gifts of mystical prayer — Passive purification — Rare participation in the Passion — Rosa’s fascination and interior greatness — Spiritual friendships in the context of the Frassinetti Associations.

Rosa’s care for her children ~ In Rosa Gattorno, the desire to be totally free to give herself to God could not be confused with her desire to enjoy divine favors, far from any of life’s concerns. We have already seen how her consecration to God daily increased her spiritual exertion in her struggle and the torment of aridity.

However, alongside her deprivation of inner consolations, which accentuated her spiritual poverty, we find in Rosa an utterly generous dedication to others, in every kind of effort and labor to win their souls.

Her many penances and assiduous prayers did not in the least prevent her from thinking of her neighbor; on the contrary, the activity of the generous widow, a member of many charitable institutions and always ready to respond to the needs of the various situations of poverty which existed in that difficult period of history, gave rise to deep wonder.

However, Rosa was first and foremost concerned with her children whom she loved tenderly; she devoted her whole self, brimming with faith, to her two tender creatures in order to give them as good an upbringing as possible and a full and happy childhood, and soon saw with surprise that she had passed on her own generous kindness to them.

Carlotta, the deaf-mute, was growing up innocent and pure, but because of her disability it was not easy for her to assimilate her mother’s teaching; to prevent her being retarded or at any rate unable to live as befitted her social rank, the decision was made to send her to the Regio Istituto dei Sordomuti (Royal Institute for Deaf-Mutes) in Milan, directed by an enlightened priest: Eliseo Ghislandi.

Rosa took her there at the beginning of 1864, and stayed several weeks in Milan to help the little girl become gradually accustomed to the new kind of life. Indeed she succeeded so well in her intention that she left her daughter very happy in the institute, where, because of her gentle manners and goodness, she captivated everyone.1

On the other hand, Alessandro remained a little longer at home; from his first years he had shown intelligence and openness and a very lively and affectionate temperament which soon drew from his mother generous feelings of kindness. In autumn 1864, when he was nine years old, since he had often said that he wanted to be a priest, she thought of sending him to a private school (moreover this was the custom at the time); the school for initiation to ecclesiastical studies in Carignano was chosen.2 Four years later, Alessandro entered the ecclesiastical college run by the Priests of the Congregation of the Mission. It is true that later this boy had a somewhat tormented life, but his affection and esteem for his mother were once again his salvation; having come to himself in the last years of his short life, he died, as we shall see, at peace with God.

As well as looking after her children and giving charitable assistance to the poor and the sick, Rosa also took the most loving care of her parents, especially her mother, who had always suffered from bad health. Rosa’s total dedication to others while day by day she became visibly weaker, made the smile of goodness that she spread around her even sweeter, making people think that she had a superior strength, certainly different from the kind that is born of natural affection.

Lofty gifts of mystical prayer ~ Meanwhile, an array of supernatural gifts were embellishing that generous soul; gifts which Rosa avidly acquired like the precious pearl of the Gospel, sparing nothing nor herself in the service of the kingdom.

Her determined desire to please her Good always made her more anxious for sacrifices: there was no renunciation of natural pleasures, sacrifice or penance known to her that she did not immediately try to put into practice, to give God a tangible proof of her love.

She allowed herself a short rest at night, which she often took stretched out on the bare floorboards; she spent the rest of the time almost constantly in prayer, of which she could never have enough.

“I do not understand”, she wrote a few years later, how “certain good souls who know God so dread suffering and seek every possible way to alleviate it; they do not want to be convinced that it is God’s will and that their souls must pass through this purification to become beautiful” (M 1, 1.p. 79).

So God, as we have mentioned in the previous chapter, granted his humble handmaid exalted gifts of mystical prayer, which opened her mind and inflamed her spirit to sublime outbursts. She herself speaks of the intimate union which absorbed her for hours and hours in her Beloved. She also tells of the lofty knowledge she had about the truth of faith, of the ineffable delights, of the raptures with which her Good deigned to regale her, especially in the secret of her cell, because she had asked and obtained from Jesus that in public he would not allow anything extraordinary to be noticed in her demeanor. These tended to occur on the occasion of great feasts, such as Christmas and Easter, but also frequently on other days, when she had just retired to pray or was receiving Holy Communion. For fear of being betrayed in public by visible emotion, she sometimes had to distract herself from the object of her contemplation and leave the church when the homily was particularly attractive to her spirit (cf. M. 1. 1, pp. 21; 24).Thus in that blessed soul, spiritual life was a real cascade of pearls.

Passive purification ~ However, Rosa certainly could not and did not lack those terrible trials which in mysticism are known as “passive purification”. She tells of them simply, making felt her anguish and the pangs of her spirit, but also singing of the victory she gained over them, ever sustained and comforted by her Beloved. St. John of the Cross, in speaking of these purifications of mystical life calls them “dark nights” and distinguishes the night of the senses, that is the privation of tangible consolations, from the night of the soul, which is an accumulation of sorrows, doubts, remorse, fears and diabolical torments. Now this twofold night very soon descended on Rosa’s soul to sharpen her virtues, the better to prepare her for her nuptials with the Lamb.

Already in 1861, after the Feast of the Immaculate Conception on which she took the vow of poverty, she encountered these trials. “Again”, she wrote, “I am in the midst of tribulations, the worst that can be described. Patience! Oh, how sweet it is to suffer for the love of Jesus, deprived of all consolations! Oh, how much rarer they are continuing to become!” (M1.1, p. 16).

A few months later, a great consolation which she had on Holy Saturday was followed by a terrible storm of doubt: “You have disappeared”, she said to Jesus, “now I find myself on the rough seas, a poor little damaged boat, immersed in the waves: only I cling closely to the anchor of the holy Cross, not to be submerged, and to reach the blessed haven of my Good. Oh! Terrible trials! Everything is over for me, except sufferings! Ah, my Love, it is not that I want to flee suffering and tribulations, no, but my pain at having disgusted you saddens me. Oh, you know well that I do not want to flee suffering, because I would give a thousand lives for you my Good, but oh, the fear of having offended you is the most excruciating pain! Pressed to my breast is my beloved standard of the Cross, but give us the strength to carry it well and to climb the mountain of pain, Calvary, and victorious always, close to you, to die with you, crucified” (M. 1. 1, p. 23).

Thus, among her laments, the fiat learned from Jesus in the agony of Gethsemane brushed Rosa’s lips and so, like him, she was granted the tenuous comfort of a few flashes of light which then gave way to even greater suffering.

Further trials came to add to her dryness and sorrows, temptations and anguish, which in accordance with God’s way accompany the call to higher favors and greater undertakings. In that darkness, Rosa turned with full humility to her spiritual director, Fr. Giuseppe Firpo, but could find no comfort in his response.

“I find no comfort anywhere”, she wrote, “nor is the voice of my director able to give me even the smallest grain of comfort, so that only suffering and torment are my companions. This is what my beloved Jesus wants; may his will be done” (M 1.1, p. 26).

She also felt the pain of doubt about all her past confessions and the devil provoking her to make a general confession, for fear of seeing herself at death’s door surrounded by sins she had not confessed or had improperly declared. Here her director’s adamant “no” and his clear order got the better of the enemy’s suggestions, so that Rosa found peace in obeying him.

However that year was to be memorable in Rosa’s interior life. The unconcealed harassment of the devil became so extreme that Fr. Giuseppe Firpo believed he should have recourse to exorcism, thinking that she was prey to a real obsession; he therefore wished to ask the Archbishop for the faculties. But Rosa begged him to forbear from this, firmly declaring that it was not at all an obsession and, finding it somewhat difficult to convince him, decided to change director; however through prayer she felt dissuaded from doing so.

At last her director was also convinced that these were trials of a different kind; he was still persuaded that Rosa was inwardly guided by a superior light, and that God was acting in a unique way in that chosen soul, enabling her to know the way to take, also by interior voices. Therefore in spring 1864, after six years of experience and attentive examination, he wrote to her to abandon herself totally to the inner impulse she felt. “Concerning the account you give me of your poor spirit”, he wrote in that letter, “I will tell you: oh, how incomprehensible is God’s wisdom, and how many ways does he use to attract to himself the souls who are his beloved brides! You no longer exist; you no longer live, it is your Bridegroom Jesus, your Love, your All, who lives and works in you. You are therefore dead and no longer live, let the One who lives in you dispose all things; in his exalted and loving plans, you must serve him only as the miserable instrument that you are. Once you have completely died in the arms of your Love, you will enjoy that unchangeable peace and patience which is always the same, in prosperity and in adversity, in temptation and in consolation: and in any event, never doubt or mistrust the One who orders all things for his greatest glory… In these holy days when the Church is celebrating the greatest mysteries of the Passion and Death of your crucified Love, who knows what he will require of you? I am sure that he will give you the grace of sharing his suffering with you; but you are already dead, you no longer live, and it is your All who lives in you; may his most holy will be done in you”.3

Rare participation in the Passion ~ These last words of her spiritual director allude to a phenomenon which, it seems she had been experiencing within herself since 1862: that is, the gift of a rare participation in the Savior’s Passion. Now and again she would feel acute pain in the palms of her hands, in the soles of her feet and in her heart. The pains in her heart were different from another pain, caused by the little crucifix which for several years had been tightly bound to her breast and had made a wound that bled, especially when she bent down to wash the floor in the hospitals.

Therefore beneath the modest elegance of the secular clothes which her family’s class imposed upon her, this great woman, wearing all her instruments of penance and tormented by all kinds of austerities, preserved in her heart the treasures of God’s gifts as in a precious alabaster casket; vital and sanctifying gifts which, although they were kept under the veil of the deepest humility could not pass unseen among those who were close to her; the ceaseless fragrance they discreetly exhaled exerted a mysterious fascination upon everyone, even the unbelieving or indifferent who lived beside her. But for good souls, that fragrance was the sign of Christ, which explains how Rosa gradually attracted many distinguished figures of Genoese society who were filled with wonder and timidly curious before that interior greatness, but even more, were eager and confident that she would bring them to the Lord.

Rosa’s fascination and interior greatness ~ Girolamo Custo’s widow radiated that unassuming air of those who are now above all common concerns, people who are distinguished by humility and tenacity and dominated by love and who strive for a superior good. People saw in her a woman so sorely tried by events, so mercilessly beaten by human selfishness, so alone in her young widowhood as she faced her children’s future; and yet they marvelled at her, resigned and even serene as she confronted events with the mysterious resistance of a faith all the sounder the more silent it was, as though it were a quality she had responded to which had been formed long before as the foundation of her spirit. As well as this strength, moreover quite common in Christian widows, in Rosa the truly rare grace of spreading around her the beneficial smile of love and hope was visible, for she seemed eager to approach every kind of unhappiness and turn it into peaceful joy.

This is why many distinguished Genoese ladies who, like Rosa Gattorno, belonged to the Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate, became her intimate friends and faithful disciples. They included in particular: Giulia Calleri, Adele Bensa, Countess Carolina Gavotti, Marchioness Emilia Negrone and Teresa Morasso, who closely shared her intensely charitable life.4

Spiritual friendships in the context of the Frassinetti Associations ~ Rosa opened her beautiful heart to these friendships, but directed the trust put in her to nurturing the desire for Christian perfection in her friends’ hearts.

Several of the letters preserved give us some clues to this constructive communication. Her friends wrote to Rosa as though to a spiritual guide and confided their most intimate secrets to her; they said they were happy to collaborate with her in the humblest works of charity. They are almost all letters from married people, yet they show such dynamism in the service of God and such a desire for perfection that they give rise to a pleasing wonder. Many of these friends were certain that Rosa had received from God the gift to read hearts; for this reason they asked her to show them the negative aspects that might exist in the heart of each one. A cousin with the same name, Rosa Gattorno, Giustino’s daughter, wrote these words: “Among the many benefits which, although so unworthy, I have received from God, I include this one too; to posses your friendship, because it is a truly good friendship and is already striving for the benefit of my poor soul… Yes, you are right, your reprimands are only too correct, and your advice is more than salutary and fitting… I am surprised to see that you read my heart without me speaking to you…”.5

“Dearest Rosa”, another friend wrote to her, “be kind to me, tell me all the sins which I have in my heart and give me a remedy for them, I assure you that you will be doing me the greatest of favors. You penetrate hearts: mine is infected, I need to be healed, but first you must reveal all the rotten things to me …”.6

Yet another, finding herself in difficulty, wrote to her: “I called you hundreds of times; I was about to describe to you all my thoughts, but you, who have the gift of knowing them and of being familiar with them, I need tell you nothing else”.7

However, the confidences of those souls about their common determination to serve God were more frequent.

“Oh if only I had your virtues, your charity and, completely detached from earthly things, were to live in the world like [you]… entirely abandoned in the heart of divine Love! Pray for me, dearest friend, pray the Lord that he deign to uproot all earthly affections from my heart …”.8

However the lady, Giulia Calleri, who wrote these lines, was already well advanced in spiritual life, to the extent that she was happy to cooperate with Rosa in the humblest services to the poor.

“I cannot express”, she added in the same letter, “the pleasure you gave me in admitting me in those days to the service of holy charity. This is a new proof of your kindness, for which I shall always be grateful. Your poor old women send you thousands of blessings, and would like to see their great benefactress soon”. And in another letter, deeply penetrating her great friend’s heart, she exclaimed, “Ah, my dear Rosa! You can tell me to fully carry out the plans of our heavenly Father! Indeed, what is lovelier and holier to you than the sacrifice of a soul who, banning every thought of this world, devotes herself to the service of those who are suffering, and considers all human beings as brothers and sisters in the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus?”.9

These tones of admiration were not an artifice of worldly kindness, but sincere expressions of hearts that beat in unison with the Christian faith; these friends drew great spiritual help and comfort from their contact with Rosa Gattorno’s soul, and were very fond of talking about it.

At the end of 1864, while Rosa was in Milan visiting her daughter Carlotta, she received requests to return promptly to Genoa.

“In your absence”, one of them wrote to her, “which already seems too long to me (for my heart longs for you and my soul needs to be nourished by your holy words), in your absence, I say, your letters are a great comfort to me, for in them your constant resignation and your lively charity shine through”10.

Thus from Rosa’s exemplary life there emanated the beauty of the mortification of Christ, which St. Paul urged us to carry into the world together with our members sanctified by baptism, for the renewal of pagan society. And so other souls, though bound by family ties, were fired with apostolic charity.

“I went to see our Monsignor”, a friend who was the mother of several children wrote to her, “and he consoled me, but he pointed out that in my position I can do nothing… and who knows, he said, whether in time the Lord may dispose of me for his glory. Would that it were so, dearest friend: today the vigil and tomorrow the feast! I truly hunger for charity and have a burning thirst for the good of souls; but circumstances are against my working, and so spiritual hunger and thirst alternate in my spirit and make me groan in this wretched state of mine”11. “Remember me”, the same lady wrote later, “implore God’s mercy for me, a miserable creature, and ask him to put an end – if it is for the good of my soul – to my stifled position, so that I may throw myself with lively ardor into the work for the glory to which I so earnestly aspire”12.

The tone of dozens of letters from Rosa Gattorno’s friends is very similar; they do not stop at the desire to do good, but for the most part they tell of generous works accomplished or in progress, about which they like to inform the one they regard as their teacher: girls in danger to be placed, poor people to be helped, meetings for charitable works, preparations for religious feasts, sacred furnishings for altars and similar works are the subject of this correspondence, in which there always spreads the fragrance of a delicate dedication and of a deep love, so that these souls habitually call one another sisters, even when separated by social standing; they help one another to know themselves and always take leave in the name of Jesus.

When Christ fills a soul with himself, it becomes a balm that gives off the fragrance of life.

Paul says in his second letter to the Corinthians: “For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Cor 2:15).

(1864-1865) Frassinetti’s Pious Unions — Enrollment in the Daughters of Mary Immaculate and other associations — Rule of the Pious Union of the New Ursulines: President of the Daughters of Mary at Frassinetti’s request — Mediation for the approval of the Rule and extraordinary enlightenment on the corrections to be made.

Frassinetti’s Pious Unions ~ The presence and activity of God’s Spirit in a soul are witnessed by its consonance with the Church’s way of understanding. Now the Catholic Church, from the very beginning, was a wise coordinator of forces and took care to inspire and promote the most varied associations, especially among lay people, foreseeing their abilities and tastes and offering adequate responses to their needs, in accordance with the times and moments.

This group activity is a feature of the Church, since she alone has been able to coordinate ideas and sentiments in every epoch in such a way as to attract to her projects in wonderful harmony people of every race and culture, whose contributions are all the more effective when they stem from their freely given dedication and are not imposed upon them. The result is an almost comprehensive network of institutions through which the living Gospel flows to the ends of the world, everywhere retaining its eternal youth.

The multiplicity of these groups and the apparent inconsistency of some of them should not therefore arouse any surprise other than at the conquering tenacity of God’s kingdom.

Thus in mid-19th century Genoa, many religious associations flourished; they were founded precisely to increase and revive the practice of faith and to remedy the disorders caused by the recent revolutions, as well as those caused every day by the political upheavals which spread anticlericalism and aversion to the papacy. It was necessary to reawaken the sense of piety and solidarity in their most varied forms, to give life to charitable initiatives, to spread the Christian teaching, and at the same time to defend the patrimony of revelation in accordance with the Magisterium of the Roman Pontiff.

Rosa Gattorno clearly foresaw this situation. Full of esteem for the sodalities then being founded by good priests, she took a generous part in them; in offering to become a member, she also had an opportunity to meet people of great faith who immediately became aware of her deep spirit, and became more than friends, sisters.

As for the pious unions for the exercise of devotion, Eucharistic adoration was particularly dear to Rosa, which is why she could be seen diligently praying in the Metropolitan Church of San Lorenzo, in the Church of Rimedio and elsewhere, as was discovered from the many invitation cards which she jealously preserved. She was not satisfied with the hours prescribed for her, usually around midday, but chose other times for her devotion, finding immense joy in remaining before the tabernacle.

In this regard she had one rather strange adventure but which had a happy outcome. Finding herself free, as we believe, from her children whom she had settled in boarding schools, she willingly obeyed the impulses of her soul. So one evening, as she was passing a church and feeling more eager than usual to remain for a while with Jesus in the Sacrament, she tried to enter it, but found the door locked. She hesitated a moment on the threshold of uncertainty when, it is not known how, the door swung open for her; so she went in, closing it behind her. Prostrate before her Lord, she was so deeply immersed in prayer that she was unconscious of time passing. The next morning, when the sacristan came in to open up the church and found a woman there, he was quite distressed; but Rosa said to him immediately, “Don’t worry, don’t be alarmed, I am Mrs. Gattorno. I wanted to do some adoration and yesterday evening I came in and I closed the door behind me”. The sacristan, who must have known her, was satisfied and said nothing more.1

Rosa found an immense field for the apostolate in other associations whose heart and soul was Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti,2 the very active Prior of Santa Sabina since 1839. A cultured and intelligent man, practical, brave and tireless, he strove to spread goodness in every way, but mainly through the press and his associations. Collaborating with another excellent priest, Fr. Sturla, in 1832 he founded the “Ecclesiastical Congregation of Bl. Leonardo of Porto Maurizio”, which was all the more useful to the Genoese clergy the more it was opposed by the liberals.

Enrollment in the Daughters of Mary Immaculate and in other associations ~ Two societies founded by Frassinetti are of special interest in our history: the “Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Most Holy Immaculate” and the “Pious Association for the Preservation and Development of the Faith”.

The Daughters of Mary were established in 1856. The first idea of this institution came into being in about 1852 in the town of Mornese, a small town of the Monferrato district in the Diocese of Acqui, through the efforts of the 18-year old Angela Maccagno. She did not simply conceive of a group of pious people with a devotion to Mary Most Holy, but of a form of religious life in the world. In agreement with her confessor, Fr. Domenico Pestarino, the young woman compiled a draft of the Rule which he sent to Frassinetti, his mentor, to be corrected and possibly modified. Frassinetti postponed the task for two years and in 1855 drafted the Rule of the Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Most Holy Immaculate along the lines of the rule he had received. He then sent it to Mornese where a first group of young women founded the Pious Union on the Sunday after the Feast of the Immaculate Conception. Among them was Maria Domenica Mazzarello, later foundress of the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, with St. John Bosco.

Bishop Modesto Contratto Cappuccino of Acqui approved the above-mentioned Rule for his diocese on 20 May 1857.

However, on 16 August in the previous year, Fr Giuseppe Frassinetti had founded the Pious Union in his own parish, Santa Sabina in Genoa, and for this occasion had given the said Rule to the printers, but limiting the number of copies so that the Rule would be kept secret until it was definitively divulged.3

The Pious Union founded by Frassinetti should not be confused with the association known throughout the world by the name of the Daughters of Mary, aggregated to its first base in Rome, Sant’Agnese. This Union was founded at least ten years later and had a simpler rule of life, suited to ordinary girls. Instead, Frassinetti’s Pious Union had higher aims.

Its members resolved to honor the most holy Virgin in her purity, abstaining from all sins, even venial. In his other institutions, Frassinetti was also a fervent supporter of this struggle against sin and relied upon the solid structure of St. Alphonsus Liguori.4

This approach showed his priestly courage and the serious attitude of those he called to join his associations. In fact, he directed the members in this lofty religious practice to teach them, in a certain sense, to live the evangelical counsels, in so far of course as secular life would permit; they received daily communion and practized mutual fraternal correction, and undertook works of mercy and a very practical apostolate in their families and milieus.

Unmarried women were admitted by preference, but young widows of good will who had decided to live in continence were also accepted.5

So Rosa willingly put her name down, and found herself in the company of other excellent ladies.

It is not surprising that although this association consisted of rather small groups in every parish, it spread rapidly in Genoa and the suburbs, forming a chosen band of active souls. San Torpete became the center of the whole Pious Union and Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti himself presided over it. He made it amazingly lively, so that other parish groups also drew vitality from it. Indeed, Rosa frequented the San Torpete center with her friend Isabella Lamba Doria who was then president. She took an active part in its various works and very soon was not only admired for her rich spirituality but also for her organisational capacities in charitable works, so that in February 1864, as we shall see subsequently, she was asked by Frassinetti to accept the presidency of this Pious Union.

The regular assemblies, at which the directors and local presidents imparted the appropriate instruction and established the tasks to be undertaken for the subsequent month, contributed to the members’ spiritual formation.

Then every year spiritual retreats were held to fortify the members and to open new horizons to people of good will. These courses of spiritual exercises were so intensive that their method might seem surprising or excessive in our day; as has been learned from the invitation cards kept by Rosa, each retreat lasted for eight whole days and was held in one or other of the religious houses under the guidance of an able preacher, while each participant could only bring with her the booklet of the Imitation of Christ and the well-known course of Spiritual Exercises by Fr. Vigitello. Rosa Gattorno helped prepare these retreats.

As well as the Unions of the Daughters of Mary, the “Pious Association in Honor of Mary Immaculate for the Preservation and Development of the Catholic Faith”, founded by Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti in 1851 was also flourishing in Genoa. At the first the sodality consisted of men only, who made a special effort to spread good books; but it soon had a feminine branch and combined various charitable works under a common administration. The feminine branch held its meetings in the oratory of Sant’Ambrogio, and was sometimes honored by the presence of Archbishop Charvaz on whom it directly depended. According to the various social needs of the time, in addition to a good quality press, the members promoted other specific works for the instruction of youth in the Christian doctrine; they also supported the perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament and saw to protecting young women at risk.

Rosa Gattorno took part in all these initiatives. In January 1865, when the commission for the above-mentioned young women had just been formed, she agreed to be its vice-president, since her good heart and capacity for the successful management and administration of this delicate and beneficial work were widely recognized.

Since during that period Rosa was in Milan with her daughter Carlotta whom she had placed in the Institute for Deaf Mutes, her election was communicated to her by letter.6

When she returned to Genoa, she threw herself into her work with great enthusiasm: she wrote a circular letter to wealthy citizens7 to collect the necessary funds and immediately set about saving from danger the young girls of the city and its environs, turning to her friends for help.8

Rule of the Pious Union of the New Ursulines: President of the Daughters of Mary at Frassinetti’s request ~ Rosa found she had an important role in this institution which had previously already been part of her apostolic activity; in fact, since 1861 her concern for it emerges from her relationships with friends and with her confessor, Fr. Giuseppe Firpo.9

In 1863, Frassinetti rewrote the Rule of the Daughters of Mary, and realizing that it had a concrete affinity with the work of St. Ursula founded by St. Angela Merici, he called it “Rule of the Pious Union of the New Ursulines Daughters of St. Mary Immaculate under the protection of St. Ursula and St. Angela Merici”. This Rule was approved on 5 February 1863 by Bishop Giacomo Filippo Gentile of Novara, and printed that same year in Genoa with the approval of the ecclesiastical authorities. Frassinetti would obviously also have liked to have the approval of his Bishop, Andrea Charvaz10. Being unable to obtain it, he turned to Fr. Firpo to convince Rosa to intervene with her mediation, and begged her to accept to be president of the sodality in Genoa. Rosa Gattorno was in fact highly esteemed by the Archbishop and beloved in the milieu of the associations in which she worked. She accepted this mission and visited the Prelate, presenting the Rule to him and begging him to deign to approve it. As soon as he saw it he said that he knew it and did not feel like approving it unless some modifications were made. He also expressed a certain doubt about Frassinetti’s willingness to make the corrections.

Mediation for the approval of the Rule and extraordinary enlightenments on the corrections to be made ~ Rosa immediately dispelled his doubts, insisting on asking him what amendments he desired.

“I would like you”, answered the Archbishop, “to guess what I dislike in this Rule”.

It is easy to imagine Rosa’s astonishment and dismay at his suggestion. “Go”, he added, “and return when you have made your notes”. And he ended the talk.

At home, mulling it over in her room, Rosa placed the Rule at the foot of the large crucifix before which she normally prayed, saying: “My Love, if I must obey, you give me suggestions”. And she thought no more about it that day.

Late at night, Rosa knelt to pray before her crucifix as usual; she took it in her arms together with the manuscript of that Rule and prayed to know the points which were causing problems.

In this way she discovered that the Archbishop had been right to refuse his approval and clearly saw the modifications required. Having thanked her Good, she sat down at her table, and leafing through the booklet, wrote on a sheet of paper the observations which had come to her mind. When she had finished she felt a great sense of relief, folded the sheets and then again took her crucifix in her arms and continued her prayers with thanksgiving.

The next day, Rosa went to ask Fr Frassinetti whether he would agree to remove what the Archbishop did not like about the Rule, promising that on this condition it would be approved. The holy priest, as can be expected, declared that he would be very pleased to accept any proposal of amendment.

Although Rosa had received extraordinary enlightenments in prayer, she judged it prudent to consult trustworthy people about the corrections, as can be seen from an unfinished letter of 9 April 1864 which because of the similarity of handwriting can be attributed to Adele Castelnuovo of Turin, who was a friend of hers.11

She returned to the Archbishop towards the end of June, presenting to him the requested observations, but not mentioning the enlightenment she had received. The prelate was astonished on reading those notes and declared that she had guessed his thoughts exactly, for those were precisely the corrections he had hoped for12.

Some months later, at the Archbishop’s order, Rosa made a fair copy of those corrections, as can be seen from Fr. Giuseppe Firpo’s letter of 16 October 186413. Archbishop Charvaz then gave his verbal approval to the Rule in question14, to Fr. Frassinetti’s great joy; for the Decree of approval, however, they had to wait until the following year15. While waiting for the required corrections to be submitted to the Bishop, some of the Daughters of Mary lived, probably from 1863, according to the Rule of the New Ursulines, as appears from the correspondence between the Marchioness Lamba Doria and Mother Rosa.

“Here are a few lines”, Miss Redabue wrote in May 1864, “to let you know about that prodigal Ursuline who has left the fold […]. Meanwhile I do not forget my good sisters and my dear Superior”16.

And again: “… give my affectionate greetings to the three dearest Ursuline sisters and companions of that dear retreat in Sampierdarena”17.

With Archbishop Charvaz’s verbal consent to Frassinetti’s Rule, an important period in Rosa Gattorno’s life also came to a close; we shall see later how this event was the occasion of a very great gift which God bestowed on his faithful servant, and which was to be the beginning of a history of blessings, the opening of new and unforeseeable horizons of charity.
