(1864-1866) A year of the strictest fasting and the first inspiration — Rosa’s inner conflict — Letter to Archbishop Charvaz and conversations with the Archbishop — Mgr. Magnasco’s Rule — Journey to Rome and private audience with Pius IX — Offering of her children to the Sorrowful Virgin in San Marcello al Corso.

A year of the strictest fasting and the first inspiration ~ In Rosa’s spiritual life two elements, which more or less always accompany holiness but in her assumed quite unique and superior proportions, were becoming ever clearer: prayer and physical participation in the Lord’s Passion. Grace urged her on these paths, because God wanted to pour extraordinary gifts into that privileged soul and make her an instrument of great mercy for suffering humanity.

From what can be deduced from the Memorie, at the beginning of 1864, to be precise in February, Rosa concluded a year of continuous fasting which she had been inspired to undertake by “her Good” and to which her spiritual director had consented.

She had spent that year without taking any other food or drink than a piece of bread and a sip of water every twenty-four hours, and had taken this meagre refreshment beside a skull and at night.1

Yet throughout the year she never lacked strength for her busy work with charitable activities and the associations, nor for her other religious and penitential practices. In this she felt a clear divine intervention and deduced that something great was being prepared. Indeed, at the end of that year, she received two exceptional gifts. On New Year’s eve, she had felt enlightened in prayer to correct the Rule of the Daughters of Mary (New Ursulines), in accordance with the wishes of the Archbishop of Genoa, as we have seen. But on that precise occasion she also quite unexpectedly received her greatest and most precious gift: the first plan for the Institute which she was called to found.

While correcting Frassinetti’s Rule, clasping her crucifix to her breast and thanking the crucified Christ for the illumination she had been given, Rosa felt her mind filled anew with the vivid idea for another Rule. In it was outlined the foundation of a new work, whose wonderful identity and distinction from the others in which she was wholeheartedly involved was clearly defined. She instantly jotted down her thoughts in accordance with the impulse she felt at that moment, folded the page and put it in a safe place; then she continued to pray and thought no more about it.

Several days passed and she told no one, not even when she had to see Archbishop Charvaz for the approval of Frassinetti’s Rule.

Rosa’s inner conflict ~ However, it was not long before she felt an impelling need and a certain consternation that prompted her to reveal what had been suggested to her so mysteriously during the second part of her prayer.

She finally decided to turn again to her Good and in compensation received the call to that new life which was to take her from the world and make her a humble and great servant of God’s Work.

Indeed, the more she prayed about it, the more she felt she should show the Archbishop what she had written that night: God wanted that work which was to be an important one; she herself was called to create it.

The first moments of a vocation are truly ineffable: who could describe the emotions that accompany the soul’s impulses? Surprise at a treasure discovered, at the revelation of new, unimaginable horizons; and everything melts away before the gift which enriches the soul. But poor human nature is sometimes so comfortable with its own securities that the unforeseen and unpremeditated new things give rise to dismay: it is then that nature struggles with grace.

Since the plan for the work required total detachment from her family, and especially from her children, as well as the duty to undertake such important and burdensome tasks, Rosa felt deep dismay and an extreme reluctance to obey. The thought of her children and her elderly parents to whom she was bound by the most tender love caused a lump to rise in her throat, and she felt she was dying.

“Oh, my God”, she exclaimed, “I feel that my strength is not equal to doing what you command; I feel myself dying only to think of it… I have not the courage, I can’t!” (M. 2, pp. 11-12).

Even these moments of weakness were precious; they served to make her experience the nothingness of her nature before God’s great enterprises and to prevent her from attempting to cheat God of his glory by attributing some merit to herself in the future events. Rosa clearly perceived her role as a pure instrument in the hands of the Artisan; so throughout her life she would call the Institute by the one name: “Work of God”.

Letter to Archbishop Charvaz and conversations with the Archbishop ~ Consequently several months passed before Rosa resolved to speak. At last she unburdened herself, but under secrecy, to her confessor, Fr. Giuseppe Firpo. As soon as he heard of it, he harshly reprimanded her for hesitating so much and so long, enjoining her to speak to the Archbishop. Rosa burst into tears, obtained permission to put it all down in writing again first: to recount that is, what had happened to her and what dispositions had so perplexed her. The priest went carefully over this account which accompanied her plan for the new Rule, and with fatherly concern suggested corrections and the way to present what she had written to the Archbishop.2

When Archbishop Charvaz received Rosa Gattorno’s writings, it was already autumn 1864; so the anguish caused by the conflict between God’s pressing call and the love, equally sacred, for her children and elderly parents had been tormenting her motherly heart for about eight months; for her conscience would have liked to be able to reconcile these two loves in the sacrosanct duty of caring for her children, hence in the conviction either that it was the task of others to execute the plan, or that it might all be a deception.

When the Archbishop had read Rosa’s account he had her summoned.

“I do not know”, she says, “how to describe my confusion and sorrow; I trembled like a leaf. I was so agitated that in arriving at his feet, there was no [way] I could speak. He realized the state I was in, and knowing my temperament, limited himself to saying that he would see that the Lord’s orders were carried out and that the Work would certainly be a very beautiful one. All that was needed was to weave the internal regulations into that [Rule]. Overcome with confusion, I said yes to everything” (M. 2, pp. 13-14).

Mgr. Magnasco’s Rule ~ Having agreed in this way, Rosa was dismissed from the audience, but after a few days she was recalled by the Archbishop who told her he had designated Mgr. Magnasco, Penitentiary of the Metropolitan Chapter, to help her to compile the desired rule. Thus Rosa was several times to find herself together with Monsignor Penitentiary for this purpose; but she humbly preferred to leave everything to him, despite her inner conviction that his ideas did not correspond with the plan she had received from God. This was confirmed by the fact that the Rule, which the Monsignor subsequently presented to the Archbishop, did not please him and was not approved.

In the meantime, at the beginning of December 1864 Rosa went to Milan to spend some time with her daughter Carlotta at the Institute for Deaf-Mutes. Fr. Giuseppe Firpo, believing that Mgr. Magnasco’s work was good, was expecting its approval from day to day; but in vain. Therefore, he wrote to Rosa in Milan expressing his somewhat disappointed surprise.

“Nothing so far, Canon Magnasco tells me with regard to the practical note: perhaps one has not been sent yet. Then every day I pray for you, so that your Jesus will give you strength and help you to respond to his call…” (he wrote these words on 15 December). And on 23 December he added: “nothing so far, the Canon Penitentiary told me, with regard to the documentation: I myself do not know what to make of this silence”.3

But Rosa well knew the reason for that silence and she was not in a hurry.

Returning to Genoa the following January (1865), she was summoned by Bishop Charvaz and questioned about the Rule drafted by Mgr. Magnasco; the Archbishop wanted to know whether she liked his articles. Rosa was confused, and in her embarrassment did not want to express an opinion; however, at the Archbishop’s insistence, she made it plain that her opinion was unfavorable, saying that some points of that Rule did not seem to her to be in conformity with the inspiration she had received from God.

“I don’t like them either” the Archbishop replied, and wanted Rosa to mark the passages she did not like with her fingernail, so that Mgr. Magnasco would not notice the corrections. Rosa took the fascicle home, did what she had been ordered and then, accompanying it with a letter, forwarded it to the Archbishop.4

All this happened in spring 1865, when Rosa thought it appropriate to abandon Fr. Giuseppe Firpo’s direction. For some time she had been rather reserved with him, limiting herself almost solely to confession; in May she deserted him completely.5

It is supposed that the reason for this decision may have been that in the meantime she had met Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, famed for his holiness, and that she had begun to take his advice.6

However, we know that at the beginning of 1867, when she had already founded the Daughters of St. Anne, Rosa returned to her filial relationship with her former director.7

Journey to Rome and private audience with Pius IX ~

Meanwhile the Archbishop of Genoa had not given up the idea of a foundation which he believed would be providential and most beneficial to his diocese.

Therefore at the beginning of the autumn, he summoned Rosa Gattorno to tell her that Mgr. Magnasco’s Rule needed so many corrections that it would be better to set it aside; preparations should be made to rewrite it. Rosa, getting wind of the Prelate’s aims, felt in her heart a harsh conflict of different sentiments and tried to shield herself from this duty. Taking up the question of principle, she remarked that it might perhaps have been inspired by the devil, for it seemed impossible to her8 that God could ask her to abandon her loved ones, especially her children.

“Oh not that”, she repeated, “it will never be, I cannot leave them!” And she asked the Archbishop if, before thinking about the Rule, he would permit her to consult the Holy Father Pius IX (cf. M.2, p. 17).

How she came to this bold suggestion we are not given to know; perhaps it was on the advice of those following the matter or perhaps it was prompted by a desperate appeal from her motherly heart, since she hoped, as she wrote later, to be released from that obedience and to make others responsible for founding the Work. Once again the weakness of her nature had got the upper hand, so that next to the greatness of God’s gifts, God would fully manifest human poverty.

“The Good Pastor”, Rosa wrote, “granted me to go to Rome and equipped me with letters of recommendation. It seemed to me that I had already won the victory. Never, I repeated to myself, will Pope Pius IX allow a mother to leave her children… Ah no, my Beloved, he will never permit it! Your Vicar will give me peace and relief in this cruel battle…” (M. 2, pp. 17-18)

When Rosa told her parents of her desire to go to Rome they consented with pleasure, certain of doing something that pleased her and, perhaps, happily surprised to see their daughter at last taking some respite. Her father, Francesco, prepared letters of recommendation to his Roman acquaintances and reserved places on one of the best steamers for her and her traveling companion, Teresa Porta, the widow of Mr. Morasso, who was one of Rosa’s great friends. The voyage from Genoa to Rome had to be made by sea as far as Livorno at that time because only the stretch between Livorno and Civitavecchia was connected by railway. Rosa left Genoa on 30 December 1865.8 Her father himself accompanied her to the steamer and, with fatherly concern, warmly commended her to the captain. The voyage started well, but at about 2.00 a.m., a heavy thud shook the whole ship and alarmed the crew: one of the paddles of the steamer had broken and there was a serious risk of being stranded at sea. Rosa, hearing of the engineer’s desperation, was so frightened that she fainted. She was unconscious for so long as to distress her companion and make the captain deeply worried, after Mr. Gattorno’s insistent recommendations. She came to when the damage to the ship had already been repaired and it was once more on its way. Her friend wanted to restore her with some cordial; but Rosa refused, so as not to be deprived of Holy Communion which she was intending to receive in Livorno

.

They reached the port at midday precisely on Sunday, 31 December. The two ladies immediately went to church; Rosa took communion and heard Mass after which she was unable to eat anything but two small cold potatoes, because her stomach balked at anything else.

They resumed the journey by train to Civitavecchia and arrived at 5.0 a.m. They then continued on to Rome by diligence and arrived there at daybreak on the same day, 1 January 1866.

There had been some upsetting incidents on the journey, but Rosa was consoled by compensations as great as the former had been painful. On Christmas Eve, shortly before setting out, after a bitter sorrow that had afflicted her for many weeks, she had been granted an unexpected interior illumination concerning the important matters she had to deal with in those days. And during the journey from Livorno to Civitavecchia, although exhausted by the hardships she had had to bear, she received divine favors.

The day of her arrival and the following day were devoted to rest and to receiving the various persons notified of her visit to Rome. In the meantime, the private audience requested with the Holy Father Pius IX was arranged for 3 January, Wednesday, at 5.00 o’clock in the afternoon.

“Oh, that day”, Rosa writes, “I shall never forget it! My hopes vanished and the sharpest knife came to wound me deeply” (M. 2, p. 23).

She had had the Rule inspired during prayer before her beloved Crucified Christ presented to the Pope some time before. When she was ushered in to the audience, she prostrated herself at the feet of the Vicar of Christ with the deepest emotion; Pius IX gave her a fatherly blessing, took her hand to help her rise and told her immediately that he had read her Rule and had found it truly beautiful; and that therefore she should not hesitate to put it into practice. Rosa, deeply impressed by these words, again threw herself onto her knees and in tears pointed out to the Holy Father that she had elderly parents who would not bear her leaving them and two children who were still young and in need of her motherly care.

“It is not relevant”, Pius IX answered her, “This is what God wants”.

“Oh no, Your Holiness,” Rosa added, “According to the Holy Gospel, God will ask me to account for my children!” (M. 2, p. 15). Tears stifled the words in her throat and she could not continue.

“Now”, the Pope then said rather severely, “if you do not do what God wants of you, you will feel remorse for the rest of your life; your conscience will prick you and you will never have peace again” (M. 2, p. 25).

The Vicar of Christ’s serious words of wisdom reminded Rosa of the supreme rights of the Creator over the affections and inclinations of his creatures; the wounds of her Savior crucified for the world’s salvation once again seemed to remind her of the voice of the Pope threatening her with terrible remorse for a refusal which could henceforth no longer be justifiable. So, her heart breaking, she bowed her head and answered: “Your Holiness, I want to do God’s will”. From that fiat was born the new Institute which would later be called the “Daughters of St. Anne”. Pius IX was inspired to add: “This Institute will spread in all the parts of the world as swiftly as the flight of the dove. God will take care of your children: you must think of God and his work” (M. 2, pp. 25-26).

Then, inviting Rosa to his desk, he gave her two photographs of himself with a few words of dedication and comforted her in a fatherly way, saying: “Your father and mother will resign themselves, you will lack nothing, you will be given everything. As for those [Rules]”, he added, “I will keep them; you will, of course, have another copy and will see to giving them the proper form for a rule” (M. 2, p. 26).

Moreover, showing that the Archbishop of Genoa had told him everything, he asked Rosa whether she had also received in inspiration the name she had given to the Institute, since he had read in her Rule: “Daughters of Mary Immaculate”.9

Rosa answered that she had not received its title from on high but had chosen it because, since she was deeply devoted to Mary Immaculate and a Daughter of Mary, she wanted the religious of the new Institute to be known by that name.

“Good”, the Pope continued, “for the time being let it stand: but when you receive the true name, if God wants it to be something else, you will obey and immediately give it the name the Lord assigns to it” (M. 2, p. 34).

Rosa, leaving her hand in the Pontiff’s who was holding it tightly in a paternal clasp, could only say: “Yes, Your Holiness, I will obey you” (M. 2, p. 34).

Finally, Pius IX blessed her and dismissed her.

Offering of her children to the Sorrowful Virgin in San Marcello al Corso ~ So Rosa Gattorno came away from that audience with the serious responsibility of the new foundation and returned to the house where she was staying where several people were awaiting her. Quickly taking leave of them, she retired to her room and gave vent to the fullness of her feelings. She spent the whole night in tears and prayers; she had no further reluctance to making the sacrifice because God’s will had been manifested, but her soul was pierced by the sharpest sword. The holocaust of her mother’s heart was necessary so that grace would fashion a new heart within her: a heart as large as the new family that was to call her “Mother”, as would the hordes of unfortunate people whom her Institute would rescue.

As soon as it was light, she went to the Servites’ Church of San Marcello al Corso, and there, prostrate before the altar of the Sorrowful Virgin, in floods of tears she reiterated all her pain and anguish at the separation from her children, remembering how Mary too had suffered from being separated from Jesus when he stayed in the temple.

“Mary, my Mother”, she said, “what knife is this? It pierces me to the very marrow of my bones!” (M. 2, p. 37).

While she was praying, she was absorbed in deep contemplation: she dried her tears and immense peace flooded her heart. When she came to herself she found that her heart had completely changed: it was filled with a generous strength that knew no bounds; so before that same altar she offered her children to God, protesting that she was ready to do his divine will and promising that she would never complain or be tempted to go back on her word. This was the conclusion of the two years engaged in the battle between frail humanity and the power of grace and, possibly, of an excessive sentiment of her own smallness before an arduous and unknown undertaking.

The struggle had opened her eyes wider to the way she could entrust herself to her God.

In her humility and littleness Rosa had approached the different levels of the ecclesiastical hierarchy even to the point of coming to Rome, to the feet of the Supreme Pontiff. Here, in contact with the vestiges of ancient greatness impressed in the heart of the Church, her visits to the great basilicas and relics of the Passion and the martyrs must have nourished her with great ideas and given her a fresh impetus for the purpose to which the Vicar of Christ had directed her.

Consequently it was a Sorrowful Way, but an eminently providential one; it led Rosa Gattorno to the very sources of spirituality so that her new charitable work would spring from them.

Rosa and her companion remained in Rome for 25 days, as can be seen from the stamps on the permit from the Spanish Consulate in Genoa. (AF-SA A.1.4). They were begged to stay on by many Bishops and Cardinals, who also offered Rosa many gifts for the chapel of the first house she would open: she received chalices, ciboriums, chasubles and other church ornaments and vestments which were all shipped to Genoa. Among the other gifts was a beautiful picture of the passing of St. Joseph which is still kept in the little chapel of the house in Piacenza. But the gift dearest to Rosa’s heart was a hand-written rescript from Pius IX granting her the faculties to keep the Blessed Sacrament at home (Rescript of 22 January 1866, AFSA B.3.81).

It also seems that in those days a sad and serious secret was revealed to Rosa which filled her with affliction: the fall of Rome which was to occur a few years later, and the devastation of Paris by the incendiaries10.

Note that this was in January 1866, when, by human reckoning, the Franco-Prussian war could not be foreseen, and much less the defeat of the French under German pressure, with the consequent abdication of Napoleon III and the grim revolution of the Paris “Commune”, during which there were massacres and fires caused by the notorious “petroleurs”.

As for Italy, there were indeed vague forecasts of war with Austria for the conquest of the Veneto, as happened six months later, but no one was even remotely thinking of an advance on Rome11.

Undoubtedly Rosa was to draw from these facts too a clearer idea of her work. Charity towards one’s neighbor was not to be concerned only with the body, and the new religious Congregation did not intend to be just any form of service of God. The new Institute was a living and concrete response to invading secularism and to the real situations of poverty of that difficult and troubled period of history; it was the small yet great “yes” of a humble, generous woman of Genoa which gave rise to a new evangelical reality marked by the most genuine and gratuitous charity.

The nascent Institute was to reach out not only to the sick in their homes or to girls in danger, but in the future to embrace the whole of suffering and marginalized humanity with the great and most tender heart of Rosa Gattorno, who had but one great love: her Good, and him crucified.

Fr. Luigi Cogrossi ~ If it is true that in life nothing can be left to chance, for believers it is equally certain that the mysterious hand of Providence disposes events and circumstances in such a way that everything is arranged to reach a predetermined goal.

Already in 1864, as has been said, Rosa had met a rather enigmatic figure in Genoa, a certain Fr. Luigi Cogrossi1 and, impressed by his aura of fame for holiness, had chosen him as her spiritual director. Indeed, it was probably Cogrossi who organized her journey, and he certainly accompanied Rosa and Teresa Porta on the occasion of the visit and to the audience with the Supreme Pontiff Pius IX.2

Cogrossi introduced the future Foundress to many important figures in Roman society including some eminent ecclesiastics, and advised the Mother to start her foundation in Piacenza where he had priest friends who would be able to help her.

Fr. Iriarte says in his previously cited book: “Mother Rosa’s awareness of her charism was clarified to her, and I would say grew in her gradually. Without her realizing it, God made her mature through a series of liberations from her conditioning, which might subsequently have prevented her from full collaboration in the divine plan”.3

The city of Piacenza, perhaps not completely unknown to Rosa,4 thus became to all intents and purposes the first cradle of the Institute, the center of the outreach of the splendid and most generous charitable activity of Rosa Gattorno, who, it is certain, was unable at that time to depend on human wealth and relied solely on the power of the One who had wanted the work and was to guide its miraculous growth.

Negotiations for the foundation in Piacenza ~ It was also Cogrossi who suggested, as has been mentioned, that Rosa contact two excellent priests in Piacenza, the Chiappini Canons whom she immediately recognized as priests “with an excellent spirit”. When she had revealed her ideas to them and recounted her journey to Rome, the Chiappinis were immediately convinced that they had to do with a soul of God, motivated by him to do great things.

The plan for the new Institute fired them with such enthusiasm that they naturally offered to help with it. So they insisted that Rosa Gattorno start the work in Piacenza; they praised this city as being peaceful and good and governed by a very zealous Bishop who looked kindly upon charitable works; they were pleased to volunteer to help her and undertook to search for temporary premises for it without delay. Later it would be easy to purchase a building among the many on sale during that time of political turmoil.

Rosa gratefully accepted their offer of help, but did not want to make any decisions as she thought it would take some time before she could start the foundation. Consequently, having relegated the matter to the back of her mind, she went on to Genoa where knottier problems were waiting to be solved: the choice of her first companions, the search for the necessary means for the foundation, the leave-taking from her family.

She said nothing to her parents, who welcomed her festively, about the true purpose of her journey to Rome. Instead she went to an audience with the Archbishop, told him precisely of how things had gone with the Supreme Pontiff, but said nothing of her stay in Piacenza and the talks she had had there.

Archbishop Charvaz, pleased to see his desire confirmed in Pius IX’s command, encouraged Rosa to undertake God’s Work immediately and already rejoiced at seeing his Genoa enriched with the new religious family from which he hoped for so much good. Therefore in dismissing the generous woman he concluded: “So let us set to work”.

While these thoughts were uppermost in her mind and she was considering what was to be done, Rosa received a letter from Piacenza which astounded her. Fr. Luigi Cogrossi had already spoken to the Vicar General and obtained his permission for the foundation; indeed, the Vicar, in agreement with Bishop Ranza of Piacenza, wrote to her in the following terms:

“Most distinguished Madam,

The Very Reverent Father Luigi Cogrossi has told me about your project of founding a religious congregation of women devoted to works of Christian charity; this project deserves full collaboration; but my prelate, extremely busy with the work of his enormous diocese with whose demands he can scarcely cope, can give you no help: however, he is not opposed to the plan, and indeed will rejoice in the good it will do; times are sad and most unfortunate and seem contrary to foundations; but if the work is desired by the Lord, it will be crowned with happy success and will correspond with your most pious desires. I assure you of my esteem and veneration,

I remain, most distinguished Madam,

Your most humble and respectful servant,

Canon Prevost ANGELO TESTA

Vicar General5 Piacenza, 7 February 1866”.

The Chiappini Canons also told her that they had already found a comfortable house at a good price, but they wanted a prompt reply in order to draw up the contract. How could she decide? Rosa renewed her offering to God and made the definitive break; as she herself says, feeling endowed with strength, she answered the two priests that they should indeed arrange for the house: she would move in with several friends in early March (cf. M. 2, p. 43).

Once this commitment had been made, she had to think about how to put into practice, and she had only a few weeks before the appointed time; but now nothing could restrain her. Silently and unbeknown to her parents, she gathered together her things with the other necessities and what had arrived from Rome, and through her trusted serving women had them sent to Piacenza. A few days later she left with her usual friend Teresa Morasso. She said not a word to her parents, letting them think that she was going to Milan to visit her daughter; instead her goal was Piacenza. She saw and quickly arranged the rented rooms with the furniture and other items that had already arrived; then after a few days she returned to Genoa.

Thus the Lord’s little house was ready,6 and there was no lack of generous daughters to live in it: Teresa Porta, the widow of Mr. Morasso, Rosa’s well-known friend; Giovanna Bixio, the widow of Mr. Marchi of Genoa, who had been staying in Fr. Giuseppe Firpo’s house; Angiola De Grossi of Genoa; Anna Grasso of Pontedecimo; Luigia Rocca, the widow of Mr. Ferro, of Genoa.

They were also joined by Amalia Custo, Rosa’s sister-in-law, (we do not know for certain whether she wanted to be a member of the new religious family or merely to stay with them as a guest).7

Taking leave of the Archbishop of Genoa and her parents ~ So it was only a question of leaving; but the most serious difficulties arose at precisely that moment. The Mother herself recounts in her Memorie: “I told my confessor all I had done and he was somewhat surprised [about this]; he too feared for my parents and for the Archbishop. I plucked up my courage and told everything to the Archbishop who was loath for me to leave Genoa and told me that he was not giving me his approval […]. I spent the saddest days; my confessor also disapproved of the decision I had taken” (M. 2, pp. 46-47).

At this point she could only have recourse to prayer, asking the Lord for illumination: she prayed prostrate upon the ground before her crucifix, examining the events that had occurred and especially her stay in Piacenza on her return from Rome. Here she had listened to the advice of enlightened priests; was this enough to understand the divine will, or had it all been an illusion?

So she begged the Lord for an answer, and as a sure sign that it was right for her to go to Piacenza, she asked that the Archbishop might change his mind and agree with her choice and give her his blessing; she would not have gone ahead with her intention against his will. A simple and straightforward prayer to which an inner voice replied: “it is entirely my will that this should happen; be at peace, everything will be ironed out” (M. 2, p. 47).

Rosa soon returned to visit the Archbishop and indeed found him pacified; he at last approved that she start the work in Piacenza and blessed her, but nevertheless expressed his sorrow at her departure. He did not want to accept her resignation from the post of President of the Associations whose active leader she had been, and added that it would be sufficient if she were to return to Genoa every two months to keep them going. Rosa accepted the Pastor’s request and said a peaceful farewell. The divine sign was manifest.

It remained for her to say goodbye to her parents; only to think of it was heart-breaking. However, she decided to speak and told them without tears of what she had decided: the work to which she would devote herself, her new residence in Piacenza, her decision to leave with her companions as soon as possible.

It was a thunderbolt out of the blue, for the sweet peace of the family then seemed to depend especially on Rosa’s presence and authority; her two elderly parents were at first stunned then burst into tears, nor would they let themselves be persuaded, or far less acquiesce.

However, faced with their daughter’s calm and decided affirmations, they became aware of her determination; so they watched her constantly for fear she might escape.

Finally the morning of her departure came: it was 13 March 1866. Rosa, having completed her usual devotions and a few household tasks, prepared for the journey and presented herself to her parents for the last farewell.

A dramatic scene followed, of the kind that are sometimes recorded in the lives of saints and which seem madness, they so exceed natural human feeling and sensitivity. Her elderly mother, who had decided to oppose her daughter’s departure in every possible way, sat down on the threshold of the house, saying with tears and dismay: “I shall see if you are brave enough to step over me!” Her father burst into tears and it was the first time that Rosa had ever seen his eyes veiled by tears; her brothers and sisters joined their parents in begging her to stay and to desist from her resolution.

She was pressed for time; her companions were already at the station because they had decided to take the 10.00 o’clock train. A flash of grace then passed through Rosa’s mind; she suddenly rushed through the door, leaping over her mother and so reached the landing. She ran down the steps and arrived at the station. She had made the move; she could now say with the psalmist: “you undo my fetters. I will offer you the thanksgiving sacrifice” (Ps 115 [116]:16). This offering of thanksgiving and glory to God was to last throughout Rosa Gattorno’s life, and in a unique way if one thinks of what her children were to go through; it was also to perpetuate itself in the Institute of her religious, sent as apostles to every part of the world to prophesy gratuitous and supportive love.

Departure for Piacenza ~ The first reunion of the new religious family took place on the train that was leaving Genoa. They were called “Daughters of Mary Immaculate, Minims of St. Francis of Assisi”. With fearful anxiety about the future, those six women saw the places of their youth flying past; how many memories they were leaving behind them! Among all these memories, two especially alternated in their thoughts just then: the homes where they had been born and lived with their families, and the churches where they had prayed. Two extremes within which their lives had been woven, their characters formed, and the true joy of living frequently expressed. Again, between church and home the first idea of that important decision had been born and from it had sprung the impulse of unreserved dedication to God; the misery of crucified humanity, felt tangibly day after day, had given birth to their generous plan. They now comforted each other and joyfully called one another “sister”, thinking that thereafter they would be sharing the same roof, the same table, the same efforts, for ever focused on the heart of their whole existence: Jesus in the Eucharist, who would take up residence in their house from the very first day.

As they gradually drew nearer to their goal Rosa felt a superhuman strength, she was so determined to overcome every kind of obstacle.

They reached Piacenza in the afternoon and took possession of the rented premises at 3 Via Fodesta.8

Hostilities of the Liberals ~ The negotiations for the rental contract had been managed by the lawyer, Achille Cattaneo, and it did not escape the attention of the Liberals in Piacenza who were prompt in attacking the new institution with a hostile article published in the Corriere Piacentino on 14 February 1866. This actually said: “We received by post a letter whose text we do not deem fit to be published in its entirety for it is written in a style not at all proper, but its gist is: that a choice gathering of “Genoese Ladies” has come to settle in Piacenza under the usual cover of pious works […] which in the main is another invasion of “Jesuitesses”. For God’s sake! Haven’t we got enough of them? […]. O Liberals, Liberals! Let us take a little look around us and think just a tiny bit about the future! […]. Don’t you realize what traitors our railway carriages are constantly sheltering?” (Corriere Piacentino, 12 February 1866).

The first attack was followed by others (25 August and 12 September 1866) so that the lawyer Cattaneo was obliged to defend himself by writing a letter to the Independente on 21 October 1866.

Nursing the poor sick in their homes ~ On the other hand, Bishop Ranza gave a fatherly welcome to the generous first fruits of the new Institute; he blessed their resolution to do charitable work among the humble and the sick, assuring them of his protection as well as of his trust in their success.

The little community immediately set to work. Its name was already a program and an incentive for the lifestyle they were to adopt even before presenting themselves to the people in a religious habit. They were called “Daughters of the Immaculate, Minims of St Francis of Assisi”. Their time was therefore divided between prayer and visits to the poor sick.

Their living environment was characterized by an almost squalid poverty: on their table no meat was to be found and their food became even skimpier with the Lenten fast which was then very strict; their habits, clean and simple, without affectation and serenely modest, impressed a gracefulness upon their bearing that opened the hearts of the humble. From the outset, the most generous love for the lowliest marked the lifestyle of these unusual creatures; gladly giving what little they had for God, they felt gratified merely by seeing a smile bloom and Providence blessed.

First witnesses of the charity of the “Genoese Ladies” ~ Their passing among the wretched was immediately noticed in the city. A young teacher, Onorata Colli, witnessed an episode in those early months of 1866 which she recounted many years later, leaving her memory of it in writing.

On her way out after visiting family friends, she encountered two ladies who were entering the same courtyard and walking towards the steps of the dwelling. Having noticed her, they nodded their heads in greeting and started climbing the steps to a miserable garret. Up there lived a woman, ill with phthisis of the intestines, who was the wife of Carlo Cella, a poor news vendor who earned barely a few pennies a day from his humble job; this was all that he, his wife and their three young children had to live on.

The school teacher, overcome with curiosity, waited a long time in the courtyard until she saw the two ladies leaving; then she too visited the sick woman’s little room. She found her in bed, clean and combed; she was wearing a nightdress of the finest material and her sheets were freshly laundered. Next to her was a little table riddled with wood-worm on which lay a good supply of ground coffee, sugar, pasta, a bottle of wine, a small bottle of orange-flower water and other delicacies. Marvelling at the sight, the young woman asked her where these lovely provisions came from. The woman answered that she owed them to the kindness of the two ladies who had just left, the “Genoese ladies”, as they were called in Piacenza, who likewise benefited many other sick people in the city. The good teacher was astonished. She said goodbye to the poor sick woman, ran down the steps and wept; she was deeply moved and blessed those two consoling angels. A few months later, she recognized Rosa Gattorno as one of them.9

Similar events soon gave rise to deep esteem and affection for the newcomers in Piacenza. But their life was full of thorns, and all the tears of the sowing had to fall upon the ground if they were to yield an abundant harvest later. Their meagre funds, the austerity of food in the house and outside it, the toil of nursing the sick day and night in their homes without taking any refreshment there, were burdens which in addition to the newness of community life, soon exhausted some of Rosa’s first companions. She had to bear with their odd moods and sorrowful contradictions, although she was convinced that their desertion of what she considered the delights of the Cross was due only to human weakness. Of those five companions Anna Grasso and Luigia Rocca did not persevere; Teresa Morasso was hesitant from the start, and later ended by leaving.10

Contract for the purchase of Palazzo Dal Verme ~ Rosa was not disconcerted by these defections, more confident than ever in the Lord whose call she did not doubt; instead, since the first days in the Piacenza house, she had been thinking about obtaining a large house in which to establish God’s work permanently. For this she turned to Bishop Ranza, who advised her to rely on a good notary whom he knew. Rosa quickly agreed with this man and on 26 Mary 1866, was able to stipulate the contract for the purchase of Palazzo Dal Verme in the Stradone Farnese. She immediately made arrangements for moving into the new house11 which then belonged to the Sforza Pallavicini family.

Various benefactors, including Cardinal Consolini whom she met in Rome, helped Rosa Gattorno collect the necessary sum to cover the great expense.12

This rapid action is a reminder and a confirmation of what Rosa’s brother Francesco said of her: “She was strong at critical moments, quick to make decisions, and had no fear of danger” (Proc. Genov., Sess. XI, fol. 59).

Palazzo Dal Verme was a massive building. Its broad facade and simple style still make it stand out today among the houses along the great avenue which took the name of the Farnese. The entrance leads into a hall with columns that gives onto a courtyard, decorated with flower-beds and closed at the sides by the two wings of the building that project from the long mass of the facade. To the left of the entrance is a grand stairway that gives access to the floor above which covers the whole area of the hall and is connected with a succession of large rooms decorated in the 17th-century style; above this floor and in the rest of the building are many rooms, which were rather humble in appearance and destined for various uses.

During her brief visit in advance, Rosa had not really taken in the real state of the building and she had thought it would be habitable with very few modifications; instead, when the time came to settle the community there, she realized the precarious condition of many rooms and the number of alterations that would be necessary. “Oh, what have I done!”, she writes in the Memorie, “a house whose only good feature is its facade!” (M. 2, p. 54). However she did not lose heart; she immediately set to work, and in less than two months it was ready to give a dignified welcome to the Daughters of the Immaculate. All this happened at the beginning of May 1866.

It is worth mentioning the circumstances. Times were sad and most unfortunate, as the Vicar General had written to Rosa, and seemed contrary to foundations. The rumors of war were more and more threatening, and the war between Italy and Austria for the conquest of Venice was to break out on 18 June. Meanwhile a sectarian current was taking action against the Church and specifically against religious orders. In Piacenza subversive laws regarding ecclesiastical patrimony and others requiring the suppression of monasteries were already being applied.13

Thus to give birth to a religious foundation at that time seemed a reckless act. But Rosa knew that it was God’s Work; her steadfast faith freed her from all fear and made her suited to walking on the troubled waters of a world without peace.

“I had the strength of a giant” we read in her Memorie, “however heavy the work was, and [I] covered in penances, I felt nothing” (M. 2, p. 54).

Through love and fidelity to her vocation, she was oblivious to the efforts and sacrifices which burdened and would burden her; entering that house which was to be the mother of many others, once again Rosa Gattorno felt her smallness but, at the same time, the greatness and omnipotence of God.

She would always have a special affection for the Mother House, as can be noted from the correspondence in which she expresses her attachment to the roots of the Institute in moving tones. “As you see”, she writes to her friend Emilia di Fitalia, “I am in the cradle of the Institute; although there is no elegance here or what you will, yet here we were born and developed, and it always seems to us the best place and one for which we understandably feel affection”.14

Bishop Ranza paternally wished to inaugurate the new religious house; he blessed the little chapel and celebrated Mass there, leaving the Eucharist.

The little room, poorly furnished at the time but prepared with great love, is still preserved intact in all its simplicity. An altar supported by little brick pillars beneath the picture of the passing of St. Joseph, which Rosa had been given in Rome; a few deal kneelers and straw-bottomed chairs crowd before the altar, for the space is so small that it barely holds ten people: this was the first sanctuary of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. Rosa would spend whole nights there in rapture, for the hours of common prayer were not enough for her to treat with God about the grave problems of the present and the future.

She allowed herself scant rest, sometimes barely an hour, which she took leaning on a table or lying on the altar step; the rest of the silence of the night she devoted to prayer.

The defection of two of the first companions was soon made up for by other generous recruits who, in that month of June and in the following months, made their consecration to God and to the service of the poor. The charity of them all in nursing the sick won the goodwill of the citizens, so that various gifts poured in to furnish the house; among the first of these were a relic of the Holy Cross and a large refectory table, which seemed to Rosa a sign from heaven. “The Lord’s Work”, she would say, “will never lack crosses, but neither will it lack Providence!”

The great house in Stradone Farnese was still empty, but it was not enough for the Foundress’s plans and desire to do good; in her fervent mind other designs were already taking shape and her gaze was turning elsewhere in search of works of charity to which she could devote the strength and the heart of her religious.

On the very day she signed the contract for the purchase of Palazzo Dal Verme, Fr. Eliseo Ghislandi, director of the Institute for the Deaf and Dumb in Milan, wrote her a letter inviting her to accept a house in that great city or its surroundings.

The letter makes it clear that Rosa had already told Fr. Ghislandi that she was willing to receive some deaf-mute girls in the Mother House15. The proposal, most flattering because of the great advantages offered by the Lombard capital, nevertheless set a condition to which Rosa would never have agreed: the directing and teaching staff, although leading a monastic life, were to form an Association, not a religious Congregation. Moreover, it was desired that “any form of monastic habit” be excluded, as appears from other letters. Mother Gattorno replied declining the invitation, and she held firm in the following years too, despite that priest’s insistence.

Once again, then, she gathered her great thoughts in the vast silence of that house which from that moment was to be called the “Mother House”; there, in the practice of humility and mortification, in work and in prayer, the daily practice of charity was to be learned. This was to be the novitiate of those first Daughters of the Immaculate.

It was the uncertain but promising dawn of a great day for the new creature born of the Father’s provident love and of Rosa’s generous response; a dawn already pervaded by the creative brightness of the immense good that was to spring from this union in which, once again, God had been pleased to manifest his power in poverty and human frailty.

(1866-1867) The first community — Meeting with Fr. G.B. Tornatore — Proposal of the name for the new Institute — Apparition of St. Anne and the change of name — First clothing — The Mother’s little room: gifts and trials — Onorata Colli meets the Foundress — Clothing of Mother Rosa — Particular features of the Institute

The first community ~ At first, the life and charitable activity of the new Institute were organized on the basis of a Rule whose origins are unknown, but which certainly reflected the first draft which Mother Rosa presented to Archbishop Charvaz.1

It does not seem out of place to presume that the first program of daily life given to the Institute may have been inspired by Mother Rosa’s experience in Frassinetti’s associations. Later, as community life was reinforced, precise times were specified which punctuated the day in a typically monastic manner.

From a mere glance at some of these timetables, one is immediately struck by the length of time devoted to prayer: almost three hours after rising, which was always at 5.00 a.m., another half hour before lunch and two hours in the afternoon.

Great attention was paid to meditation, for which the Mother herself usually dictated the topics, sometimes giving an hour of instruction in the morning on the theme of the meditation. Novices had one hour of nursing school and one hour of study. Vocal prayer would alternatively assume tones of asking forgiveness, of praise or of thanksgiving.2

Marked by the radical nature of the Gospel was the detachment from family ties or friendships developed prior to entry, with an attitude of total renunciation that aimed for a superior well-being and a total gift of self.

With such a grounding in spiritual principles, one can understand that the life of poverty and obedience which really was so harshly tested in those early times must have been reasonably easy to all.3

The sisters lived on spontaneously offered donations, or, more frequently, on what they obtained with their humble collections; many of Rosa Gattorno’s letters have been preserved in which one can read of her recourse to all kinds of people to obtain aid for the needs of the Work. Their donations served mainly for the poor and sick to whom help was given, whereas the community limited itself to very ordinary food and never meat. Obedience governed every office and occupation. For assistance to the sick a series of norms were established in which one can admire the Christian prudence and spirit of sacrifice that enhance the value of charity: “In assistance to the sick”, they say, “all sorts of persons of both sexes should be assisted, whatever their condition or illness, by day and by night. By day [the nurses] must be replaced twice; those who visit them in the evening should stay in the house of the sick person until the morning […]. Then, should the person be seriously ill, they should never leave him alone, being relieved by another two. They should not accept anything in the sick person’s home, neither money, nor food nor drink, other than a glass of pure water in the case of need”.4

All this is only a rough outline of the kind of life that was imposed upon the new Institute, and one can see the immense concern with which an effort was made to foster an absolutely gratuitous and disinterested spirit of dedication in the sisters.

Meeting with Fr. G.B. Tornatore ~ In the meantime, a figure entered Rosa’s life and work who was shortly to acquire a remarkable importance in the foundation’s history: Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore.5

We describe his providential entrance on the scene by following the Mother’s own account in her Memorie: “The day before concluding, that is, signing the contract, two of my friends together with a priest who had come from Genoa to spend two days with me, invited me to go out with them. They were going to visit a missionary, [a] certain Tornatore; they said to me: Let’s go and see him! I gladly agreed because he was said to be very ascetic […] As we were leaving, he said he would come and pay us a visit. The next day one of my two friends came to tell me that both priests were there, both Tornatore and the other one […]; I allowed a moment to greet them; they were just leaving and I did not see them for long” (M. 2, pp. 51-54).

So it was a casual meeting, but there is no doubt that it was marked by Providence.

Proposal of the name for the new Institute ~ Surprisingly, as soon as he met Mother Rosa, Fr. Tornatore began an important correspondence with her. In fact his first letter is dated 27 March 1866 and accompanied a small donation to the Institute. He also included several little images of St. Anne and three copies of the Life of St. Anne for the month dedicated to her.6

In further letters of 31 May and 20 June (AF-SA A.1.1) that same year, Tornatore again proposed the devotion to St. Anne with a certain insistence, presenting three candidates to the Institute and describing them as “…true Daughters of the august and glorious St. Anne”. This information is corroborated by the testimony of Sr. Anna Santina Solenghi, who says: “The Servant of God accepted in her Institute some women who were getting on in years but were full of enthusiasm and, in particular, had a great devotion to St. Anne; and having entered the Institute, they were deeply edifying to me because of their rare zeal”.7

On 4 July 1866, Fr. Tornatore made Mother Rosa an unexpected suggestion concerning the new Institute’s name: “I would be curious” he said, “to know whether the nuns I saw in a dream, years ago now, in the month of the glorious St. Anne (I believe that the dream was truly divine) were yours, and which was the one who, with a heavenly look, took the relic of the glorious Saint and marked my heart with it. Enough: my St. Anne must have a family, and the most respectable one to have emerged and to be about to emerge from God’s Church. Oh, if I could but have on my grave a little of the dust trampled upon by the feet of such heavenly daughters, sisters of Mary Most Holy!”.8

On 9 September, he returns to the same subject in a postscript, saying: “The daughters of the Immaculate motherhood of St. Anne do not yet exist: pray that God will soon bring then into being, since it is they who must console the world”. And again, on 27 September, after speaking of St. Anne, he repeats the words cited above: “If I could but have on my grave a little of the dust trampled upon by the feet of the chosen and wonderful daughters of the Immaculate motherhood how refreshed I should feel! […]. Pray Jesus that he make these blessed days for the Church come soon”.9

Apparition of St. Anne and the change of name — We know from the Memorie that shortly after moving into the Dal Verme house, Rosa made up her mind to go to Fr. Tornatore for confession for since her arrival in Piacenza she had found no permanent director. “The first time”, she recounts, “I liked him, but I felt there was something a little frightening about him. His direction was so utterly different from my former direction! Enough! I was not worried about it because my guide was Jesus in everything and for everything” (M. 2, pp. 55-56). And Mother Rosa truly let herself be guided by the Spirit alone, by that interior impulse which assured her that she was living entirely in accordance with the will of her Good.

As we have had the opportunity to say, she used to like to spend long hours at night in front of the tabernacle in the humble chapel of the house. On one of those nights, while she was absorbed in prayer and experiencing great intimacy with God, all at once she saw the chapel illuminated with a great light and the Virgin Most Holy appeared to her with St. Anne; lower down, as though kneeling and turning to the Virgin, was St. Francis of Assisi. “I would like the title of the Rule to be ‘Daughters of St. Anne’, my mother”, said Mary Immaculate distinctly and in a clear voice (and she pointed her out to me). “I willingly cede this work to my mother. Do not be troubled, I will always take whatever you do for it as done for me” (M. 2, pp. 58-59). And she vanished immediately.10

Coming to herself after a while, Rosa felt perplexed; she remembered her obligation to tell Pope Pius IX if she were to receive the communication of another name for her Institute. Time was pressing (indeed her clothing was planned for 8 December); so she decided to write to Cardinal Patrizi and include a letter to the Supreme Pontiff. She immediately received an answer, telling her to call her Institute “Daughters of St. Anne”, and was again urged to draft the Rule (cf. M. 2, p. 60).

She therefore told the Bishop and the sisters who were about to take the veil, but she told them only of the order she had received from Rome;11 she did not of course have time to change the frontispiece of the booklet of the Rule approved by the Bishop of Acqui, which remained the same.

First clothing ~ As the Novena of Mary Immaculate approached, Rosa asked Bishop Ranza for a priest to preach the retreat for those who were about to be clothed as religious, and was assigned Fr. Tornatore (we know from a letter dated 2 July 1866, that Mother Rosa had already asked Tornatore to give a course of spiritual exercises to the whole community, AFSA A.1.1).

It is easy to imagine how full of trust and admiration for that priest Rosa must have felt, after the vision had confirmed what had been suggested to her regarding the Institute’s name; she truly considered him a person inspired by God.12

Moreover the community was very pleased with the retreat, so that henceforth Fr. Tornatore had great credit with the Daughters of St. Anne and paternal authority over them.

At last 8 December 1866 dawned: the Feast of the Immaculate Conception. A history was beginning for the new Institute which, it was hoped, would be rich in heavenly blessings, fruitful with holiness and good works, although not without the thorns that sometimes also mark the most gratuitous acts, and above all the great undertakings desired by God. Rosa knew that her Institute was also rooted in the Cross.

Because of the need for space, since the first chapel was no longer big enough, she had moved it to a larger room, but left the little chapel of St. Joseph intact. The new chapel was blessed on 7 December 1866, the eve of the Feast of the Immaculate Conception.13

It would really be superfluous to describe the state of mind with which the ceremony of the clothing was prepared; it is known that for the occasion some new oremus were composed, suitable for the circumstances and for the new title (cf. M. 2, p. 60), and that the rite was celebrated by the Vicar General, Mons. Angelo Testa, since the Bishop had been detained in the cathedral to celebrate the solemn pontifical Masses. Bishop Modesto Contratto of Acqui had also been invited, but was obliged to refuse the invitation (cf. letter of 9 January 1867 AFSA B.1.61).

However, Rosa was unable to be among this first group. She was prevented from receiving the veil that day by serious family reasons and by the good of the Institute for whose existence she was responsible. She remained merely a spectator of her companions’ joy. They were five: Giovanna Bixio, Angela Degrossi (who had been the first to arrive in Piacenza), Rosa Podestà of Novi Ligure, Luigia Camisa from Cortemaggiore and Teresa Merlano who entered after the community had taken up residence in Stradone Farnese.

Mons. Testa, thanking Rosa Gattorno a few days later for a gift presented to him in gratitude, wrote to her: “Your community, like the Lord’s works, is being born in the shadows: it must grow with them and among them; the day of light will come and the time to work in public and openly; for the present, it is right to work in silence”.14

The truest and most timely words, but those who knew of the difficult path she had taken in the past and the future horizons for which she was aiming wondered at her courage and tenacity.

“I admire your extraordinary self-denial”, the Bishop of Acqui wrote, “and the continuous sacrifices, both spiritual and temporal, which you make to the good Lord, for his greatest glory and for the benefit of the souls to whom you are dedicated without reserve. There is no doubt that the Supreme Giver of every good will bless your zeal and that of your establishment, and will prepare for you a most precious coronation of glory in heaven, for the richest treasure of merits which are being accumulated by your most exemplary virtues in this vale of tears”.15

God’s blessing was immediately evident in the flourishing of vocations. In the month of November five postulants entered, some from Genoa, others from the Piacenza region where the Institute was rapidly gaining trust and admiration. Early in 1867 a crowd of young women (more than twenty) came to ask for admission to the Daughters of St. Anne. Rosa thanked the Lord for them, seeing in all this not only a clear sign that he was pleased with the work, but also the possibility it implied for putting into practice the extensive assistance to the sick and the other works of charity of which she had so often dreamed.

In this period the Mother had many serious worries, due not only to the inevitable uncertainties and difficulties of the beginning of the foundation, but also because she was forced to change her mind about the priest, Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, who had at first been her adviser.

Because of certain regrettable incidents, she presented the disagreement, her own and that of the Piacenza community, to Bishop Ranza; distressed at having been disappointed in him, she dismissed him in August 1867.16

There was also the care of the many postulants who needed spiritual formation, the internal organization of domestic life and religious practice, which in those early days had yet to be defined, mounting tension in the face of the imminent political events, and the foundation of new houses, requested as from January 1867. All this meant a mass of work which might have oppressed or at the least wearied any great mind.

Yet all this could not distract Rosa Gattorno from her intimate attention to God or from her zeal; indeed, she felt in greater need of him for her own preparation to receive the veil and for the conception she had of the new work. Rosa saw it as a humble participation in the Church’s apostolic and charitable mission and in the work of the Redemption; she was therefore bound to rely on God above all and to support herself with those means used and indicated by Christ himself: prayer and sacrifice.

The Mother’s little room: gifts and trials ~ With an admirable simplicity of spirit which can well be described as the wonderful insight of saints, Rosa resolved to start a journey of deeper identification with Christ through the spontaneous martyrdom of the cross.

To this end she chose a small, solitary and unassuming room in that large house which later had the privilege of being next to the wall of the chapel where Jesus in the Sacrament was preserved. As has been said, at the end of 1866 the chapel was transferred to a larger room on the first floor.

She had a window made in the wall of her little room which would give her a view of the tabernacle in particular. A small wooden staircase, barely half a meter wide, led to that lonely place which Rosa had forbidden every one from entering. Here she would meditate for a few hours during the day and always at night, not so much to rest as to abandon herself to contemplation or to inflict harsh corporal penances upon herself.

In it she put a low iron bedstead and a rough pallet stuffed with leaves and maize, without either mattress or blankets. She would snatch brief moments of rest there, wrapped in a black shawl; sometimes, on the contrary, she would even remove the pallet and stretch out on the old iron bedsprings, so that her sleep, already so scant, would be even more uncomfortable. More often, as she said in an account to her director, she liked to lie on a large black cross which she sometimes placed on the pallet and sometimes on the bare floor: thus stretched out on that wood, she seemed to feel more united to her Redeemer.

She would rest her head on a rough and heavy chain which she had coiled up, while around her temples she had tightly bound a crown of iron with spikes, like a crown of thorns (M.1.1, p. 71 and M.15, p. 5).

Her keen desire to participate in the Lord’s Passion impelled her to work out ever new ways to make her body like that of her crucified Good. Later she also wanted to experience the agony of her Jesus as he hung on the cross: “I slept”, she says, “clinging to a cross, and then I climbed up [first] upon another, and hung on the cross like my Good” (M. 15, p. 3).

To do this she bound together with chains and cords two rough tree trunks which she had furtively dragged up there so as to make a cross, which she set upright fixing it to the wall; she put a support for her feet on the vertical trunk while on the transversal one she used hooks like those used to lower buckets into a well; she would insert her wrists into these, staying there with her arms extended as in a crucifixion. How many times she clambered up that cross, remaining there in prayer! But once a rather painful incident occurred.

“I hung on the cross like my Good”, she recounts, “while I wanted him to make me feel, as he did, that wrenching of the nerves as he was hoisted by those terrible torturers. Once, I don’t know how, I missed the support where my feet were at the bottom of the cross and was left suspended by my hands alone. Oh how the bones of my chest suffered, they were dislocated, and I can feel it still! I have never recovered…” (cf. M. 1.1, p. 83; M. 15, pp. 3-4).

No one else will ever be able to tell of the sublime raptures in God which Rosa enjoyed in that squalid solitude, deprived of every worldly object but full of heavenly delights.

In reading the brief accounts in her letters and in her Memorie, one glimpses the abundance of extraordinary gifts and light that Rosa drew from the wounds of Christ crucified, more than from any other source.

The evil spirit’s dogged persecution could obviously not be missing, both so that she might remain humble and so that patience might perfect all her virtues. In November 1874 she was tormented for several days; indeed, she writes in her Memorie: “Oh, if I could write down all the insinuations and incitements that infernal dragon continues [to make] to me! I would have to write volumes and I have no time…” (M. 1.2, p. 52).

Rosa clung to her Crucifix imploring comfort, but her trials often went on and on.

In his book already cited, Fr. Iriarte says on this topic: “It is no wonder that Satan should have launched his attacks particularly against God’s great friends, and even more fiercely against those who, like the Apostles in the Gospel and founders of religious institutes, were instrumental in spreading the kingdom”.17 However, these trials were frequently followed by the rare caresses of the Lord, which reassured his servant that he was constantly beside her and that she had nothing to fear.

Then Rosa would descend into the community from her solitary refuge of love and strife, of sorrows and illuminations, to carry on the duties of daily life.

She was always first in chapel in the morning and was concerned that all the sisters should start the day well with a fervent and heartfelt prayer. Usually she would read the meditation or expound on the subject following her inner impulse, and she most frequently dwelt upon the mysteries of the Passion.

Zeal gave her such eloquence that even after many years those who had been present still remembered her tones and the inner joy they had felt.

One morning, instead of the Passion, she chose hell as her subject, and read about it from a book. Having finished the reading, they all remained silent in meditation while the Mother was immersed in the contemplation of Christ’s wounds. Suddenly an increasingly loud banging could be heard and no one could tell how this happened.

The sisters were frightened and since the banging was growing louder and louder, they became upset. Rosa, shaken from her meditation, realized that this was how the infernal enemy wished to intrude upon the prayer of the religious: she secretly ordered him to stop, and everything fell silent. Then she continued to comment on hell with unusual eloquence.

“I do not know how”, she writes, “I was able to give that meditation on hell or what strength I found. Oh, those words were not mine but Jesus’! And wasn’t the strength also his ?” (M. 1.1, p. 76).

Onorata Colli meets the Foundress ~ The Mother’s intensity and great absorption in prayer were visible to everyone; she would be totally absorbed especially after Holy Communion, and for so long that to speak to her, it was necessary to shake her hard. However, in her working hours she was brisk and seemed tireless. She sought to do humble kitchen and household tasks, as soon as she had her obligations as superior out of the way. In the first four years of the Institute’s existence she often did the washing up during the community meal, despite feeling great pain in her hands because she could not tolerate the hot water. The testimonies at the trials are full of such examples and do but confirm Rosa Gattorno’s way of life already at the beginning of God’s Work.

Thus she shone like a lamp in the Lord’s house, showing everyone the way to holiness. Her face also reflected a certain majestic beauty which seemed to radiate something superhuman so that many people, even outsiders, felt an irresistible fascination, sensing that she was imbued with an arcane sense of piety; some found themselves prostrate at her feet, without knowing how. “A year afterwards [the reference is to the episode of the Genoese ladies, recounted in Chapter VII], I was sent by the Headmaster of the schools to talk to the Most Reverend Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne, who lived in the Mother House, to find them the teacher they needed. After waiting in the parlor for a few minutes, a door opened and I saw before me a sister so divinely beautiful that I was enraptured. I soon recognized her as one of the two angels of Providence who had left me with such sweet memories. Without knowing how, I found myself prostrate at her knee, just as one prostrates oneself before a holy person. I then realized that I was facing the Most Reverend Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno, the exceptional woman who, when she was very young, motivated by the most ardent love, had renounced the world with its enticements to serve the Lord by blessing him”.18

Clothing of Mother Rosa ~ In this greatness and fervor of spirit, the day of Rosa’s clothing came. She had arranged for it to take place on the Feast of St. Anne in 1867. The ceremony was held in the new chapel where a beautiful picture of Mary Immaculate had been set upon the altar, the gift of the Landi, a noble family of Piacenza who lived opposite the Mother House, while the picture of St. Anne was on the side altar. The chapel was actually called the Chapel of Mary Immaculate.

A lovely group of twenty novices took the habit with Rosa Gattorno who had already experienced a great change of feeling concerning St. Anne who was now the titular of the Institute, as will be explained, while previously she had only had a common devotion to her.

In taking the veil on that day, the Mother also decided to precede her baptismal name with the name of Anne, and the novices who had been clothed on 8 December did likewise. Notice of this was sent also to those far from Piacenza (by that time the house in Cento had also been opened): from then on they were to put the name of Anne before their own, as is still done throughout the Institute today19.

Particular features of the Institute ~ From that memorable day it was established that the new Congregation should present itself to the faithful and to the Church with these particular features: “The end which the Daughters of St. Anne have in common with all Christians is to please God through faith, hope and charity and the practice of good works; their own end, which distinguishes them from every other religious body, is to profess a very special devotion to the glorious St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate […]. The Institute [professes] moreover, among other virtues, the compassion of the heart of St. Anne, by nursing the sick in their homes night and day: and this service must be free of charge. They likewise take in poor girls in danger, to keep them from losing their innocence and virtue; and in this too they honor the care which [St. Anne] had for the Immaculate Child and the zeal which, because of this care, the Saint must have had to see all the young girls of the world innocent”20.
