(1867-1885) The epidemic in Piacenza: abandoned orphans — Assistance to cholera victims and acceptance of orphan girls — Interventions of Providence — Education of the orphans — Poss Mill — Acceptance of several deaf-mutes: negotiations with Ghislandi and with Fr. Aquilino Marelli — Administration of the Scalabrini Institute for Deaf-Mutes and the Deaf-Mutes Tertiaries Daughters of St. Anne.

The epidemic in Piacenza: abandoned orphans — The peace of Vienna, ratified on 3 October 1866, ended the Austrian domination of the Venice region which passed to the Kingdom of Italy after almost 70 years of foreign domination. A pall was cast over the event, which at last ended a disastrous war after only three months of hostilities, by a mortal epidemic that took a heavier toll of victims than many battles.

It was not long before the outbreak of cholera began to manifest itself in various regions of Northern Italy. Because of the lack of measures of hygiene at the time, the disease spread rapidly, giving rise to consternation among the people and bereavement in many families.

In addition to the sorry spectacle of the many war-wounded who wandered about begging was the equally pitiful spectacle of children left on their own after the death of their parents and relatives.

The public authorities of the time, although showing good will, were disconcerted by the devastation of the disease and the spread of contagion especially since, still burdened by the many problems caused by the war, they found themselves facing really serious emergencies with very slender means.

In Piacenza the cholera appeared at the beginning of June 1867 and raged throughout the months of July and August, sowing death among all the social classes.

A section for treating persons infected was arranged in the hospital of Campagna, but, with the mounting impact of the disease, it was considered prudent on 31 July to transfer it to Torricelle, outside the inhabited area. A private commission spontaneously offered to collaborate with the municipality for measures of hygiene, and the official notices posted by the city administration gradually guided people to implementing the provisions deemed appropriate to prevent contagion, and managed to keep the peace among those terrified by alarmist rumors.

To tell the truth, the press did not show the sense of dignity and correctness for which it should have done its utmost: on the one hand it published criticism as biting as it was childish, and on the other, displayed an exaggerated optimism which savored of irresponsibility; nor was there any lack of pretexts to diffuse a little sectarian poison against priests. In spite of all, it must be said that the public authorities’ concern greatly reduced the harm of contagion and did as much as possible to relieve the common people from the disaster.

From 3 June, the first day on which the disease broke out, to 21 August, there were 2,513 cases of cholera in the Province of Piacenza with 1,320 deaths: in the city, there were 443 cases and 257 deaths. On 27 August, it was announced that the disease had disappeared. Obviously the information concerning the figures recorded in historical texts and by the press of that period do not always tally.1

The mayor, Vincenzo Rovera, confronted the disaster with wise and generous administrative measures to help the poor. However, he was particularly concerned by the state of neglect in which many of the orphans were living, deprived of all their relatives; orphanages were overflowing and families were sought to assume the care of these innocents with compensation from the municipal funds. Even more than food, the little ones needed moral protection against the speculation of false protectors. These, prompted by greed and equally poor, would take them in to profit from the public funding but neglect them and leave them deprived of affection.2

Assistance to cholera victims and acceptance of orphan girls ~ In this deplorable situation, Rosa Gattorno found a domain for her great charity. When the disease first began to spread, she and her sisters devoted themselves to helping the afflicted, the sisters taking turns to visit their homes; and to protect the community from any danger of infection, she arranged for the nurses to stay in very modest rented lodgings located in the Strada della Morte at n. 34bis, next door to the suppressed convent of the Minims of San Francesco de Paola.3

Twenty-four of the most generous sisters devoted themselves to caring for the cholera victims, that is, nearly all the Daughters of St. Anne who then belonged to the Institute, including several postulants. In the meantime, Rosa had given hospitality in the Mother House to three poor little orphan girls; she entrusted them to the care of a good-hearted young novice, Sr. Anna Giuseppa Troni, more easily acceptable to the unfortunate little girls since she came from Cortemaggiore, hence from the same region.4

However, when the worst of the epidemic was over at the end of the summer and more people were available, Rosa decided to open the Mother House to all abandoned girl orphans. It was easy to accept the ones who had been left on their own, but she could not touch those who had been taken in by foster families receiving municipal aid without the authorities’ intervention and without provoking resistance. So trusting in Providence and not giving a thought to the Institute’s poverty during that first year of its foundation, she decided to offer the municipality free maintenance for an unlimited number of orphan girls, and wrote the following letter to the mayor:

Distinguished Mr Mayor,

Since the undersigned has been informed that in this city many little girls have been orphaned of both their parents because of the cholera which has stricken us this year and knowing that many of them are abandoned with no means of support or shelter, I have thought it through thoroughly and feel it my duty to turn to you and to make available to the said poor girls the home for abandoned daughters, opened by the writer of this letter at n. 49, Stradone Farnese.

You will therefore be able to arrange to have sent here all those girls in the above-mentioned conditions, whom you deem worthy; the undersigned assures you from this moment that the said girls will also receive in addition to free maintenance the education required by their condition, and is flattered to hope that one day they will be good mothers of families and good citizens.

Since this is a newly founded hospice and not yet sufficiently equipped with the necessary small beds, the undersigned asks you kindly to make available to the little girls who will be accepted, the number of beds you deem fit, in addition to a modest sum for uniform clothing”.5

Rosa Gattorno’s action went far beyond any human calculation and once again showed the power of her boundless charity. The mayor, Rovera, was deeply moved and at a council meeting put forward this proposal which was accepted with unanimous applause; in answer, Rosa Gattorno was sent a splendid letter which is vibrant with the city’s gratitude and full of human admiration.

“Piacenza, 11 November 1867.

I received with great pleasure your most gracious letter in which you offer free maintenance and education and other things, in the house you have founded in this city, to the poor little girls orphaned of their parents because of the cholera which has afflicted this district in the current year.

While this offer does not surprise those who know the spirit of charity of the pious and philanthropic institution you have founded, at the same time it cannot lessen my obligation to show you the most sincere gratitude. To give priority over any other good to the supreme happiness of the exercise of charity, thereby diminishing humanity’s sufferings, is a deed that it is not for human beings to compensate. It is heaven alone that must reward you a hundredfold, as I wish for you with all my heart, and you can be certain that the citizens will be just as grateful and will always remember your beneficial deed.

The Municipal Administration, also eager to help you, has arranged that to assist the poor girls you have taken in, n.12 beds complete with bedding will be provided, together with the sum of a hundred and sixty lire to provide for their uniforms. Please accept, Madam, the sentiments of my most respectful consideration”.6

The style of this letter, rather unusual in official documents, especially in those times when secularism prevailed, displays the significant involvement which Rosa’s charity inspired in the representatives of the public administration; indeed, it was subsequently very favorable to her.

After the news had spread of the work established in Stradone Farnese, requests to take in abandoned little girls also came from other places; Rosa welcomed them with her warm motherly heart; consequently, the Mother House was soon gladdened by a lovely array of seventy little girls.

Interventions of Providence ~ The maintenance, care and instruction of these innocents and of the growing community cost a substantial daily sum. To cover it, every now and then they depended on the help of Providence which was effectively never lacking, although it sometimes made them wait until the last minute. It was in these circumstances that Rosa Gattorno’s steadfast faith shone out in its full glory.

In this regard, Sr. Anna Apollonia Marchetti recounts an event which has something of the miraculous.

“I was a postulant”, she says, “In 1869 in the Piacenza house: one day there was nothing to give the sisters for lunch. Since I was cook and was unaware that there wasn’t any food, when midday approached, I asked the sister in charge of the dispensary for the necessary amount of pasta because the saucepans were boiling; but she told me to be patient and gave me nothing. When midday came, she answered my repeated request by telling me to go to the Servant of God and look for the pasta. In the meantime the sisters were already trooping into the refectory. I managed to attract the attention of the Servant of God and she emerged from her room. She told the sisters to return to the chapel to pray fervently for a most important grace, and said that they would be called to the refectory by the sound of the bell. We all went into the chapel. I do not know exactly how long we spent in prayer, when we heard the bell in the porter’s lodge summoning myself and the dispensary sister, Sr. Eufemia Mirasole. We went there and saw two carts, one drawn by four oxen, the other by two, laden with all kinds of provisions and accompanied by a lady who presented herself at the porter’s lodge. Everything was unloaded and the dispensary sister told me to inform the Servant of God. I asked the lady if she had a note, and she answered,: “Why don’t you do as the sister tells you?”. But then, putting her hand in her pocket, she gave me an envelope, telling me to give it to the Servant of God. I ran to her study immediately and told her of the arrival of all the provisions; the Servant of God opened the envelope in my presence and found all that was written was “Commend me [sic, perhaps ‘commend yourselves’] to St. Joseph”. The Mother, smiling as she spoke, told me to bring the lady in. I ran to the porter’s lodge, but the lady and carts had vanished; I went out into the street and looked this way and that, down the long road and in the neighboring streets; there was no one there, not even the carts, which moreover, drawn by oxen, could not have disappeared in an instant.

The miracle was even greater since we were not only left with the provisions, but also with the recipients, which suppliers normally reclaimed!

I turned to the Servant of God to tell her and she smiled and said: “Go and prepare the pasta for the nuns”. All the sisters were convinced that it had been miraculously provided through the intercession of the Servant of God”.7

Another time, as Sr. Apollonia Marchetti told several of her sisters, there was no coal for the kitchen. The cook warned Mother Gattorno, who answered: “Go and see, you will find there is enough”. Indeed the sister went to the place where shortly before there had not been any and found the necessary amount.8

A similar event occurred with the wood: there was not a single piece in the wood-store, and Sr. Nazzarena who had clearly noted that there was none and needed firewood, told Mother Rosa. She answered: “You are mistaken, there’s plenty, come with me”. Together they went to the wood-store, and found it full.9

In his testimony at the ordinary process in Rome, Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte said that her prayers for the serious or urgent needs of the Institute were liberally granted by heaven; in her drawers she would find that the few funds she had had which were insufficient for its needs had been increased. To explain, the Cardinal added, how it happened in these cases that funds were lacking, it was enough to mention the taxes she was obliged to pay to the government from one moment to the next for the property possessed by the Institute, as well as for the important construction of the Generalate in Rome.10

Here is an example. Once when the Piacenza community had no money at all to pay the suppliers of bread and other foodstuffs who had already waited some time for payment, they finally became impatient; and one morning they came to the door to complain. At that time the religious were in church at Mass; meanwhile they realized that the Mother had disappeared without telling them why. As they did not see her, they went to look for her in the house and found her coming down from her room, her face lit up but calm and smiling; she told them in answer to their questions that she was going to the porter’s lodge to pay the suppliers who were waiting, and showed them a quantity of brand new shiny gold coins with which she settled the debts.

The sisters asked her how she had managed to get hold of the money; Mother Gattorno smiled and passed them without answering, but they were all convinced that she had received them by a miracle, praying before her Crucifix.11

These loving acts of Providence were indeed a comfort to the charity of Rosa and her sisters but did not dispense them from their daily efforts, continuous sacrifices and diligent care to provide for the needs of so many people. The miraculous graces mentioned were also obtained at the price of sacrifices and self-denial: her long nights in prayer, rigorous daily fasting and continuous work, prove clearly how Rosa nourished the poor. She did not want the little orphans to lack anything, even those innocent enjoyments which are necessary to make the poorest children happy.

Education of the orphans ~ One of her first concerns was to give the little girls a proper education; Rosa paid a secular teacher, Miss Maria Colli, to do this and arranged for them to have two days of schooling a week, fulfilling the government programs then in force for elementary classes. Then to introduce the older ones to work and make them useful for their own sake, she equipped a workshop for weaving fustian, setting up thirty looms in a large hall on the ground floor, to the left of the entrance.

Rapidly becoming skilled at this craft, the young girls were able to satisfy commissions from outside, such as from the Brigidini Company and other city merchants. Even in this humble endeavor, Rosa was the first to set an example. She herself worked such long hours at the loom that she found it difficult to hold a pen in her hand when she set about writing letters, as we read precisely in one of those she wrote to Sr. Francesca Camisa.12

Poss Mill ~Later the Poss Mill was opened in Piacenza for the manufacture of silk. The proprietor himself asked Rosa Gattorno for a certain number of her orphans to do this work, giving them lodgings at the factory as well as a salary. Mother Gattorno accepted the offer, but appointed several sisters to look after them also during working hours; for their education she wished them to have lessons with the teacher, Onorata Colli, on their free days.

Mr Emilio Poss’s workshop started well. Sixty orphans from the Institute of St. Anne were sent there. Assisted by the excellent Sr. Anna M. del Buon Pastore, they behaved so well that they earned the business man’s praise.

At the beginning of 1874, requiring an additional number of workers, Mr. Poss asked and obtained from the Province of Piacenza permission to receive another hundred needy orphan girls in his establishment; he came to an agreement with Mother Gattorno and entrusted them all to her sisters.

New dormitories, a kitchen, a refectory and a decorous and capacious chapel were prepared to accommodate them. Rosa accepted the burden of the large family because of her splendid humanity and boundless trust in Providence, since the meagre pay of twelve lire a month per person was certainly not enough for their full keep. In addition, it was not a religious house that belonged to the Institute, but a work of social assistance, affiliated to the Daughters of St. Anne. Nonetheless, great good was done by initiating many of the girls to an honest hard-working life and preparing them for a peaceful and dignified future. Poss himself, negotiating with Rosa Gattorno when setting it all up, wrote to her on 5 February 1874: “I am convinced that this letter will put the true state of things before your eyes; I thought that the horizons of your influential and beneficent purpose would be considerably broadened; that the merit and satisfaction of having such a number of girls under moral protection would not only open your heart to joy, but would enable you proudly to call yourself the rescuer and regenerator of abandoned girls”.13

This was precisely the case: Poss had understood the great heart of Mother Rosa who knew only one form of pride and a holy one: the boundless pride of charity.

However, the work soon ran into serious financial difficulties and the silk mill had to be closed. Meanwhile other orphans had filled the Mother House in Stradone Farnese, so there was no room for those who had been dismissed from the Poss Mill; but many were now able to fend for themselves and Rosa Gattorno soon found work for them. Some of the younger ones were placed in other orphanages of the Daughters of St. Anne and lastly others, who had an unmistakable vocation, became religious.14

Acceptance of several deaf-mutes: negotiations with Ghislandi and with Fr. Aquilino Marelli ~ During the disastrous cholera epidemic, Rosa also had the opportunity for a new work: for deafmutes. It is easy to understand how Rosa, the mother of a deaf-mute daughter, was particularly sensitive to those unfortunate beings, especially in view of the difficulty of giving them an all-round education. In fact, her daughter Carlotta had had to delay her First Communion until she was 14 years old. With the instruction she had received in Milan, she had finally acquired a sufficient religious formation to receive the Eucharist on 4 July. Rosa was present at the celebration with her mother and other relatives.15 She then invited the priest Eliseo Ghislandi, director of the Institute for Deaf-Mutes in Milan and Carlotta’s teacher, to Piacenza for the month of September, so that he could celebrate Mass in the Mother House and the girl could again receive communion. Accepting the invitation, he asked Rosa Gattorno to do him a favor: recalling the plan she had made a few months before for a house of that kind, he suggested that she accept in Piacenza a certain Milanese deaf-mute whose family name was Villa, who had completed her studies with the Canossian Sisters but, having to return to her family in Baggio, would be in a precarious situation since some people in the village were threatening her honesty.

“Oh! Mrs. Gattorno”, Ghislandi exclaimed, “wouldn’t she be the cornerstone of the building? Remember that you have a deaf-mute daughter. She would be an excellent companion for your daughter, and should you want others just as good, with time I could supply them galore”.16

On 8 September, after only three days, he therefore repeated his plea but he had no need to, because Rosa had already enthusiastically accepted his proposal and offered to take in the young girl in danger free of charge.

On the 25th of that month, shortly after visit Fr. Ghislandi’s, Miss Villa arrived in Piacenza with another deaf-mute, a certain Cecilia Racasi from Merate; they were joined a few days later by an eight-year old dumb little girl from Parma, Itala Stefanini. They were all so taken by Rosa’s motherly care that the two Milanese girls could not refrain from telling the priest about it rapturously. Writing to Rosa, he said: “I hear that the Villa and Ravasi girls would have liked to return to Milan to kiss my feet, they are so happy to be there. Tell them to kiss the Crucifix for me instead”.17

Rosa, with admirable energy among the many worries the cholera epidemic was giving her, immediately set to work organizing a school for deafmutes with suitable and well-trained teachers. Since she had a young girl in the house who was “very well educated by her rather rich family”,18 she managed with entreaties to the Ministry of Public Instruction and other recommendations to have her take the diploma exams privately. She then sent her to the Institute for Deaf-Mutes in Milan to acquire experience in this special kind of teaching.

The young woman was Colomba Della Cella. She responded very well to Mother Rosa’s plan, and on her return to Piacenza was able to take charge of the deaf-mutes. Mother Rosa also had someone else study for the teacher’s diploma, Sr. Angela Degrossi,19 to teach in the external schools she intended to open.

Ghislandi, deducing from these and from other signs that Rosa Gattorno was an able person for that difficult apostolate, reiterated his proposal to come to Milan with her sisters and open a charitable institution for deaf-mutes already trained and in a civilized condition. The priest had taken this work very much to heart; he had received a substantial donation for it from a lady whose husband had died of cholera. In addition, a wealthy country priest had come to him for advice, wishing to gather the deafmutes of the Milanese district in his town of Cerro, and whose keep he intended to pay for with his own means. All things considered, given the difficulty of the times, were these not providential and lovely opportunities to found an institution in Milan and devote herself to such a necessary form of charity?

Yet along with such attractive invitations, Fr. Ghislandi imposed a difficulty, or, rather a condition that he considered indispensable: “my fear”, he wrote, “is that the Sisters of St. Anne might not want to submit to those disciplines which I consider appropriate for the well-bred and wealthy deafmutes. Therefore I say and repeat to you frankly that I intend them to dress like the latter, without uniforms: to go out walking even on feast days, without having an escort of persons dressed as nuns; and to lead a good life, but in a community; otherwise people would not think well of the institution for them, they would not stay in it willingly and disasters would ensue. Therefore, Madam, if you do not feel disposed to the above, you must tell me frankly, so that I may think about training staff for it. Those who do not pay are more easily resigned to discipline, but the relatives and girls who pay want certain conditions. To do good, one must adapt to the circumstances of the day: I tremble at the thought that the deaf-mutes in the Institute might think they were being forced to lead a monastic life: I therefore want to forestall any suspicion of it”.20

Mother Gattorno, probably preoccupied with the difficulties that had arisen in Cento where already her religious did not wear habits as will be seen later, did not at all share Ghislandi’s views; and since she realized she would never be able to agree with him, she tried to come to an agreement directly with the parish priest of Cerro, Fr. Angelino Marelli, to set up the work for poor deaf-mutes as her own spirit motivated her. For the time being, this was impossible because of the obstacles set in its way by the Archbishop of Milan and the climate of aversion to new foundations which existed in that city.

Ghislandi’s Institute for Deaf-Mutes was taken on by the society of the Pious Ladies of Nazareth, recently founded in Corso Magenta: a little later they opened another house in Saronno. Rosa indeed had to send back the first two she had accepted in Piacenza, the Villa and Ravasi girls, because their parents and parish priests wanted them closer to home. Nor did the proposal of even just a temporary house for the assistance of the sick at home come to anything.21

In 1881 the same parish priest of Cerro, Fr. Aquilino Marelli, suggested to Rosa that she take on the administration of the Institute for Deaf-Mutes, which had in the meantime been opened in Legnano and entrusted to lay women called the “Mothers of Charity”.22

Aministration of the Scalabrini Institute for Deaf-Mutes and the Deaf-mutes Tertiaries Daughters of St. Anne ~ Three years later, the Mother who had always had an unconcealed inclination for this type of work, agreed to direct the Scalabrini Institute for Deaf-Mutes which Bishop Scalabrini of Piacenza had founded in 1879. Here, on 8 December 1884, the first clothing of five deaf-mutes, Sisters Adorers (Sacramentines) took place, with specific aims such as the perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament and the production of sacred vestments.

The Daughters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul had been put in charge of the Scalabrini Institute first. However, in the report for the Ad limina Visit of 1 November 1885, Bishop Scalabrini explains: “With humble gratitude to God I would like to mention that in the course of the past three months one of my heart’s deepest desires has been granted with the regular and canonical creation of the Institute for Deaf-Mutes. I have entrusted the care and administration of this institution, which of its nature is strictly ecclesiastical (in fact, I created it and I direct it myself), to the Daughters of St. Anne. The marvellous improvement of the deafmute girls in their studies and in acquiring the capacity to articulate sounds and words is due to their zeal and tireless work”23.

Bishop Scalabrini, who had perceived in some deaf-mute girls the desire to live some form of religious life, formed, as has been said, a group of consecrated women whom he affiliated to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, placing them under Mother Gattorno’s direction. He called them “Deaf-mute Tertiaries of St. Anne, Perpetual Adorers”, and gave them a Regulation and real Constitutions modelled on those of the Daughters of St. Anne. This work, which never received approval as a religious Institute, nevertheless continued for many years. The last Sacramentine died in 1974.

So, in the whirlwind of dark and dramatic events, Rosa knew only one way, that of the Crucified, in whose footsteps she walked with invincible fortitude. And from that source her immense charity also drew its strength, a charity marked by prophecy and therefore so true and so far above every human consideration.

First foundation in Cento ~ At the unforgettable audience of 8 January 1866, the Pontiff Pius IX had said to Rosa Gattorno, encouraging her to found her Institute: “The Institute will spread in all the parts of the world as swiftly as the flight of the dove”.

Hardly a year had passed since the clothing of the first Daughters of St. Anne when, in January 1867, the opening of the first new house came in sight.

The Capuchin, Fr. Giambattista Tagiasco, former chaplain of the Santo Spirito Hospital in Rome and a member of the Institute of Hospitaller Brothers, Sons of the Immaculate Conception, had had the idea in collaboration with his Superior General, Fr. Bernardi, of adopting a new strategy to introduce themselves into the hospital milieu, given the difficulties of that time in history and the recently approved laws suppressing monasteries (cf. note 13, in chapter VII). With this aim, they planned to present themselves as a lay association called the “Società Ospitaliera Umanitaria” (Humanitarian Hospital Society), stipulating the agreements on 5 January 1867 with the Congregation of Charity in Cento, establishing that they would take on the service of Dell’Annunziata Hospital on 1 February. They consequently found themselves urgently in need of nurses to assume responsibility for the women patients and to be in charge of the kitchen and laundry. Finding no available institutes, they turned to Rosa Gattorno.1 It is thought that in so doing they may have been advised by Mgr. G.B. Fratejacci, a friend of Bernardi whom the Foundress met in January 1866.

For the new congregation only just taking its first steps, this was a crucial and delicate moment; the sisters would have had to present themselves, together with the Hospitaller Brothers, as a lay association, and would obviously have had the problem of keeping their own spirit and identity intact. Furthermore, the Institute’s principal aim was assistance to the sick at home and the protection of young women in danger; this new request, in a certain sense, lay outside these aims and presented certain risks, which furthermore were foreseen by Fr. Tornatore, to whom Mother Rosa and Cogrossi turned for advice.2 In a long and well-argued letter, Fr. Tornatore actually expressed a negative opinion,3 but despite this, Mother Gattorno, perhaps at Cogrossi’s insistence or because she was following the impulses of her boundless charity, accepted the invitation. From the outset the Institute had shown that it was free of rigid plans and open to requests prompted by the real needs of the moment. On 2 February 1867, Rosa took some nurses to Cento and stayed there for about a month, to initiate the young women to hospital service.

While she was there, she received a lovely letter from her former spiritual director in Genoa, Fr. Giuseppe Firpo, who had been informed of the new Work.

“At this moment”, he told her, “I am sure you are already in your foundation, and I hope the Lord will give you sufficient strength to accomplish his work and so his holy will may be done. What a lovely context the hospital is for you to give vent to that love through which your soul, by a privilege of grace, draws fervor from the most holy wounds of the divine Heart of Jesus! It is precisely the place to which your crucified Love has already been attracting you with his grace for some time. Yes, he demands great perfection of you, that is, continuous contemplation of the mysteries of the Cross together with an active life of great love, resembling his own as a wayfarer on this earth who healed the sick everywhere and did good to all. I have expressed this sentiment to you because the Lord inspired it, and because in your letter you still call me by the name of Father, which gives me confidence, and I hope that you will be glad to hear it. Then, as the first witness and depository of all the graces the good Lord has bestowed upon you, I have very much at heart that you respond to your sublime vocation and this is why, in my wretchedness, I wish for the success of the work begun within you, and I pray him to hear you and to bless you, so that it will all be fulfilled and to his glory”.4

In Cento, as had been predicted, she found herself obliged to face many difficulties. In the meantime, nothing had been prepared for the nurses’ arrival, not even accommodation to welcome them. Rosa, without losing heart, immediately devoted herself to making temporary arrangements for her daughters, and as for herself, having glimpsed an empty bed from which the corpse of a woman had just been removed, she settled down as best she could and spent a peaceful night on it. What seemed to her quite natural on the contrary made a great impression on the sisters who never forgot that generous act, stamped with the style of real charity, to which she gave herself without reserve.

Until then, a few lay people had volunteered their services at the hospital; it had a secular administration.

The work of the Daughters of St. Anne was to be approached in a new way, drawing inspiration from the most disinterested love, for the benefit of the sick. It was decided that the nurses would be fully responsible for its management, including the laundry and cooking; but it was all so badly organized that the Mother immediately realized it would take days to put it in order and arrange everything properly.

“You told me”, she wrote to Piacenza after two weeks, “that you were expecting me any day. My dears, how could this be, given that in so few days it isn’t even possible to find the soup ladle? So don’t let us deceive ourselves: the Lord’s works require patience and sacrifice”.5

With regard to sacrifice, Rosa truly did not measure it and her patience was harshly tried in that first foundation. Since, as has already been mentioned, the Hospitallers and the Daughters of St. Anne presented themselves as a single secular association, Mother Rosa was under constant tension, striving to claim autonomy for her nurses; there were also such injustices in financial dealings that the Mother House in Piacenza was also obliged to provide for the keep of the community at Cento (cf. Virga Jesse, op. cit.).

It is true that Rosa’s trust in Providence was boundless, but here we must recall that at that time she had taken into the Mother House a large number of cholera orphans and was living on donations.

She was also more in demand than ever for the moral ordering of the community, especially since she had to reckon with the lay spirit that motivated the administrators of charitable works at the time.

She therefore stayed more than a month in Cento, directing everything and setting an example in the various activities; that work of total dedication to the sick was very dear to her.

Epistolary relationship with the first sisters ~ In those exhausting days, Mother Gattorno never lacked concern for the daughters she had left in Piacenza. Late in the evening, tired out by her day’s activity with the sick, she would give free reign to her feelings in prayer. She then sat down at the table to write letters in which the tenderness of her motherly affection accompanied her wise advice and generous encouragement to be dynamic in serving God. It is easy to imagine how much that first separation must have cost the new family of St. Anne which, among the countless uncertainties of its first steps, was sustained by affection and esteem for the Foundress; the Mother fully understood this state of mind.

The oldest of the novices, Giovanna Bixio, formerly a close friend of Rosa’s in the world, was unable to resign herself to being so long without her conversation, accustomed as she was to confiding in her the many sufferings of her troubled spirit.

Caterina Rapallino, who had only entered the Institute a month before, was upset by her absence. Others felt uncertain and bewildered, as though the bleak winter that enfolded the large house in Strada Farnese were also numbing their souls.

It is therefore not surprising that the most sorrowful letters arrived in Cento. Mother Gattorno answered them all with solicitude, stealing time from the briefest of naps that she usually allowed herself.

“After midnight”, she writes to Giovanna Bixio, “I want to have a little chat with you, my dear friend. Firm patience and resignation: your mother is working for Jesus, so it is inevitable that the daughter also feels her weariness and absence; but courage and peace…”. Here follows a long series of detailed suggestions for spiritual peacefulness and religious observance. She gives Caterina Rapallino a lesson on the detachment of heart which was valid for them all: “God”, she says, “prefers sacrifices to great promises […]. Jesus sacrificed himself for us and, until the very last, drank the bitter cup: and we make such a fuss about being closer and not separated! Ah! Come my children, let us cast off our blindfolds, go forward in the heart of the Eternal Father, and beg him to do with us what he pleases…”.6

So the little flock that had been separated from her felt the warm affection and strong encouragement of the one and only Mother.

Well into March, Rosa returned to Piacenza leaving as superior Sr. Anna Luigia Camisa, one of the first to be clothed on 8 December 1866; she was replaced about a month later by her sister, Francesca, only just a postulant, but who had shown signs of such human and religious maturity that she deserved this trust.

The mountains of work in the Mother House, the novitiate that was teeming with novices, their formation and other commitments could not distract her mind from her concerns for Cento. Hence the very detailed letters to the young superior, in which one feels her motherly apprehension for the dangers in which her inexperienced daughters came to find themselves, and one can read the most detailed advice on religious conduct, keen calls to the holiness of work done as a service to Christ in suffering humanity. She truly glimpsed the divine face in the poor and the sick, and deeply and coherently lived the dimension of sacrifice and of the Cross, bringing her daughters with her on the same path with a truly overwhelming enthusiasm.

Against the uncalled for practices of penance to which people who have not yet achieved a healthy balance might be inclined, she wrote: “…for pity’s sake, do not practice abstinence to save money; eat, spend whatever you want, eat well as your condition requires. If you have no money, write and tell me so that I can send you some immediately. No dear friend, I had no intention of telling you off for the expenses! Poor thing! Please believe that I see everything and I am very pleased with your exaggerated economy! Continue to keep the girls happy”.

At the same time, she urged them to look at the work entrusted to them with a deep sense of duty: “How fortunate you will be when the day comes on which you can say: I am dying through having worn myself out with acts of charity. And then you can be certain that our dear Mother St. Anne will be waiting for you at the gates of Heaven, to receive you, blessed and holy, for eternity. Be comforted, you who are working for your Jesus! Ah, you are always talking to Jesus, because in touching those sick people with love and such great love like that of your dear Mother St. Anne […] I assure you that I am dying to come and to be with you, to be part of your love”.7

In the summer of 1867, the cholera was raging in Piacenza and in various parts of Italy. Rosa also wanted her sisters in Cento to be ready to help those who were infected.

“Isn’t the cholera threatening you at all?”, she wrote to the superior, “If it does, you can let it be known that you will be prepared to provide nurses, you understand, I will send you some from here; make this known”.8

In fact, something happened which immensely increased the trust of those first Daughters of St. Anne in their Foundress.

Sr. Anna Annunziata Chiodelli, was stricken by an ailment that did not at first seem serious, so that the superior did not think to tell Mother Rosa of it. However, the sick sister suddenly took a turn for the worse so that she was brought to death’s door, and the doctor considered her past saving. Notified by telegram, the Mother hastened to Piacenza; it was the first time that the danger of death had shown itself in the new Institute. Reaching the sister’s bedside, she asked her with indescribable affection, “My daughter, what is wrong with you? How do you feel? Courage Annunziata, tomorrow you will come with me to chapel, to receive Holy Communion”.

There is no doubt that those present took these merely as loving words of comfort; but it happened that the next day, the sick woman, already considered dead by the doctor, got up by herself and went to the chapel with Mother Rosa.

Shortly afterwards the doctor arrived and went directly to the sister’s little room; finding the door open, he entered, but seeing the bed empty, was convinced that she had already died. Coming across the nurse, he asked her whether they had taken the body to the morgue.

“Quite the opposite to the morgue”, she answered, “Sr. Annunziata is in chapel receiving communion with Mother General!”.

“That’s impossible”, the doctor added, “I don’t believe it!”.

“Well, go to the chapel and see with your own eyes if I am telling the truth”.

The doctor went into the chapel and to his surprise he found Sr. Anna Annunziata there, having just received communion with the Mother. As they were coming out, making a point of meeting Rosa Gattorno, the doctor exclaimed: “Excuse me Mother, but this is a true miracle”. The Mother smiled and changed the subject.9

That first hospital however, was not destined to have good fortune. On 16 November that same year 1867, the Congregation of Charity of Cento were ordered by the Vice Prefect to dismiss the Hospitallers. Although the measure did not concern the nurses, nevertheless they were partly included in the aversion: slanderous rumors were spread about the work, letters that arrived from Piacenza were read and many of them intercepted; as a result, when Mother Gattorno saw her communication with the sisters seriously threatened, she complained to the director, Giuseppe Rusconi, and sent a letter of protest to the President since it was a matter of the honor and charity professed by the Institute. “Understand in the name of Jesus”, she wrote, “that the charity I profess is loyal, and has nothing to do with sinister purposes…” (AFSA A.1.4, minute n. 2).

The energetic protest had a positive effect and the honor of the religious was then acknowledged in a public attestation by the Vice President of the Congregation of Charity.10

However, this was not the end of the hostilities: since it was impossible to attack the integrity of the sisters who were giving so much evidence of generosity and dedication in their diligent assistance to the sick, other expedients were used to procure their dismissal, thereby injuring the very authorities who were protecting them.

It should be noted that in October that year, on the day of St. Francis, some of the postulants had been clothed with the habit of the Daughters of St. Anne: but the celebration had been kept secret; immediately afterwards, the young sisters had returned to secular dress as Mother Gattorno had temporarily ordered, so as to avoid provoking further disputes. In December, Sr. Anna Francesca Camisa, whose health was uncertain, was withdrawn and replaced by Sr. Anna Giuseppa Troni who had common sense and was very faithful to the Foundress. However, nothing could improve the situation.

Mother Gattorno, although in anguish, sought with every possible means to iron out the difficulties; the contradictions served only to purify the charitable impulse of herself and her sisters but never managed to break down their courage.

“They are making a secret and evil fire to burn you”, she had written to Francesca Camisa towards the end of November, “I assure you that I am extremely upset. For pity’s sake do not discuss it with anyone.”11

On her part, she redoubled her sacrifices for the hospital of Cento. That winter between ’67 and ’68 took a great toll on the straitened circumstances of the new Institute; in the House of Piacenza, where there were so many orphan girls as well as the novices, even firewood was lacking; some sick sisters were sent to Bettola to convalesce, but there was not even the money to pay the cart driver for the short drives, and it was hoped that some shawls could be sold.12

Death of the first Daughter of St. Anne ~ To alleviate such poverty, Rosa had them pray, work and ask for money; she herself asked for alms, visiting various people and also writing humble letters to relatives. At most she collected a few small sums and sometimes refusals and humiliation, but she considered all this the price to be paid for obtaining day by day the bread of divine Providence. Therefore whatever she was able to collect she spent, and always found a way to send something to the extremely poor sisters in Cento.

They continued with that unlimited trust for the whole year, until, with suffering heroically borne, one of the first flowers of the Institute died: Sr. Anna Daria Vagni of Cremona, who had entered it in 1867 and had been clothed with Mother Gattorno on 26 July, died in the Cento Hospital at the end of August 1868. Her simple goodness had made her beloved by all as was testified by her beautiful funeral, offered by the people. But no heart so treasured her memory as that of Mother Gattorno, who throughout her life kept beside her the portrait of that first daughter of hers to die.

At the end of 1868, with the change in the board of administration of the Congregation of Charity, unacceptable conditions were proposed to the Daughters of St. Anne which made it impossible for them to continue their service.

Mother Rosa wrote a final letter which bore the mark of her typical determination and clear ideas: “I can see clearly that my nurses, who are every inch the spirit of philanthropic charity, cannot mix with mercenary persons who strive only for vile interests, so that if my nurses can, they will remain as they have been, otherwise I shall be obliged to withdraw them; and should they remain, I am ready to attest to my warmest gratitude to this city by doing any disinterested charitable service”.13

As the Congregation of Charity refused the conditions requested by Mother Rosa, on 21 April 1869 the decision was taken to dismiss the sisters. They left Cento at the beginning of May (cf. Virga Jesse n. 6 [1986], op. cit.).

Foundation of the house in Sampierdarena — While the house of Cento was thus nearing its end, another foundation was looming on the horizon: that of Sampierdarena, which although it originated in tribulations and at first very painful events, was nevertheless blessed by God with abundant fruits.

Fr. Angelo Ricchini, the priest who wanted to use his inheritance for a religious work, had conceived of a house that would take in young people at risk and a school for abandoned children. Since his available capital was insufficient for his purpose, he turned to Rosa Gattorno while she was in Genoa in October 1868. Rosa willingly accepted the proposal of a new charitable work, trusting herself to Providence. On the evening of 14 November, five Daughters of St. Anne arrived at Sampierdarena with Mother Gattorno; they stopped at the door of the Church of the Madonna delle Grazie, known as the “Madonetta”, and were greeted by Fr. Ricchini, its custodian, and the people. When the candles on the altar were lit, they recited the Te Deum and various prayers to the Immaculate Virgin and to St. Anne. They then withdrew to the humble house they had been allocated, opposite the church.14

They immediately began their assistance to the sick at home, and opened a school for poor children who flocked to it.

A lay woman, Carolina Pezzoni, was headmistress of the school; she subsequently became a Daughter of St. Anne. The sisters taught and helped with the housework. It is obvious that not everything was perfect: they worked with simplicity among young people who were rather rebellious, who had been taken in from the street, who had to be gradually taught moral values and civilized coexistence. The effort, more often than not unappreciated, produced a certain amount of dismay and had its repercussions on the community’s functioning; then came illness.

All these afflictions were poured out in letters to the Mother who in the meantime was involved in the last battles for the Cento House; her motherly heart had to find and give comfort, although she was suffering the torture of so many hardships. She accomplished this mission magnificently, as can be seen from the letters of that period.

The following spring, the community moved to the neighboring Villa Gattorno, rented from Rosa’s father; its farm buildings were also adapted to serve for the Work’s uses. In particular, a fairly large chapel was created there which was decorated little by little, and a picture of the Sacred Heart, commissioned for it in Rome, was placed in it. The results of the sisters’ activity were soon visible, the number of little girl boarders they helped rapidly reached about 30 and their day pupils were very numerous. They were all the object of the tender attention of the community which took charge of their human and Christian formation. The sick poor, whom they helped so lovingly, also showed them immense gratitude.

About a year later, the parish priest of Sampierdarena attested that the religious had “with every kind of self-denial and sacrifice always achieved exactly three times what they had set out do, to the pleasure and edification of all”.15

First slanderous accusations against the Mother — However, while Mother Gattorno was busy arranging and founding that house, she became the target of a real hostility which wounded her religious spirit and her work as Foundress. A secret battle was waged against her by one of the first of the five sisters who had been clothed with the habit, whom she had so trusted as to make superior of the Mother House of Piacenza in 1867: Sr. Anna Luigia Camisa, the elder sister of Sr. Anna Francesca. She was unable to adapt to the harsh life of poverty that was such a vivid feature of the Institute’s early days and corresponded to the lofty idea of the radical Gospel life which, on the other hand, was lived by the Mother. She began to spread slanderous rumors against Mother Gattorno and soon had several supporters among the religious of Piacenza.

The Foundress was blamed for the difficulties that the new Institute was encountering, with the pretext, as has been said, of its great poverty and the critical conditions of the Cento house. Sr. Anna Luigia had the audacity to write to her from Piacenza that her daughters were complaining of her, saying that she was the ruin and scandal of God’s Work.

This blow hit her in Sampierdarena on the very day of the opening of the new house. Far from feeling indignant, the Mother lowered herself with humility and wrote a very noble letter to that superior, as though her accusations were true and were a beneficial revelation to her soul.

“After having had a good journey”, she said, “a very happy arrival and, today, a beautiful day, the heavens are rejoicing with us and seem to echo the hoorays of the little girls. My God, except that this servant of yours finds herself immersed in every kind of trouble, and tastes nothing of all the relief and contentment that nature is offering her […] Ah, dear sister! if you but knew how painful to me is […] the thought that I am your ruin, your scandal, that I serve only to spoil the Lord’s business; I feel my innards wrenched, and continue to thank my God for having removed me and sent me away from you. You others will therefore be able to have greater providence from heaven and will no longer have with you this most shameful woman to impede it. Thus your hearts will receive from the hand of the Holy Mother […] spiritual gifts, graces and enlightenments, to observe closely the holy book of the Rule. My God, what will happen to wretched me? Pray for pity’s sake that you will not have to lose me […] Yet, my dear, I can assure you that this wretch has done everything, and my every word and thought was always for your good. And yet there are some who say I am your ruin. My God, how wretched I feel inside! Why [Lord] did you not rid of me before of this state of blindness? Ah, if only I had not so scrambled the matters of my conscience, I would be less unhappy! Dear Luigia, forgive me for all I have done to you, and also obtain the same forgiveness for me from the community…”.16

However, full of trust as always, the Mother did not even suspect that those accusations were the product of a wicked mind. A month later, receiving a letter in Cento from the superior herself who complained that the Institute had many enemies, she replied in the perfect good faith of her affection, imbued by her love for the crucified Christ: “Dear Daughter and Superior, I, your poorest Mother would like to take the time to answer your letter today. As I imagine your dear delights, for my wickedness I must make do without them. After sins, repentance is needed! Blessed hand of my God, I kiss you a thousand times, while I feel you are crushing my back. Yes, Daughters of St. Anne, let us rejoice amidst tribulations, our only security and comfort. Ah! Blessed be that soul who knows so well how to rejoice in tribulations and receives the blows of divine justice with pleasure and consolation […]. You tell me that we have many enemies: what consolation I felt in reading this! I only regret to see you still so anxious and giving too much consideration to these things: I would like you to make less of them and at least to be indifferent…”.17

In these lines, the magnanimity of the strong woman of the Book of Proverbs is revealed. No less was needed to give life to the new houses of the Institute among so many difficulties.

Opening of a house in Genoa and a school for poor children in Piacenza ~ Hardly had the work of Sampierdarena been opened when some sisters were requested by Fr. Costantino Peragallo for his institution for poor and abandoned girls on the outskirts of San Nicolò in Genoa.

Carolina Pezzoni was sent there to run a school with other sisters who remained dependent on Sr. Anna Francesca Camisa. They were destined to struggle and suffer because of the lack of internal organization in that house, but they did so well that Fr. Peragallo was deeply satisfied with them. However, since she could not establish a real religious community there, Mother Gattorno withdrew the sisters at the end of the year.

This only served to kindle a more ardent desire in her heart to have a house of the Institute in her native town; in spring 1871, she succeeded in opening a house of nurses there for free assistance to the sick at home, and this foundation was the most heroic of all.

Since Rosa Gattorno was totally without the means to pay any kind of rent, she requested and obtained from Caterina Rusca a few rooms in her house. According to the account of the sisters who were the protagonists of this event, this lady offered them some beds but fewer than the number of sisters, so that some nurses had to be assigned to be out at night, watching over the sick.

For their keep, their only resource was alms collecting, since the nurses’ service was entirely free. Sr. Anna Serafia Lorenzi was put in charge of these collections and several times a week gave an account of her difficult, humiliating and tiring efforts to the Mother General. From her letters, which are ungrammatical and almost in dialect, transpires an enchanting simplicity, a deep and edifying faith and a touching love for the poor.

“Dear Mother”, she writes, “with great pleasure and happiness I received the recommendations you give me to be humble: I don’t know how to act: I will try to do all I can to do everything well. Sometimes there are days when I certainly feel real repugnance about going to speak to certain men, but afterwards I pluck up my courage and I say: ‘My dear Mother has gone before me’; and I remember that, if I must repent for my sins, this is nothing: or I read your letters for a while, then I take heart…”.

“Dear Mother, I am going to tell you about my usual affairs. This morning I left the house at eight o’clock and I went around until eleven, without being able to obtain anything. Because I, a poor Daughter of St. Anne, am short of patience, I had almost decided to go home empty-handed […]. I went along, thinking these things. Afterwards I thought: let us have a little try with Marchioness Cattaneo […]. She gave us 100 francs…”.18

In this candid heart, one can feel the spirit inculcated in her and her trust in the one she so affectionately calls “Mother”.

Having collected a little money, in early autumn they were able to rent a house in the Castello district; but there was no furniture or furnishings of any kind; yet the Mother moved in with her sisters.

“I write to you from the new house”, one reads in a letter from Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino of 22 November 1871, “on a table which was sent to us by Mrs. Luigia from Sampierdarena, after we had been several days without one; we ate standing up like soldiers. Mother is busier than ever working and having work done; she has chosen the room for the chapel, tomorrow she will send for the altar […]. Mother’s health is reasonably good, that is, she is up and about. The Lord gives her the strength to work; one can really see his divine hand”.19

Nor were caresses of Providence missing; that is, those events that fill the heart with joy in privations and leave profound traces in the mind as signs of God’s passing.

“There were some days”, a sister recounted many years later, “when there wasn’t even any bread; nevertheless we were all happy and working. One day […] a lady sent us a cake as a present: it was midday and our dear Mother, blessing Providence, began to cut the cake and gave a piece to each one. That was the beginning and the end of the meal that day. We had to sit on the ground because of the lack of chairs; and I remember it as though it were now, we were so happy with that creature from whom something heavenly transpired”.20

These lovely strands of distant memories give rise to the desire for a more detailed account of events to piece together the history of those early times, but almost no one then thought of keeping a record or of writing diaries; they worked in simplicity to serve Christ in his poor, to whom they gave not only a glass of water, but truly their whole lives.

This house of nurses was the only one in Genoa that put down deep roots; others were opened but were soon closed, while the humble house in the Castello district was moved to larger premises close to its first site. It experienced days of extraordinary apostolic fruitfulness in its mission, which was the Foundress’ first idea and favorite activity as a young lay woman: serving the sick.

In autumn 1870, the municipality of Piacenza granted Mother Gattorno the use of the building in Via della Morte (today Via Gregorio X), to open an elementary school for poor children. The building adjacent to the house which then served to accommodate the sick sisters, was joyfully occupied by Mother Rosa. She arranged that the children be given soup at noon every day; she closely followed the schools’ progress and enjoyed encouraging the children with her presence during examinations. In the first year, there were about a hundred small pupils, and in the second, a hundred and forty eight.

“All in rags and tatters, real leftovers from prison”, Mother Rosa wrote to Fr. Agostino Donadio in Rome, “If you had but seen them! Barefoot, and some of them with their shirts hanging out through holes in their trousers. They did very well, and the examiners were satisfied; they certainly did not expect so much from such dreadful little ragamuffins”.21

Indeed, all the authorities had been present at that performance, they admired the sisters’ effective work and later supported them with some donations, but the greatest support always came from the alms-collecting of the Daughters of St. Anne.

Foundation in Ferrara ~ There was another foundation in 1871: in Ferrara. Countess Trotti of Bologna, because of a grace received from St. Anne in a certain litigation which had a successful outcome in her favor, gave the Institute Palazzo Obizzi in Ferrara as a base for various works, including home nursing for the sick. After six months, what with promises and preparations, it was inaugurated on 10 October with great solemnity since Cardinal Vannicelli, Archbishop of that Diocese and Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne, was present in Ferrara and saw this foundation with the greatest joy. The beginnings were truly splendid: the Countess had undertaken to give a subsidy of 300 lire a month, to which she added other benefactions. The young superior was that same Carolina Pezzoni who two years earlier had run the schools in Sampierdarena as a lay teacher; she had entered the Institute in 1869, taking the name of Sr. Anna Adelaide, and had given herself with great generosity to the Lord’s Work. Most docile to the enlightened directives of the Foundress, Sr. Anna Adelaide ran the house with tireless energy and practical sense. The day pupils of the school were numerous, there were many calls to nurse the sick, the boarding school was also well under way and a good number of the girls were taken in free of charge.

Everything thus seemed to be sailing along smoothly, and perhaps not a few people who saw things only from the outside thought so. But the law of authentic charity is modelled on the example of Christ, who redeemed mankind and consoled the afflicted by his total sacrifice.

So difficulties arose for the house in Ferrara too, and they were not only those of poverty.

From the very numerous letters of the superior, Sr. Anna Adelaide Pezzoni, a reality emerges which is at times truly disconcerting: her very frank character, full of affection for her Mother General, sets daily events before our eyes like a film sequence; there are tears, together with serene abandonment to God.

The Countess’s gifts in fact soon dwindled considerably; the unhealthy premises caused various illnesses and some weaker souls felt the burden of fatigue too heavily; but in the end love for God’s service always won.

“Mother”, the superior wrote, “this morning St. Anne sent me a little bit of providence: it seemed a great deal to me, because I was really without anything and did not know which way to turn […]. I do the little I can, what charity requires”22.

“How much good is being done here in Ferrara”, Mother Gattorno wrote to Fr. Agostino Donadio, “a hundred and thirty-nine little girls […] what a consolation this is! We have admitted so many to their first Communion: what mercy of God for these foundlings! We are already beginning to take them into the house, rescuing them from sin. The calls to nurse the sick increase every day. God be blessed!”23.

Opening of a hospital and a school in Nizza Monferrato ~ In January of that year (1872) Rosa at last succeeded in opening the hospital in Nizza Monferrato as well, which the Congregation of Charity entrusted to the Daughters of St. Anne. Instead of the large convent of St. Francis which had been promised some time earlier, the small Chiodi building was given for the purpose. So they began with ten beds and an annual allowance of 3,000 lire for the upkeep of the sick and the sisters. These humble beginnings were blessed by the Lord, for the religious immediately won the hearts of the townspeople. In the following month of April Mother Gattorno also opened an elementary school in the same town, much desired by the authorities and the citizens.

As usual, she trusted in Providence for the necessary means. She paid a lay teacher and provided everything needed for the school and for the pupils, who soon numbered more than seventy.

The hospital too, owing to the increase in patients, had to move to other premises.

As soon as this foundation in Nizza had been made, Mother Rosa had to face the long and painful matter of the approval of the Rules, as we shall see, and for some time she had to suspend the acceptance of postulants and the opening of new houses.

God’s Work was to receive from the Church a new structure, from which it would draw strength for wider and more beneficial expansion. But those first six years had already been a fine proof of Rosa Gattorno’s sincere and heroic charity. The six existing houses lived on joyful sacrifice, born as they were solely of gratuitous love for one’s neighbor and of longing for the Kingdom of God.

The first foundations of the Institute, as we have seen, seem clearly to mark out an arid and stony path which constantly sets before our eyes poverty, effort and abandonment. It is still and always the lesson that comes from the Cross, which demands choices and attitudes that have the depth of self-immolation. Only in this way does love become fruitful, for it is a sharing that implies belonging: not giving something, but giving oneself, and totally.
