1. Hostile rumors about the Institute — Slanderous episode and the Mother’s forgiveness — Attempts on her life; further insults — Dispute with Fr. Ricchini — Intense prayer and extraordinary penances — A retrospective look at a conversation with her brother, Francesco.

Hostile rumors about the Institute ~ On 30 August 1898 Mother Gattorno’s name day was being celebrated. The twilight of her intense life was now on the horizon, but she could gaze at her works, widespread throughout the world, as at a fruitful harvest; God’s Work, after those thirty-two years, looked truly great. The Mother addressed words of thanks and exhortation to the religious who had gathered round her, offering their congratulations. Among other things, she recalled the fidelity they owed to their vocation.

“Daughters”, she said, “I want one promise from you today, and that is that you will be faithful to the Institute, to the Holy Mother and to the Church. No, my daughters, do not let troubles, slanders, desires or anxieties cause you to lose your holy vocation, the sublime grace you have received from God. I have also been slandered, despised and abused, but I never had the slightest doubt about my vocation”.1

Indeed, Rosa Gattorno’s life was truly lived beneath the banner of the Cross, folly from the human point of view, as St. Paul says in his First Letter to the Corinthians, but for believers, the power and wisdom of God. He himself also says: “When we are cursed, we answer with a blessing; when we are hounded we put up with it; we are insulted and we answer politely…”. (1 Co 4:12-13). Rosa too was slandered, despised and abused, but throughout the long course of thirty-two years she could only understand and forgive.

Troubles began immediately in the humble house that welcomed her in Piacenza when she went there to found the Institute. Even among her first companions, there were some who fell by the wayside; but this is not surprising: it can happen merely because of the weakness of human nature, without wickedness.

That first group of friends included Rosa’s sister-in-law, a certain Amalia Custo; as has been said, we cannot be certain whether she went to Piacenza to become a religious, or simply as a guest of the first community. In any case, she changed her mind after four months and left Piacenza bitterly hostile to the Mother; in a series of letters that she wrote from Genoa, it can be said that out of resentment she did everything she could to wound and humiliate her.

This wickedness must have caused Rosa Gattorno particular disappointment, since it was a sign of the spread of malicious gossip against the Institute which was still very new. Indeed, it was manifestly expressed in Genoa a few months later, when it became known that Fr. Luigi Cogrossi had been dismissed from the Mother House (August 1867).

“For your information”, her father wrote to her, “it is beginning to be rumored here that [your] establishment is disintegrating, and that you will shortly all be returning to your homes; and it is not known where these rumors started”.2

So the abuse threatened to become really damaging to the institution, discouraging or deviating the vocations that were starting to flourish in that city.

However, the only sign we find of Rosa’s reaction to these offenses is the care she took to soothe the friction in her family and among her relatives, procuring the good of their souls.3

Nonetheless, about a year and a half later, a truly terrible storm was to be unleashed on Mother Gattorno.

In the previous chapter, mention was made of a letter she received from Sampierdarena on the very day of the opening of that house: 14 November 1868. The evil mind of the person who wrote it became more and more poisonous, to the point that she hatched a real plot against the Foundress in the Mother House.

Slanderous episode and the Mother’s forgiveness ~ In March 1869, Rosa was at Sampierdarena attending to urgent matters concerning the house; she saw that they were expedited with redoubled efforts, since the proximity of her relatives demanded particular attention. Moreover, her son, Alessandro, then almost 14 years old and living in her father’s house, was in a very disturbing state of health; he had a rather serious illness and it was thought that his leg might have to be amputated. In these circumstances a letter suddenly arrived which recalled her immediately to the Mother House.

She left that very evening, and unusually, on her own. She arrived at the station in Piacenza at 11.30 p.m. and at midnight was knocking at the door of the Mother House.

She was made to wait and then there were difficulties about opening the door. Having entered, she asked for the superior, wondering at not seeing her; she was told that she was in bed. Since she did not have the key to her cell with her, she went to the superior and first asked her what the matter was, and whether she felt ill. She was answered with a dry no.

The other Sisters with her stood there in silence, with an air of mystery and embarrassment. The Mother insisted, but she was given no answer. Only the cook who had followed close behind her, drew near to her whispering: “Mother, poor Mother!”. But no one took the initiative to break the ice; no one took the trouble to offer the Mother anything nor to invite her to go and rest. It was a bitterly cold night and Rosa, feeling thoroughly numb with cold then asked if she could be given a room to retire to for a while. She was told to go to the guest room. It is easy to guess the Mother’s anguish and bewilderment. But this very strong woman, giving no sign of her inner agitation, retired to the chapel to pray. At that moment it seemed that even heaven was closing: her spirit, as arid and dry as a dead tree trunk, found no comfort in prayer. She was alone in that place and the house had once again fallen silent. She prostrated herself on the altar steps, her arms wide, imploring God to give her light in all that darkness; but God wanted her just then to feel abandoned and in total darkness.

At last morning came: she received Communion with that dryness, and when her devotions were over, she went to the superior, and again asked her to explain her hostile attitude and the whereabouts of Fr. Tornatore; in fact she wanted to talk to him to have an explanation; but she was told that he would not be returning.

So the Mother wrote to him informing him of her arrival and begging him to come; instead she received a reply from him which threw her into consternation: it was a severe condemnation and the toughest reprimand, on the basis of absurd reasons deriving from slanderous accusations that were totally unfounded.

It seemed to her that her mind was closed to any consideration of what she had read; she did not understand anything at all, but inwardly felt that impassive tranquillity which stems from an easy conscience.

At last, Fr. Tornatore, summoned several times that day, sent word that he would come towards evening but would not stay. Indeed, he came, entered the parlor, called Mother Gattorno and immediately prohibited her from receiving Holy Communion. He mentioned several very serious accusations made against her by the superior and then left.

“I wept a little immediately”, writes the Mother at this point, “and then, hearing what had happened, I felt calm; but the thought that for fourteen and a half years I had never missed Holy Communion, Oh what a hardship! I obeyed, but in the evening, at last in my poor beloved cell, I scourged this monster of a body; however I continued to feel that coldness, or to describe it better, the inability to think and reason…” (M.1.2, pp. 23-24).

The following morning, when the moment for Communion came, as Mother Rosa saw approaching the altar the sister who had hypocrisy and calumny engraved on her heart while she herself had been forbidden to receive it, she was so overcome with emotion and trembling that she had to leave the chapel and take refuge in a room. As soon as she had entered it she fainted. She was revived by the cook, who had followed her, suspecting some disaster.

Fr. Tornatore arrived at 9 o’clock in the morning, to conduct a sort of trial. It took place where the sisters generally made their confession, in two small rooms, communicating through a small grille. Tornatore sat on one side with the Mother, and those who had made the accusations came in turn to the other side. The priest read a lengthy report which lasted a good five hours. The Mother listened on her knees.

Her principal accuser was the superior of the Mother House, Sr. Anna Maria Luigia Camisa. Mother Gattorno had well-founded reasons for distrusting her: in fact she had realized that this sister eavesdropped at the door even while she was conversing with priests; and she had clear and repeated proof that she intercepted, read and corrected letters addressed to the Mother General. After having thoroughly verified the state of affairs, also with the collaboration of Fr. Paolo Rossi, the community’s confessor, she thought it appropriate to inform Fr. Tornatore. At this point she had reason to believe that he had fallen into a real trap since he had not managed to discern the falsity of the superior, his penitent, and on the contrary believed that Mother Rosa’s well-founded suspicions were excessive. He therefore defended Sr. Anna Maria Luigia.4

She had formulated the most serious accusations against her Mother General, distorting offices of charity to the sick cared for in the hospital at Cento by Rosa Gattorno. Other accusations concerned the administration of the Mother House, which, as is well known, lived in great poverty. She also blamed the Foundress for the Institute’s great difficulties and its many enemies.

Her accusations were supported by another four sisters and had the effect of involving Tornatore, the victim of the plot, in an even worse deception.

The long reading of the report recounting these enormities was excessively painful to the Mother: although in her heart she felt the comfort of being humiliated unjustly like her crucified Good, she was distressed by all that was attributed to her.

In the afternoon, while the reading continued, the cook entered the little room where Tornatore and Mother Gattorno were with the pretext of wishing to talk to the Father; but bursting into tears, she started to protest that the Mother was innocent and hinted at the plot hatched by the superior with the other sisters, and at how they had wanted to involve her. At this point, the sister on the other side of the grille also began to speak, threw herself on her knees weeping, and with open arms asked forgiveness, asserting that the Mother was innocent.

It all happened like lightening; Mother Rosa, deeply moved, embraced the two Daughters, encouraging them with words of compassion and complete forgiveness. Fr. Tornatore, as though emerging from a dream, realized that he had fallen into a trap. He immediately withdrew the Mother’s prohibition from receiving Communion and sent for the superior. She had the impudence to present some bills to be paid and discussed them with both the Father and the Foundress. This coarseness should have prompted well merited disdain; instead, the Mother showed her willingness to reply, noting that with the alms recently collected it would be possible to pay them all. However, while saying this she became so upset that she could not prevent herself from bursting into tears.

She withdrew to her little cell, closed the door and gave free reign to her tears; clinging to her Crucifix she cried for at least three hours, prey to a paroxysm of weeping.

This was the second time, she herself noted, that she had wept like this. She had eaten nothing for 24 hours and ate nothing until noon the following day, but in the morning, having been able to receive Communion, her strength came flooding back (cf. M. 1.2, pp. 21-26).

In her, the purest constitution of Gospel charity was truly resplendent: she did not punish that wickedness: Indeed, she wanted to place even greater trust in the superior, and sent her to manage the House at Cento which was in a difficult plight.5

We know nothing about the other sisters who took part in the plot: it is certain that none of them were banished; their names are unknown, because the Mother did not indicate them in her writings and probably also destroyed all traces of the event in the writings of others. All that remains is a single letter, written by Sr. Anna Francesca Camisa who, as an eye-witness, declares Mother Rosa’s innocence concerning what had been imputed to her with regard to the hospital at Cento and expresses deep regret as Sr. Anna Luigia’s sister.6 It is certain that no information of the event was given to the other sisters of the house in Piacenza, and still less to those of the other houses; it is also true that not even the oldest religious were told about it.

All this shows the Mother’s care and sensitivity in removing every trace of the great offense she had received, and her sincere forgiveness, which she describes in her Memorie: “only one thing comforts me, and that is that I am not left with any ill-feelings for the one who caused me such pain, I feel deep affection for whoever might have been [to blame] and have increased my prayers for them, and always tried to do as much good to them as I could…” (M. 1.2, p. 30).

Attempts on her life; further insults ~ With the same generous heart, the Mother ensured that no written accounts remained of two further serious episodes in which another two religious played the lead, in the grip of deep hatred of her. Some suspected that they might have been sent to the Institute by sectarians, with malevolent aims. Although these events occurred about six years after the time of which we are speaking, it was felt appropriate to insert them here, because of the similarity of the virtues in Mother Rosa which they highlighted.

It was known that in the morning the Mother only took a cup of black coffee. It once happened that the usual cup was seen to have been set before her in the refectory, but after looking at it for a few moments, she refused to drink it: she had guessed, it seems, that it contained poison. This happened a second and a third time, when the poisoned cup was insistently brought to her. Then Mother Gattorno, after a moment of hesitation, abandoned herself in God’s hands and drank it.

She was immediately seized by atrocious pains and she herself asked for an antidote. Dr. Albertazzi came immediately and saved her. He wanted to report the culprit to the civil authorities; it would have been easy to identify her and she had acted with premeditation; but Rosa persuaded him with fervent entreaties to keep the matter secret.7

It was concealed as far as possible, since it could not fail to be known to the sisters of the house; but the name of the culprit has been forgotten.

Another disconcerting event which occurred on 22 April 1875 is mentioned. The protagonist was a sister from Foligno, Sr. Anna Carlotta Biagini, superior of the Mother House in Piacenza. From the Mother’s own account of it in her Memorie, it appears that she foresaw through extraordinary enlightenment certain inexplicably homicidal intentions of the sister. “Today, 22 April 1875 [I do not know] how my God suggested to me all that a superior was intending [to do]. She had planned to kill me either with poison or by stabbing me in the throat with a knife […]; I found out all about it, and summoning her, this is what I told her: You have in your heart […] (as I have written above).

Then my Good made me see what she had in her heart […] because he had opened the book of her heart to me, I say a book as it were, because I could clearly read […]. ‘You wanted to kill me with a knife that is in the guest quarters and is very sharp; you wanted to stab me in the throat with it; in the same way you wanted to poison my food, but you never succeeded because you were prevented’…” (M. 4.3, pp. 40-41).8

The next day she herself accompanied that religious to Cortemaggiore for a spiritual retreat with the other sisters of that community. In a letter written on 2 May 1875, the guilty one expressed her repentance and made firm resolutions to change her life radically. It also seems from the same letter that she left the Institute of her own free will, asking a blessing from the woman for whom she had desired such evil.9

Other unpleasant events are mentioned which occurred in the place opened by Mother Gattorno’s charity; however there is no trace of them in the Memorie or in the letters. Only one episode is recorded, which occurred in 1867 at the end of a journey while the Mother was going home, and can therefore be attributed to persons who did not belong to the Institute. “I went to Milan on the 4th of this month to see Carlottina receive Communion […]; my sister-in-law once again accompanied the girl and myself to the college, and I returned to Piacenza with my mother and Caterina; we arrived at eleven o’clock at night. They had prepared “perfumes” for us; dear you, we thought we should die. Caterina with the suffocation she suffers was overcome by the stench. It was absolutely deadly!”10

It should certainly not be presumed that because of such offenses Mother Gattorno was little loved in the work she had established; indeed, she had to struggle all her life against the affection, sometimes even vehement, which her daughters continued to show her.

Now returning to 1869, we find annotated by Rosa herself that she had to suffer another five very hard trials, although they were not as serious as the calumny mentioned. In fact she writes in the Memorie: “From ’68 and throughout ’6911, there were fireworks on all sides: without comfort, all alone! In ’70, towards the end of the year, they exploded more seldom and gave me a little respite” (M. 1.2, p. 29).

Dispute with Fr. Ricchini ~ A source of particular worry to the Mother was the bitter dispute with Fr. Ricchini, a priest of Genoa, which was taken to court and lasted many years. What specifically upset her was the indecorous spectacle of a legal dispute between holy persons and having to give witness in public trials. The quarrel flared up two years after the foundation of the house in Sampierdarena, to which Ricchini had donated 30,500 lire in stocks and shares. Mother Rosa and Fr. Tornatore were accused of having used the money for other foundations, while they insisted on declaring that the accusations were groundless; they were therefore brought to court in September 1871.

When they were acquitted in August 1872, Ricchini appealed; the painful conflict dragged on until 1877 with tremendous anguish for the Mother, but in the end her triumph was complete, not only because of the truthfulness of her assertions, but especially because of the moral responsibility of that public dispute in which the press of the time was obviously involved.12

Archbishop Salvatore Magnasco of Genoa had frequently endeavored, with the mediation of Cardinal Giuseppe Berardi, Protector of the Daughters of St. Anne, to put an end to the controversy; at last the proceedings were closed, and this precious declaration was issued to the Institute: “The undersigned Archbishop certifies that the proceedings formerly pending between the priest Angelo Ricchini and Mrs Gattorno, Foundress of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, have ended with the full victory of the latter: that the said priest, on my orders, has revoked the charges he had brought against the person whom he treated with such impropriety and which he attempted to revive; and that he deeply regrets the imputations made in that case, in spite of himself, to the said Mrs. Gattorno.

Genoa, from the Archiepiscopal Residence, 19 December 1877. Signed Salvatore, Archbishop”.13

Regarding the events which will have to be told in the following chapter, we can well say that those were the most anguished years of Rosa Gattorno’s life.

Intense prayer and extraordinary penances ~ The moral sufferings we have described were accompanied by the burden of the debts contracted to maintain the works of charity, and by the illnesses that raged in the houses founded or which afflicted her own body, already so tried by her penances. It must have been considerably difficult for Mother Rosa to keep the necessary peace of mind in these conditions, what with the intense activity of expediting the many affairs of the Institute; her sisters were amazed, yet they did not know all the inner tribulations of that great soul. However they knew and saw that she drew miraculous strength from prayer and penance.

Jesus’ precept: “watch and pray” was the sure secret of success for Rosa, in both her spiritual struggles and in the enormous activity her role demanded. Indeed, the Work she had founded, despite opposition, became more and more firmly established. Her qualities in governing aroused wonder inside and outside the Institute. She also saw that she had become the object of immense affection on the part of her Daughters, especially the best of them, and the favors she received from God in prayer were true gifts to be cherished, with an awareness of her own lowliness.

This was Rosa’s constant preoccupation. In the language of her personal writings in which she talks to herself and to her spiritual director she says such things about herself that they are sometimes wounding. At every step she calls herself “disgraceful”, she always has her “wickedness” beneath her eyes; she feels a “shapeless monster”. Her very penances seemed so wretched to her that she was ashamed to offer them to her Beloved. So it was that she made her vision and constant awareness of her own littleness the basis of her life.

This allows us to sample the sincerity of her acts of humility, which might otherwise seem empty and affected. One most special point of her life in the Institute must have been her continuous abandonment to Providence with regard to its material keep: each member had to strive to please the heavenly Father and Mother St. Anne so as not to be unworthy of her daily bread. Now: the privation or long delay of this help in coming was attributed by Rosa to herself, before anyone else, and she humbly complains of this in her letters to the superiors. On the other hand, they felt great sorrow, well knowing how the mother sacrificed herself for the glory of God and for the good of the Institute.

“My beloved Mother”, Sr. Anna Francesca Camisa wrote to her, “I hope that Providence will come soon: only one thing sickens me, and it is when you always write to me that if the Lord does not send his Providence, I am [the cause] of his shame. This is what you always say. I am telling the truth that when you write to me like this it disgusts me. If you speak like that, what should I say, who do nothing good? […]. Then what would the house be if you weren’t there? Mother, I beg of you, for pity’s sake; don’t write to me in this tone any more”.14

With the same sincerity of heart, she lowered herself to ask the forgiveness of her Daughters for certain acts which she deemed shortcomings. In Sampierdarena in 1871, after a splendid celebration at which Fr. Tornatore was present, she held a council meeting in the Father’s presence to deal with certain matters of the house. Mother Rosa showed herself to be of a different opinion than the others who participated in the meeting, but it seemed to her afterwards that she had been in some way excessive. Therefore the following morning, “before receiving her God, one after the other, she called the superior and her deputy to her room, and asked their forgiveness for having opposed them.”.15

These delicate words of her secretary, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino tell us what a lesson the Mother’s humility must have been for them all.

Obviously her humble heart was the object of God’s favors and flames of the purest love were kindled in it. The need to converse with her Beloved would have kept Rosa praying continuously, but so as not to fall short in her serious duties of governance, she dedicated a large part of the night to prayer, in addition to the time allocated to it for the whole community in day time. The attention she devoted to prayer was noted by all, because they always saw the Mother first in chapel, both in the morning and during the day; she never let herself be induced by her multiple commitments to miss a time of community prayer or to arrive late. Once, when she had stayed up working until 4.00 a.m. for urgent matters, she drowsed a little, and did not hear the bell at the common hour of rising. She asked the community’s forgiveness with deep sorrow as if for a bad example, for such was her concept of prayer for the life of a religious community.16

For her, prayer was indeed the primary means of sustaining the work she had founded. Her Memorie do not only tell us of the delights that flooded her, but show us at every step how the Mother treated with God the needs of one or other of the souls whose custodian she was, the financial difficulties of the houses, the sufferings of the Church, the Institute’s difficulties. It is moving to see how enlightening the Mother found the problems that afflicted the Roman Pontificate in evaluating her own sufferings and those of her Institute; the thought gave her such courage in embracing her cross that she declared that to remove suffering was to remove life.

Rosa Gattorno combined the diligent practice of humility and prayer with harsh punishment of her body, so that her spirit would live and be constantly fortified in serving God. She did this to pay homage to her Savior and to participate in his Passion by following him as closely as she possibly could.

Her passionate union with the suffering Christ drove her to shut herself up in her little room for the whole triduum of Holy Week, so that no one saw her on those days; she spent them in absolute fasting, in prayer and in penance. In this way, with her wounded body, she wished to help obtain the means necessary for the life of God’s Work. Indeed, from its beginning she had bound herself by vow not to eat fruit; she later made the temporary vow perpetual and always kept it, except on the very rare occasions when an express command of obedience imposed an exception out of regard for her health. And how often, when the community lacked food, she went up to that little room of hers to obtain it from God by shedding her own blood! All this made Mother Gattorno a truly strong woman: what storms could ever have bent a soul so great, so generous, so close to God? Greatness of spirit, then, even if her weak body sometimes showed the strain.

Her frequent fainting fits were witnessed not only by her Daughters but by all who had occasion to know the Mother on her frequent and uncomfortable journeys, which took up almost the whole of her life. Her body, worn out by penances, weakened by fasting and burdened with work, often gave way; the fainting fits lasted a long time and headaches followed upon fevers.

Several times her illnesses seemed mortal, so that as early as 1869 it was thought she would be lost when, after the bitterness of the slanderous episode of which she had been the victim, a strange swelling of the head and an irregular pulse had reduced her to the end of her strength, so much so that there was thought of giving her the Anointing of the Sick. But the doctors were never able to identify any illness in her, since she would not submit to any examination; judging from the symptoms that had appeared, however, they considered her survival almost a miracle.

Yet, inexplicably, for thirty years Rosa dragged that broken body, which she called the donkey of God and of his Work, across Italy on countless journeys, without illness ever being able to extinguish the ardor of her great spirit.

Here there comes to mind the fine image of the soldier of Christ which Paul presents in the letter to the Ephesians: “Therefore take up the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to withstand on that evil day, and having done everything, to stand firm. Stand therefore, and fasten the belt of truth around your waist, and put on the breastplate of righteousness. As shoes for your feet put on whatever will make you ready to proclaim the gospel of peace. With all of these, take the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one. Take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Pray in the Spirit at all times in every prayer and supplication…” (Eph 6:13-18).

Against slander, contempt and ill-treatment only these weapons avail. And it seems that Rosa Gattorno wielded them with love and skill throughout her life. Thus she overcame adversity and accomplished immense good.

A look back in a conversation with her brother Francesco ~ Her brother, Mr. Francesco, who came to visit her in Rome in one of the last years of her life, turned the conversation to the long road traveled, begun in very sad times, without the necessary means, indeed with nothing, and ended so splendidly in the Eternal City with some three hundred houses and over three thousand religious. Francesco was proud of the good his sister had done; although his religious sentiments were rather lukewarm, he was moved by the wonders of charity she had worked. And he recalled the distant times when in Piacenza, after watching over the sick at night, she returned home, where very often she lacked the necessities for a meal, so that she went without food together with the sisters, and how help then reached her…

And now she was in the house in Via Merulana, the heart of the Institute, by now solidly established and spread throughout the world.

“I remember”, he says, “that we were alone and, at [my] words […], she looked at me with those expressive eyes which understood my approval and praised her action; and she drew me out of that rapture with a sweet smile, changing the subject so as to take importance away from that past, for which she did not wish to be praised”17.

It is the deep humility of the great and of the saints. Life is work and struggle to the very end. Only in eternity will it be granted to look upon it with satisfaction as a victory.
